Katalog Berita (Halaman 8/57)

#9974. 14-year-old creates tool for AI agents to band together like a team

Autark can act without constant prompting, but leaves users to enforce their own security boundaries

Built by a 14-year-old developer, a new tool called Autark treats AI agents as a virtual team that can work without constant prompting.

Users put tasks in an inbox, where a manager agent delegates them to other agents that carry out the work and report their results. Agents can also ask clarifying questions if tasks are too vague.

“Agents do not wait for a prompt,” Autark’s website explains. “A schedule, a timer, a new task, a message or an event wakes them up. They decide what to do, do it, and can plan their own next step.”

As one would hope from a product like this, Autark is model agnostic and can be set up to connect to OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Kimi Code through those services’ CLI tools. Local models are also supported. Your mileage may vary if you choose to use anything besides Codex or Claude Code, though, as Autark’s website mentions support for other models is built in but hasn’t been tested in a live run yet, as Autark is still under active development as an open-source tool.

Autark is the brainchild of teenage Austrian developer Stanislaus Hees. He’s still in school, and tells The Register he’s deeply interested in AI and came up with Autark after being unhappy with existing AI tools.

“I could get help with individual tasks, but I still had to organise the work, remember what was unfinished and keep pushing it forward,” Hees said of his time using Claude Code and Codex. “I wanted a system that could take responsibility for ongoing work, not just respond to my next message.”

He developed Autark - or, more accurately, prompted AI coding tools to do it for him - to come up with a tool that could fulfill that want. You know what that means: It’s capable, but that capability also makes it dangerous.

Autark’s page on access and data makes clear what’s at risk if you give it unfettered access to a PC, and why you don’t want to let the thing run roughshod over a system.

“It can do everything,” the page explains, because “Autark does not put walls around its agents.”

There’s no sandboxing in Autark, no approval prompts, and no permission gates. It doesn’t stop agents from spending all the money they can get their hands on, deleting files, or sending unsolicited emails, either. Agents run with the privileges of the machine's user, with approval checks and permission restrictions disabled or bypassed. Even the safety limit parley that users have with Autark establishes guidelines, not rules.

“The first thing the AI asks is how far it may go,” the access page points out. “That is a question, not a technical barrier.”

That means agents given a task that conflicts with their stated limits may still attempt to carry it out. As we’ve seen in recent months, some AI agents have found ways around restrictions, instructions be damned.

“In our own live test runs, agents given a vague request reached real repositories, backups, SSH keys and .env files within minutes, and one changed the permissions of a file it had found,” the access page notes.

In other words, it’s probably best to stick Autark on a machine that doesn’t contain anything you’d want to avoid losing - even Hees admits as much.

“I would not claim that … the app is suitable for unattended access to sensitive systems,” the teen dev told us.

That’s not to say Autark lacks protections for secrets, though. Autark’s site explains that stored passwords and keys are encrypted and referred to using IDs that keep their values out of prompts. It also says its servers don't store user data, with a meeting server used to relay encrypted traffic between devices.

If you're willing to try Autark to see whether it can improve your workflows, you don't need to rely on its servers. While prepackaged apps are available from Autark’s website, it’s also fully open source and available on GitHub. Everything, even the meeting server code, is available for self-hosting and modification under an Apache open source license.

The bottom line is that this is a tool built by an ambitious young person, and it’s a tool with a lot of potential if used correctly. That correct usage is the major challenge, though, so be sure to build your own guardrails.  ®

#9973. A faster Easter date function

This post is a fun little side quest to kickstart my journey optimising regional calendars.

Computing the date of Easter faster is not going to matter in any real application. Even in places where it might seem to matter, like high frequency trading applications, it is probably better to just use an in-memory lookup table for holiday dates...However, no "Fast Date" series would be complete without some mention of this classic problem.

The rules for Easter were broadly decided at the First Council of Nicaea, organised by Emperor Constantine in 325 AD, ultimately landing on the first Sunday after the first full moon, on or after March 21. Later, for operational efficiency, the church defined "full moon" according to a formula, which was eventually modified by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582 ("Gregorian Easter"), with the first Easter under the new rules applying in most Catholic countries the following year.The Church of England first observed the new date of Easter in 1753, but Eastern / Orthodox churches continue to follow the old rules.

This article is about the new "Gregorian" Easter, because it is much more complex and slow to compute. For more details on the underlying algorithm, you can see Gauss's Algorithm on Wikipedia (the first known self-contained function, which basically all later algorithms build on).

The code below runs really fast.It's around twice as fast as a standard easter function that you might find in a typical date library, and I suspect it may be the fastest one made so far ð¤·.Part of that speed is attributable to using only 5 multiplications (whereas typical reference algorithms have 10 or more multiplications).

The accuracy range of around -11m â +16m years might seem a bit of overkill, but the reason I targeted this range is so that any date library that expresses dates via a signed or unsigned 32âbit "rata die", is covered by this function. This means that if you decide to not clamp the logic to years after 1582, at least it will return something resembling the correct rules, rather than garbage.

Note that this function contains more terms than traditional Easter functions, but bear in mind that the compiled assembly will be a lot smaller. So if you don't care about the speed, but want a tiny impact on binary size, that could be a reason to consider this function.

The rest of this post will briefly explain the tricks used in this function:

You'll notice that the very first thing we do is add a strange value SHIFT to the input value. This is done for two reasons:

For example, most Easter algorithms have a term like (5 + 8 * c) / 25, where c is the century (year / 100 + 1). The term 25 in the calculation of shift is responsible for aligning the century such that the constant 5 can be removed, resulting in c * 8 / 25, which is then approximated in the final algorithm with a single mul-shift: (u64) c * M25 >> 32.

Other terms in SHIFT: 19, 400, 30 are all doing similar things related to the 19-year-cycle, 400-year-cycle, and mod-30 steps.The term * 2 is different. Without this term, the range of coverage would be -5,403,600 â +22,363,835; which doesn't quite cover the range we wanted, which for signed 32-bit rata die, is Â±5.88m years. Including * 2 increases the value of shift by exactly 5,700,000, which is how many years it takes for the Easter pattern to repeat, and gets the range we are after.

If you like this type of optimisation, but are not a fan of the low-level bit-shifting and so on, then you might prefer to use this function here below. It is a much more readable version of the function, which only has these higher-level optimisations applied.

Note that unlike in the main function presented earlier, MOD 30 needs to be a positive-modulus function (even for positive dates), and that the nextSunday helper is anchored to the internal logic of the function, not related to Unix day-counting.

Note: a variant in the C++ repo has some small optimisations not shown here (fast day-of-week and fast mod 30), and a range of [-73,803,600 .. 70,208,581].

Computing year % 19 is a staple of Easter algorithms.It's related to the Metonic cycle, where every 19 years there are nearly exactly 235 full moons.

It is traditionally used in Easter algorithms in two ways:

We are going to compute these same things using a single multiplication.These steps seem unavoidable at first, but they can be eliminated. We'll begin by expanding the first one:

(11 * (year % 19) + ... ) MOD 30(11 * (year - year / 19 * 19) + ... ) MOD 30(11 * year - year / 19 * 209 + ... ) MOD 30(11 * year + year / 19 + ... ) MOD 30

The last step there might be the least obvious. It works because we can add any multiple of 30 to the multiplier and get the same result (a property of MOD), so add 30 Ã 7 = 210, which means we can remove the multiplication by 209 and just invert the sign.

This leaves us with only two terms related to year which can be computed efficiently in parallel, however using a 64âbit multiplier, we can actually merge these into one (fixed-point multiplication by 11 1/19):

u64 constexpr M19 = (1 << 32) / 19 + 1 + (11 << 32)((year * M19 >> 32) + ... ) MOD 30

This is the only 64âbit multiplication in the function, and a 32-bit compiler should have no trouble turning that back into the previous pair of multiplications.

The algebra above relies on MOD 30, which is different to % 30 in C for negative numbers.The value being computed does not go negative over our range, so the substitutions remain valid.

Now on to the other term: (year % 19) > 10. It is a well known trick to use the low bits from the mul-shift of division by 19 as a comparison cutoff, and the version used in my function is u32(b) > 0x90000000. The extra term in our multiplier (11 << 32) has no effect in the lower 32âbits, so this still works. Cassio Neri has written about things like this, if you want to read more you can start with this Overload Edition 154 .

So, this is just one multiplication plus the MOD 30, which is usually an additional two multiplications, but we'll eliminate those later in Trick #4.

There's always a % 7 term in these Easter functions, which is then subtracted from a final result. This is because Easter is on the âfirst Sunday after [...]â.

Clearly we are going to use the fast-mod-7 trick from the weekday article. If you haven't read that article, you should. You won't understand this section otherwise, and frankly, it's a better article than this one.

The same mod-7 trick as before, but notice that the mapping is reversed? (The numbers track anti-clockwise)

So why not just subtract the result of % 7 like everybody else? Well, that would make the final line be: j - m + C (for some constant C). This does not fit the pattern of a single-operation LEA instruction on x86.

Instead, we adapt the fast-mod-7 code to use a fixed-point multiplier of 6 / 7 (rather than 1 / 7) before the right-shift-29, which means this line actually counts mod-7 backwards for us! This means the final line can be j + m + C, which fits LEA and saves... one cycle ð (depending on the compiler and CPU...).

This one is pretty obvious if you've been following this blog series.MOD 30 can be calculated faster by using our favourite identity:

This was introduced and proven in the weekday article, and utilised more notably in the time-of-day article.Here setting D = 30, c = 2 gives us the useful version where we can apply MOD 32 (same as & 31).

This final bit, I'm not sure if it's been done before exactly like this.

Easter can only ever be in March or April (month 3 or 4), and luckily March is 31 days long, which means we can use % 32 to truncate dates there. A straightforward modulus would cause March 32 to overflow to April 0, a non-existent date, so we add the term v >> 7 which increments the date when it overflows (a lucky coincidence relying on April, month 4, being a power-of-2).

I have seen similar things done before using % 31, but I have not seen this with the clean bit-mask approach.

So, that's it. A bunch of fussing about to make a simple streamlined function that is next to impossible to read... but fast.

This article was prompted by Twitter/X user Dirk Loss replying to one of my posts with a link to a ChatGPT thread, where he used AI to compute Easter faster. See ChatGPT thread.

The AI actually did a pretty good job. It used learnings from my prior blog posts to apply various optimisations, but also came up with new twists on these ideas. It produced a function that is really fast, and that is accurate over the range 1498â14,544. The range is a fairly reasonable choice given that the modern rules for Easter took effect after 1582, and nobody really needs Easter further into the future.

In a serious case of "Not Invented Here" syndrome (on behalf of human kind), I had to see if I could beat the AI. I clearly did, otherwise there wouldn't be this blog post. The wider-range algorithm presented in this article has around 5-15% higher throughput across tested platforms, and similar latency (despite the wider range).

My algorithm was adapted from the one presented in Calendrical Calculations (Reingold and Dershowitz).I did not apply any learnings from the ChatGPT one, though we settled on several similar steps.

I suspect this function could be optimised more, as it still has the same overarching structure of existing algorithms going back a very long time.I tried for a little while to find a shortcut solution using the Python "Z3 Theorem Prover", which found an alternative which is a further 15-20% faster than my main one, however it's only accurate over a micro range [1894 .. 2199]. It is available in the testcase repo . If you can find a function of similar or faster speed with a wider range, feel free to let me know and I will update the repo and this page!

Although I beat the AI in this case, itâs a pretty mild victory as it was just a basic model with a moderate amount of compute. Itâs sad to know that if frontier models were pointed at the problems Iâve been tackling in this blog series, they would probably unearth every last jewel of optimisation left in the blink of an eye. I hope that I have time to explore this space more before it becomes barren.

If you enjoyed this post, you should follow me on X to get notified when I publish more date and algorithm related articles.

Exhaustive tests of the ranges asserted in this article can be verified via the testcase code: https://github.com/benjoffe/fast-world-calendars .

The same repository is used for benchmarking, where a large set of random years are loaded into memory and tested.

All results were obtained by running the benchmark with -repeat=10 and recording the median results.The -batch flag runs each computation 3 times before loading the next entry from memory. This ensures that the processor is not bottlenecked by memory access.Latency results use the same command but replace the batch flag with -latency. This mode feeds the result of each computation into the next, so there is no parallelisation.

The number in a small font size represents the number of nanoseconds per year computation.The larger number is the ratio of these results compared to the New function as a baseline.

Note: the benchmarks compute "Days since 22 March" (not day and month), as some of the reference algorithms only return this value.If my optimisation of the day/month step is novel, then the speedup would be larger than presented here.

#9972. Multi-Vector (Late Interaction) Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v6.0 update, it gains a fourth model type: MultiVectorEncoder, for ColBERT-style late interaction retrieval. Any PyLate checkpoint and any Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint loads straight into it, and colpali-engine models for visual document retrieval can be used too, through the same familiar API you already use for dense, sparse, and reranker models.

Where a regular embedding model compresses a whole text into one vector, a multi-vector model keeps one vector per token and scores query against document with the MaxSim operator. That preserves token-level matching information that a single vector has to average away, which usually means stronger retrieval at the cost of a bigger index. It's also the state of the art for visual document retrieval, where a text query is matched against page images directly, with no OCR step in between.

In this blogpost, we'll show you how to use these models: loading the various checkpoint formats, encoding and scoring, plugging them into a search stack, running them on page images, and keeping the index affordable. Everything below runs on a plain pip install -U sentence-transformers.

This blog is about using multi-vector models. If you want to learn how to train them, see the companion Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost.

A dense embedding model reads a text and returns a single fixed-size vector. Everything the model noticed has to fit in those 384, 768, or 1024 numbers, and similarity is one dot product between two such summaries. This works remarkably well, but the compression is lossy in a specific way: a rare entity, an exact identifier, or one crucial clause in a long passage all have to compete for room in the same vector. A query with several requirements at once runs into the same wall. For "green sofa with wooden legs and rounded cushions", a single vector has to blend all four into one point, so a green sofa with the wrong legs ends up sitting close to the one you actually asked for.

A multi-vector model (also called a late-interaction or ColBERT-style model, after the ColBERT paper) skips that compression. It runs the same transformer, but instead of pooling the token embeddings into one vector, it projects each token embedding down to a small dimension (classically 128) and keeps all of them. A 9-token document becomes a 9x128 matrix, not a 1x128 vector.

The interaction between query and document is then deferred until scoring time, which is where the name "late interaction" comes from. A cross-encoder interacts early, with both texts going through the model together, which is accurate but leaves nothing to precompute, since every document has to be re-encoded for each new query. A bi-encoder, which is what the dense embedding model above is, barely interacts at all (one dot product between two finished summaries), and that is exactly what lets you encode a collection once and query it fast. Late interaction sits in between. Documents are still encoded independently and can be indexed offline, but scoring compares every query token against every document token, which leaves far more room for the two to interact.

Scoring uses MaxSim: for each query token, take its highest similarity against any document token, then sum those maxima across the query.

MaxSim(Q,D)=∑Qi∈Qmax⁡Dj∈DQi⋅Dj\text{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{Q_i \in Q} \max_{D_j \in D} Q_i \cdot D_jMaxSim(Q,D)=Qi​∈Q∑​Dj​∈Dmax​Qi​⋅Dj​

Because the token embeddings are L2-normalized, each of those dot products is a cosine similarity in [-1, 1], so the whole sum lands within [-num_query_tokens, num_query_tokens].

You can read the operator as a soft alignment, where every query token points at the one document token that best explains it, and the score is how well the document supports the query overall.

The alignment doesn't have to be lexical, since the token embeddings are contextualized. Encode "Where do penguins live?" against "Penguins inhabit Antarctica." with lightonai/mLateOn and the query token live finds its best match on inhabit at 0.94, a word it shares no characters with! That is the thing lexical retrieval cannot do, BM25 and its relatives need the term itself, so synonyms and paraphrases slip past them. Dense embedding models bridge that gap as well, of course. What late interaction adds is that it does so without giving up the other direction. When an exact match is what matters (a product code, a surname, a function name), MaxSim still has that token sitting there on its own, where a single-vector model had to average it in with everything else. It isn't one-to-one either, since several query tokens routinely settle on the same document token.

You gain retrieval quality, particularly on queries where one specific piece of a document is what makes it relevant, on multi-requirement queries like the sofa above where each requirement gets to find its own evidence, and on out-of-domain data where a dense model's compression was tuned for a different distribution. That compression is learned from the training queries, so the model learns to keep what they needed and drop everything else, which may include exactly what your production queries ask about. The effect grows with document length, since more text has to fit in the same fixed vector.

The cost is index size. One vector per token instead of one vector per document is a lot more vectors, only partly offset by the smaller dimension. Encoding 4,874 Natural Questions passages with lightonai/LateOn produced 608,414 token vectors, an average of 124.8 per passage:

That's about 42x the storage of the MiniLM index, or 62 KiB per passage. However, indexes are often compressed, e.g. the same 608,414 vectors take 92 MB as a fast-plaid index, since PLAID stores a centroid id plus a quantized residual per vector rather than the vector itself. For scale, a 4096-dimensional dense model like Qwen3-Embedding-8B would need about 80 MB for these same 4,874 passages, so a compressed multi-vector index sits in the same territory as the dense indexes people already run. Token Pooling cuts the vector count before any of that, and Retrieve and Rerank avoids building an index at all.

PyLate comes up throughout this post, so here is the short version. Sentence Transformers handled dense and sparse models but not late interaction, so LightOn built PyLate on top of it to close that gap, adding the training, inference, and retrieval pieces these models need. Much of what you'll load below was trained with it, and LightOn built an ecosystem around it too, including fast-plaid, the late-interaction index that turns up in Indexing. With v6.0 those capabilities live in Sentence Transformers itself.

With the tradeoff in mind, let's get a model running.

Multi-vector models work with a plain install:

For ColPali-style visual document retrieval, you also need the image dependencies (see Installation for all extras, and Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models for multimodal support in general):

Sentence Transformers v6.0 requires transformers v5.x, torch 2.2+, and huggingface-hub v1.x. If you pin any of those lower, plan the upgrade first. See the Migration Guide for the full list of breaking changes.

Loading a multi-vector model looks exactly like loading any other Sentence Transformers model:

To find models that work, look for the multi-vector and sentence-transformers tags on the Hub. Any model with those tags loads with the line above, whether it started life as a PyLate checkpoint, a Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint, or a ColPali-family model for visual document retrieval. We're working through the ecosystem to get that tag onto every model that works, so the list keeps growing.

Underneath, MultiVectorEncoder reads each of the formats these checkpoints have been published in over the years, so PyLate and Stanford-NLP checkpoints load directly even where the tag hasn't been added yet:

Visual document retrieval models are the exception. ColPali-family checkpoints ship in colpali-engine's own format, which carries no information Sentence Transformers can use, so each one needs a small configuration added to its repository before it loads. Most of that work is done and waiting to be merged. See Supported Models for the current state and how to load them today.

Multi-vector models carry a handful of recipe knobs that differ per checkpoint: marker prefixes for queries and documents, length caps, whether queries are padded out with [MASK] tokens, and which tokens are skipped when scoring documents. All of them live in the module configs, so print(model) shows you exactly what you loaded. Here's the original ColBERTv2 checkpoint, which pads every query to exactly 32 tokens and truncates documents at 180:

That's the classic ColBERT pipeline: a Transformer producing contextualized token embeddings, a token-level Dense projecting each of them to 128 dimensions, a MultiVectorMask deciding which tokens count during scoring, and a token-level Normalize. Other checkpoints fill in different values. lightonai/GTE-ModernColBERT-v1 uses the same four modules with [Q] and [D] prompts, no query expansion, and caps of 48 and 300.

You rarely need to touch any of this, since every released checkpoint configures its own. It matters when you build a model from a bare backbone, which is covered in Creating Custom Models.

One value is worth checking against your own data, though. document_length truncates, so anything past it never reaches the index. For example, a 662-token passage through LateOn's cap of 300 comes back as 273 vectors, with the rest of the passage simply gone. Most of these checkpoints were trained on short passages, so if your chunks are longer than the cap, you can lift it for a single call with encode_document(..., processing_kwargs={"text": {"max_length": 512}}), keeping in mind that you would be running the model past the length it was trained on and that the index grows roughly in proportion. Multi-vector models tend to tolerate that well. On MLDR, a long-document retrieval benchmark, the multilingual siblings of the pair above show the gap clearly: mLateOn scores 77.92 against mDenseOn's 51.59.

Multi-vector models are asymmetric, so queries and documents go through different prefixes, different length caps, and different scoring masks. Unlike many dense models, where the two are interchangeable, encode_query() and encode_document() are required to get correct embeddings:

What you get back is a list of 2D tensors, one per input, each of shape (num_tokens, embedding_dim). Unlike dense embeddings, you can't stack these into one rectangular tensor, because every input has its own token count. The second document is longer than the first, so it comes back as a taller matrix.

Each call applies the model's own recipe for you. encode_query prepends the query marker, expands the query to a fixed length if the checkpoint asks for it, and caps it at the query length. encode_document prepends the document marker, caps at the document length, and drops any skiplisted tokens (punctuation, for most checkpoints) from the scoring mask.

The usual encode() arguments all still apply, so batch_size, show_progress_bar, convert_to_numpy, device, and multi-process pools work the way you'd expect:

model.similarity() computes the full all-pairs MaxSim matrix:

Mars wins, as it should, though the runners-up are close behind. Saturn also contains the literal phrase "the Red Planet", and Jupiter is a planet with a red spot, so a token-level operator has plenty to latch onto in all three. The ordering is what matters.

Scores often sit this close together, as GLInt shows by measuring the spread across a full candidate pool. MaxSim takes a maximum per query token, so a document will usually give every query token some decent best match, and scores start from a floor. Contextualized token embeddings are also anisotropic, clustering in a narrow cone rather than spreading out, so even arbitrary token pairs tend to score high.

There is also model.similarity_pairwise(), for when you already have matched pairs and just want the pair scores instead of the full similarity matrix:

MaxSim sums over query tokens, so its magnitude scales with how many query tokens there are, which means you can't compare scores across models with different query recipes. LateOn encodes the Red Planet query above as 12 tokens. Run that same query and those same documents through ColBERTv2, which pads and truncates every query to exactly 32 tokens, and the scores land in a completely different range:

Within one model the ordering is all you need, but if you want scores on a bounded scale, switch the model's similarity function to MeanMaxSim, which divides by the query token count. Back on LateOn:

Now every score is an average cosine similarity in [-1, 1], although you'll only see [0, 1] in practice.

If your corpus is small, exhaustive MaxSim over all of it is the simplest thing that works. Encode the corpus once, then score each query against everything:

Those 4,874 passages encoded in 20 seconds on an RTX 3090, and each search takes about 120ms end to end, most of that the MaxSim scoring against all 608,414 token vectors. This is exact, but it scales linearly in total corpus tokens and keeps every token vector in memory, so reach for it when you have a few thousand documents rather than a few million. The runnable version of this script is semantic_search.py.

Past that size you want a real late-interaction index, which Sentence Transformers doesn't ship. It doesn't need to, because these indexes store whatever encode_document produced, so you encode here and hand the token embeddings to something built for them. Indexing has working snippets for four of the options, and the section directly below covers how to skip the index entirely.

You can also get late-interaction quality without maintaining a late-interaction index, by using a multi-vector model as your reranker. A fast bi-encoder narrows a large corpus to a handful of candidates, then the multi-vector model rescores only those:

Only the 50 candidates are ever encoded as multi-vectors, so your index stays a normal dense index and the token vectors are transient. This is the same role a cross-encoder plays in a retrieve-and-rerank stack, but a multi-vector model is considerably cheaper per candidate. You encode the documents in one batch and score them with a matrix multiplication, instead of one forward pass per query-document pair. The runnable script is retrieve_rerank.py, which prints the timings of both stages.

Several vector databases index and score multi-vectors natively: Qdrant since v1.10, Weaviate since v1.29, Vespa for years now, LanceDB since v0.15.0, and VectorChord, which adds a MaxSim operator to Postgres that plain pgvector doesn't have. Milvus joined them in v2.6.4, under array-of-structs rather than the unrelated feature it calls multi-vector search. If you would rather not run a server at all, LightOn's fast-plaid is a pip install away and implements PLAID directly, and PyLate wraps it in a fuller retrieval stack.

A few others get you partway. OpenSearch and Elasticsearch can rescore candidates with MaxSim but not retrieve on it, and the Elasticsearch field is additionally in technical preview and Enterprise-tier. turbopuffer has late-interaction indexing in private beta.

The snippets below index text, but nothing in them is text-specific. encode_document hands back the same list of token-vector matrices whether the document was a passage, a page image, an audio clip, or a video, so the ColPali-style models from Visual Document Retrieval go into any of these unchanged. There are simply more vectors per document, which is what makes Token Pooling worth reaching for sooner there.

fast-plaid, Qdrant, Weaviate, and Vespa all take exactly what encode_document returns, so the code is the same up to the client library. Here's a working snippet for each, run against the 4,874 passages and 608,414 token vectors from the Semantic Search example. Each one carries the ingestion and query times it produced on one machine (RTX 3090, i7-13700K), with no tuning beyond what the code shows, to give a sense of the shape of the work. All four answer the query faster than the 98ms model.similarity took in that section, and three of them do it on the CPU, since fast-plaid is the only one here using the GPU.

All four returned the same three passages in the same order as the exhaustive PyTorch MaxSim earlier in this post, and the three databases reproduce its scores to four decimals! That is because their snippets score every document, which is affordable at this size and removes approximation as a variable. fast-plaid is approximate by design, so its scores differ slightly. The notes under each one say what changes when you switch to an approximate index, which is where rankings start to drift.

fast-plaid is LightOn's Rust implementation of PLAID, the index ColBERT was originally built around. There's no server to start, and it reads the tensors encode_document hands back without any conversion.

The index argument is a directory, not just a label, so the index is written to disk as it is built. Pointing a new FastPlaid at the same path reopens it for searching or for adding more documents, instead of rebuilding from the embeddings each time. On this corpus it occupies 92 MB, against 311.5 MB for the raw float32 vectors.

This is the only one of the four that is approximate, and it is the one place in this section where the scores do not match the exhaustive MaxSim. PLAID prunes with centroids and stores quantized residuals, so the three scores drift by a few hundredths in both directions against the 11.9192 / 11.7591 / 11.6710 computed earlier. The ranking is unaffected here, and that is the trade PLAID is making. It was designed for corpora far larger than this one, where scanning everything is not an option.

Qdrant needs a server: docker run -p 6333:6333 qdrant/qdrant. The client also has a local mode (QdrantClient(":memory:")) that needs no server, but it's a pure-Python reimplementation, so use it for trying things out rather than for timing them.

MAX_SIM is the only comparator Qdrant offers, and hnsw_config=HnswConfigDiff(m=0) is their recommendation for late-interaction fields, since the vectors are used for rescoring rather than graph traversal. Note that Qdrant themselves suggest reserving late interaction for reranking a few hundred candidates rather than scanning a whole collection, which is the Retrieve and Rerank pattern. At 4,874 documents the full scan costs 18ms and is exact, but that doesn't extrapolate.

Weaviate needs a server too: docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 50051:50051 cr.weaviate.io/semitechnologies/weaviate:1.34.0. Multi-vector support needs 1.29 or newer, and the embedded mode isn't available on Windows.

Defaults are enough here. Weaviate's dynamic ef resolves to 100 for a top-3 query, and this ranking is already exact from about 32 upward. That margin is a property of the embeddings rather than of Weaviate, so it's worth confirming on your own model instead of assuming the defaults hold.

Weaviate also supports MUVERA encoding, which made ingestion 3x faster and queries 1.8x faster in our test. It cost far more accuracy than that speed is worth at this size though, since the correct third passage didn't appear even in its top 50.

Vespa also runs in a container, but pyvespa starts it for you, so there's no separate docker run.

Vespa asks for the most upfront structure of the four, because you're declaring a ranking pipeline rather than just an index. In exchange you get to write MaxSim out as a tensor expression and see exactly what it computes. This version puts MaxSim in first-phase over where true, which scores all 4,874 documents and is why the output matches exhaustive MaxSim exactly. It's deliberately not what Vespa recommends at scale. Their ColBERT sample app stores int8-binarized vectors and moves MaxSim into second-phase to rerank a cheaper first stage.

Moving to that phased setup needs care, because second-phase rescores only the best 100 candidates by default, and here that window left two of the three correct passages unscored entirely. Raising rerank-count to cover your candidate set fixes that, though at this size the phased version still came out slower than simply scanning everything.

Late interaction is the state of the art for visual document retrieval, matching a text query against page images, with charts, tables, and layout intact, and no OCR step. This is what the ColPali family of models does, and those checkpoints load and run through the same API, with the revision pinning the open pull request that adds this one's Sentence Transformers configuration (Supported Models has the full list). Image documents are passed as URLs, local paths, or PIL images:

Each query retrieves its own page (the diagonal), and the second query separates much more cleanly than the first, since only one of the four pages is about outlay over time.

The code is unchanged. Underneath, the processor handles the visual prompt and the image patches, and MaxSim scores query text tokens against document image patches. A page holds many separate regions, which is exactly what makes late interaction a natural fit here, since a single vector would have to average a chart, a table, and three paragraphs into one summary. That fidelity costs index space, though. The shapes above are 755 token vectors for one page against 25 for the query, where a Natural Questions passage from earlier averaged about 125, so token pooling is worth reaching for earlier here than it is for text.

These are VLMs, so plan for the memory they need. The table in Supported Models runs from 252M to 8.8B parameters, and the small end of it stays practical on CPU where the multi-billion ones don't.

Page images are the common case, but they're not the only non-text modality. Sentence Transformers accepts text, images, audio, and video, and a checkpoint supports whichever of those its processor does, which model.modalities reports. A single document can combine modalities too, by passing a dict like {"text": ..., "image": ...} in place of a bare value. Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models covers multimodal models in Sentence Transformers more broadly, and the Usage documentation lists exactly which input formats each modality accepts.

vidore/colqwen-omni-v0.1 is built on Qwen2.5-Omni and takes all four modalities. Retrieving a recorded conversation with it is the same two calls as retrieving a page:

ColQwen-Omni was trained purely on image-text pairs, so its audio retrieval is zero-shot. It never heard a training example, and there is no transcription step anywhere in the pipeline. The query says nausea where the recording says carsickness, and it still picks the pharmacy conversation out of twenty by a wide margin.

Video works the same way, but sample the frames or it will eat your VRAM. Its release blogpost is blunt about this, that video "is very memory-intensive, so it's best suited for short clips":

At 1 fps and full resolution the same pair of videos produces 8,426 and 5,137 token vectors and peaks at 20.8 GB of VRAM, against 4,240 and 2,446 vectors and 12.5 GB here, for a model that occupies 9.0 GB on its own. The ranking is identical either way. Long audio wants the same treatment, and the release blogpost recommends 30-second chunks, which come to roughly 800 tokens each.

Because MaxSim is a sum of per-query-token maxima, a ranking decomposes exactly, so every point of a document's score belongs to one query token and one document token. That lets you answer "why did this rank here?" precisely, rather than by eye.

For image documents, sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.interpretability overlays that decomposition onto the page as the standard ColPali heatmap, either aggregated over the query or one map per query token. Asking "How much was spent on water resources and power?" against the outlays page from above, this is where the water token went:

heatmap.py is the runnable version, including the masking step that lines the document embedding up with the patch grid.

Text documents have no patch grid to overlay, but the same decomposition applies. text_similarity_map.py ranks a corpus and then attributes the top hit's score token by token, here on the Natural Questions corpus from earlier with the 32M-parameter mxbai-edge-colbert-v0-32m:

rich, mond, preliminary, and final matched themselves, while when settled on since and play on game. Three special tokens contribute 22.7% of the score while carrying none of the query's content. Below this table the script prints the passage itself, with the winning tokens highlighted in place.

If the index footprint worries you, the most effective knob is to store fewer token vectors. HierarchicalTokenPooling implements the token pooling technique from Clavié, Chaffin, and Adams by clustering each document's token vectors with Ward linkage on cosine distance and replacing each cluster with its mean, keeping roughly 1 / pool_factor of the tokens. Within one document a lot of token vectors end up close to each other, so much of what you drop is redundancy rather than signal:

There are three places to apply it, depending on when you want to pay for it:

By default, pooling applies to documents only, since queries are short and are the side you can't afford to distort. On the Natural Questions corpus from earlier, the reduction tracks pool_factor closely, and pooling all 608k token vectors took about 6 seconds:

A cluster mean is a worse match for a query token than the best of its members was, and the coarser the clusters, the more that shows. The original experiments measured that cost on BEIR and found very little of it, at 100.6% of the unpooled retrieval performance on average at pool_factor=2, and 99.0% at pool_factor=3. Halving your index for free is a good deal, so 2 is a reasonable place to start. How much it costs on your data is corpus-specific though, so measure it with an evaluator before you settle on a factor. The runnable comparison is token_pooling.py.

How far you can push pool_factor is also partly a property of the model. LightOn's hierarchical pooling regularization trains for exactly that, shaping the embedding space so pooling costs less and reporting 99.4% retention at 5x compression. Training with that regularizer isn't in Sentence Transformers yet, but the resulting checkpoints are ordinary PyLate models, so lightonai/LateOn-hpool-regularized loads and pools like any other.

Multi-vector models run through the same backend machinery as the rest of Sentence Transformers, so you get torch (default), onnx, and openvino, alongside half precision, Flash Attention, and torch.compile.

On GPU, fp16 with Flash Attention is the best configuration we measured, at 2.44x the throughput of fp32 with no measurable retrieval quality loss. Flash Attention helps multi-vector models more than most, because documents are only truncated and never padded to a shared length, so your batches have widely varying sequence lengths that unpadding can exploit:

Models with non-attend query expansion (attend=False, which covers the Stanford-NLP checkpoints like colbert-ir/colbertv2.0 and answerdotai/answerai-colbert-small-v1) reject Flash Attention at load time. Flash Attention strips attention_mask=0 positions, so the [MASK] expansion tokens that MaxSim scores would never receive an attention update. Use "sdpa" for those models.

On CPU, OpenVINO is your better bet where the architecture is supported, and int8 quantization buys a further speedup at a cost of about 0.4% accuracy. See Speeding up Inference for the full benchmark details, the export and quantization helpers, and a flowchart for picking a backend.

MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator runs the NanoBEIR suite of 13 small BEIR subsets with MaxSim scoring, and needs no data preparation on your side:

This also makes it easy to check the claim from the top of this post. lightonai/LateOn and lightonai/DenseOn were trained by LightOn on the same data with the same ModernBERT backbone and the same 149M parameters, differing only in whether they keep one vector per token or pool down to one per document. Running both over all 13 NanoBEIR datasets isolates what that choice buys:

Late interaction wins on 9 of the 13 datasets and on the mean, by roughly one NDCG point. The four it loses (ArguAna, FiQA2018, SCIDOCS, and SciFact) are the shape of the tradeoff you should expect, a real gain in retrieval quality at the same model size, paid for in index footprint, rather than a universal win on every dataset. The same pair scores 57.22 against 56.20 on the full 15-dataset BEIR, a comparable gap, so the margin is not an artifact of the small benchmark.

Alongside NanoBEIR, MultiVectorInformationRetrievalEvaluator, MultiVectorRerankingEvaluator, MultiVectorTripletEvaluator, and MultiVectorDistillationEvaluator cover the usual evaluation setups on your own data. They're documented in the Evaluation API Reference.

MultiVectorEncoder absorbs the modeling, inference, training, and evaluation of both libraries. Every PyLate checkpoint loads directly, and Supported Models lists the colpali-engine checkpoints along with the revision to pass where one is still needed. If you're migrating, these are the calls that change:

The difference worth knowing about is on bare (non-ColBERT) checkpoints, where PyLate's ColBERT("bert-base-uncased") applies the classic recipe by default while MultiVectorEncoder("bert-base-uncased") builds a plain stack, leaving the prefixes, query expansion, and skiplist as explicit choices. The training loss and evaluator equivalents, and the data-handling differences, are in the Migration Guide.

Save compatibility is one-way in every case. PyLate, Stanford-NLP ColBERT, and colpali-engine checkpoints all load into MultiVectorEncoder, but MultiVectorEncoder.save_pretrained output isn't loadable by any of them.

Models carrying the multi-vector and sentence-transformers tags on the Hub are the list that stays current, and we're working to get those tags onto every model that works. The tables below are what we test against directly, so treat them as a starting point rather than the full set. For text retrieval in particular, any PyLate or Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint loads whether or not it carries the tag yet.

Some entries need a small Sentence Transformers configuration added to their repository first, and several of those are still open pull requests at the time of writing. Where a revision is listed below, pass it until that pull request is merged, after which the plain model name is enough:

These load with their trained prefix tokens, query expansion, and punctuation skiplist recovered from the saved configuration.

The NanoBEIR column reports the mean NDCG@10 (higher is better) across the 13 NanoBEIR datasets, each a 50-query subsample of a BEIR dataset, as a fast proxy for English text retrieval quality. We used the MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator to compute the scores for the primarily-English models. A - means the model was not evaluated on it. Note that NanoBEIR is a small benchmark, and its scores aren't a substitute for evaluating on your own data, which is always the right way to pick a model.

ColPali-style models embed page images as documents and text as queries.

The NanoViDoRe column reports the mean NDCG@10 (higher is better) across NanoViDoRe v3, a compact visual document retrieval benchmark spanning 8 subsets (computer science, energy, finance in English and French, HR, industrial, pharmaceuticals, and physics). Like with NanoBEIR, NanoViDoRe is a small benchmark which shouldn't replace evaluation on your own data.

Most of these are LoRA adapter repositories, with the adapter applied directly onto its base at load time. Some also have a -merged sibling on the Hub (e.g. vidore/colpali-v1.3-merged) with the adapter already folded into the weights.

The three -hf entries are the transformers-native *ForRetrieval ports. They load without any configuration, but use more modeling from transformers and less from sentence_transformers. Generally, it's preferable to use the original models instead, as the ports score approximately the same.

Late interaction in Sentence Transformers rests on a lot of earlier work. Thanks to Omar Khattab and Matei Zaharia for ColBERT, which everything here descends from, and to the LightOn team (Antoine Chaffin, Raphael Sourty, Paulo Moura, and Amélie Chatelain) for PyLate and fast-plaid, which carried late interaction for years and shaped a good deal of the API described above.

Thanks to the ColPali team (Manuel Faysse, Hugues Sibille, Tony Wu, Bilel Omrani, Gautier Viaud, Céline Hudelot, and Pierre Colombo) for ColPali and colpali-engine, which brought late interaction to page images, and to Benjamin Clavié, Antoine Chaffin, and Griffin Adams for token pooling.

Thanks as well to the core MTEB team, Kenneth Enevoldsen and Roman Solomatin among many others, for MTEB and for the kind of hidden work that keeps information retrieval research running.

And thanks to everyone who trained and released the checkpoints in Supported Models. Without them this post would have had nothing to measure.

To learn how to train or finetune these models on your own data:

See the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers.

The guide's distinction between first-stage retrieval and late-interaction reranking is useful for comparing complete systems. A practical baseline is BM25 candidate generation followed by a reranker, measuring recall at the candidate cutoff as well as final nDCG and end-to-end cost. We evaluated that pattern on a small English corpus here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). We haven't benchmarked the multi-vector models in this guide, especially on long or visual documents, so a matched evaluation would be needed.

InfoQ Homepage Podcasts Distributed LLM Inference on Kubernetes with llm-d, Wasm, & TornadoVM

In this episode, Edoardo Vacchi discusses the evolving landscape of WebAssembly on the backend, running Java workloads on GPUs using TornadoVM, and optimizing distributed AI inference using llm-d and vLLM on Kubernetes. Edoardo explains how llm-d manages cache locality (KV and prefix caches), request routing, and batch inference across Kubernetes clusters to maximize expensive GPU utilization.

Automated code transformation at scale. Fix vulnerabilities, migrate frameworks, and modernize legacy code across every repo. Try Moderne Free.

Olimpiu Pop: Hello everybody, I'm Olimpiu Pop an InfoQ editor, and I have in front of me today, Edoardo Vacchi, one of the two Italians that usually talk about boxes inside of boxes. The other one is Andrea Peruffo. Eduardo worked for a long period of time in the WebAssembly ecosystem, he did some spotting around other types of VMs, and today he's back at Red Hat and he's trying to make things easier in terms of Kubernetes and inference. Is that correct?

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. I mean, on my team. It's a few people working on this, and I'm just one of them, but fair description. We're working on distributed inference on Kubernetes specifically, and that's called llm-d, and it's part of the VLLM family of projects. So, yes, it's super exciting to be back at Red Hat and work on the bleeding edge.

Olimpiu Pop: Yes, that sounds nice. But before we go there, because that's the gist of your current work, tell us what happens currently in the WebAssembly space. And I'm asking you because, besides working on the Java side of WebAssembly, you had exposure to Wazero, if I remember correctly.

Olimpiu Pop: So, maybe just have a short refresher. I know that the WebAssembly space is moving fast, so maybe if you can just provide a short summary where it is, what changed, and what's to be expected in the upcoming period.

Edoardo Vacchi: Right. So, for the benefit of our audience, I don't know how much all of them are familiar with it, but you will know that Wasm was born for web browsers, but more recently, and by recently now it means a few years, people were also interested in running it outside the browser, and for the backend specifically. So, running software on Wasm. And in that sense, it could be seen as a sort of a similar thing to the JVM in spirit. And that's why I guess some of us that were working on the JVM were interested in working on Wasm as well. So, Wasm has changed fast in some senses, it evolved quickly in some senses, it evolved just slowly in others. So, there's been a lot of discussion around the component model, which is this new modular system that's built around WebAssembly. That is probably where a lot of the development happens these days, I'd say.

But I'd say that the space for WebAssembly on the backend has changed a lot in the last few years. I think that all of our development landscape has changed. So, things have shifted a little bit. I think it's very meaningful and relevant today, even more possibly than it was when there was much more hype, because it has a lot to do with sandboxing. And as you know, sandboxing is all the rage these days.

Olimpiu Pop: One good scoring point for WebAssembly was earlier this year I was talking to the local first community, and what was interesting was that they were mentioning that one of the libraries they built, the name is eluding me now, but what they said is that rather than just thinking about providing implementation in different programming languages, they built it in Rust, and that meant that they can just compile it to WebAssembly and then use it via WebAssembly to different programming languages. And that was the nice part from their side, and they were quite happy with the result. And I think that's where the power of WebAssembly comes. Or I think the previous year I spoke to a couple of guys that used to work on infrastructure and they spoke about Firecracker. And what was nice, is that they said that most often than not, the harder that you have in the server acts is idle.

So, what they did on top of those idle space, they just had very small WebAssembly machines... Well, containers, I think it's a better wording for that. That was doing very small things that were quite useful for other people. So, I feel that there are all those different scenarios where people are using WebAssembly.

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. I think one interesting aspect that connects to what you were saying right now is even migrating workloads somehow, like running stuff in the browser, but then you also have these WebAssembly run times that can run, even on devices or in general outside the browser, and you have the same workload that runs on your browser, and we have demos of things that are migrated, even live migrated, from the browser to an end user device without breakage. That's really fascinating. And I think these days when we talk about agentic workloads, that's an interesting space. That's where I think Wasm is still relevant. I mean, Wasm is still relevant, especially for browser related work, and many other, but these scenarios for the word that's changing a lot these days for developers, those are the use cases with really good shine.

Olimpiu Pop: Yes. As you mentioned, isolation is important and is getting more and more important these days. So, I think that's quite useful. What is bugging me for at least one week now, and probably I'll try it the following week, let's see what you are going to say to that, I'm just thinking to run a small language model inside the WebAssembly in a browser, is that feasible? Is not feasible?

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, I mean it is feasible, there are examples of that. The thing is, I've been on the receiving end of this question a few times now, so it depends is the short answer.

Edoardo Vacchi: WebAssembly is meant to run on the CPU first. And as we know, we can do inference on the CPU, but generally it works much better. And for the way LLMs, modern LLMs, I mean, the modern architectures for LLMs are designed, they are meant to be run with highly parallel architectures. And the CPU is parallel, but not as parallel as a GPU. So, long story short, smaller models, which basically make sense to run in a browser, for instance, do make sense to run in WebAssembly, much bigger workloads... Well, those in general, we probably want to run on a GPU anyway. However, there are experiments that I'm aware of to translate WebAssembly into GPU kernels.

So, yes, possibly. But the short version of it is for all those workloads that are meaningful to run on a CPU, so relatively small language models, Wasm can be used, and there are many versions of these workloads that exist. I think that Hugging Face for some of the smallest models will run them on your browser, I think. And there are a few examples, on the Wasm I/O conference, there were quite a few talks of people showing this, running these workloads in the browser especially to do inference. So, yes, it does work, it depends on your workload. TornadoVM: Translating Java Code to GPU Kernels [08:26]

Olimpiu Pop: Yes. Well, I'm going to say it anyway, it's simple, it's more about just trying and seeing how things evolved, and fingers crossed that something will happen and not just smoke. But in order to work and consolidate the point that I stated about an expert into putting boxes into boxes, you had the posts, I think last year or the previous year, about TornadoVM. I know that you just had a small exposure to it, so maybe just have a short summary what's TornadoVM and when should we use it?

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. So, TornadoVM is, we could say a flavor of the JVM or an add-on, a plug into the JVM, depends on how you see it. TornadoVM allows you to run Java code essentially on the GPU. This is the bottom line, the selling point, the very short version of it. It's a little bit more nuanced than that. But yes, basically you can, speaking of boxes inside boxes, yes. It's called the VM because it allows you to translate on the fly your Java code, and compile it on the fly into GPU-specific kernels. So, PTX for NVIDIA, SPEAR-V, whatever. And it handles for you this translation. So, you can basically write Java code and then it will translate for GPU backend. Now, the code that you write there, it is Java code, but you have to write the code in a specific way. You might have to use some libraries that TornadoVM provides you.

You cannot run basically any code... You won't be able to run Spring on TornadoVM. I mean, yes, but it will run in Java mode. You won't run Spring on the GPU, that's the point. But yes, you can write GPU kernels using Java, and that's the beauty of it. And the blog post you were referring to, I think it was last year's, I'm walking through the reader... One of the examples in the code, I think there is an example of writing a simple kernel and running on the GPU, that's one thing that we show in the blog. But then we run GPU Llama 3, which is an implementation of the Llama 3 model that runs on GPU. And this implementation is completely written in Java. So, that's fascinating. The blog post walks you through how this works.

In the latest DevOps Belgium, if people want to catch up a little bit, they had demonstrated, I think there was definitely a talk about TornadoVM, there were talks from the GraalVM team of the similar projects to run Llama and other language models using GraalVM that will do the acceleration for you, and then there was also former GraalVM team member that spun off his own startup. I think his name is Alfonso Alfonso, I remember it because his nickname is Alfonso Squared. And he started his own startup branching off some work that he did originally in GraalVM, again to run Java code, I think, on the GPU and LLM.

So, yes, fascinating stuff. And so, bottom line, the reason why I started to look into this is fan of boxes inside boxes, fan of languages and compilers, so it felt like a natural evolution of the things that I did in the past, including compilation to WebAssembly to learn about compilation to the GPU.

Olimpiu Pop: That sounds quite interesting, and it definitely makes sense these days. For instance, I saw that a lot of the big companies are just using Java for inference, and that makes perfect sense to just have this closing the loop. Today, you are part of the team at Red Hat, back again at Red Hat, that is working on llm-d. And in my understanding, what llm-d is, taking a step back, if VLLM is making sure that everything runs perfectly on one box, llm-d is trying to make sure that everything is efficient if you have a Kubernetes cluster. Is that a correct affirmation or did I understand wrong?

Edoardo Vacchi: No, no, it is correct on a high level. More specifically, so VLLM is our inference engine. So, you can think of it, if you will, as the JVM of language models. So, it has support for several language models, there's an interesting aside here, it is a platform to run LLMs. The interesting aside here is you would expect that this is a general sort of VM, and the LLMs are sort of software that you load on top of it. But unfortunately every LLM architecture is slightly different. So, VLLM has to basically include the implementation of every LLM that gets released. So, when people release LLMs, they do not release the software to run them, they release the weights. So, all of these inference engines, such as VLLM, what they do is implementing basically the software, the kernels, the components that actually load the weights and then actually do the inference.

So, VLLM is our platform to run the core and effectively VLLM is able to serve, it's a server... I mean, it's an inference engine, it's also server that exposes endpoints that you can call to do inference, and it does so efficiently. It was originally VLLM, I think the V in VLLM originally stands for virtual, as in virtual memory allocation. Because it was the first engine to implement page detention, basically a mechanism inspired by good old systems programming to do paging of memory, memory pages, but for memory that gets allocated on GPU, this is in a very high level way. So, VLLM is able to do high throughput inference. So, you can do several requests at once and VLLM will pack them and try to serve them together, and do inference in one pass for several requests at one time, this is called continuous batching. But this gets you to a point.

Essentially, at some point you have your GPUs on your machine, and your inference engine and that's it. You will not be able to scale further than the resources that you have on that machine. So, how do you scale further? Well, you can scale by having more VLLM instances, right? So, you have several VLLM instances and you want to serve your inference requests using these few VLLM, these few VLLM instances that you have. Now, you have another problem. How do you route requests across your VLLM instances? So, if you are on Kubernetes, what you will do... And most people are on Kubernetes these days, it's the standard for platforms for serving services in an efficient way. So, you can scale your VLLM instances and have several VLLM instances that serve the possible the same request... I mean that gets selected by the scheduler, by the VLLM scheduler.

If you do it the traditional way and let the Kubernetes normal router to pick across the VLLM instances that you have replicated, you won't get necessarily good performance. The reason is inference does not behave like a traditional service, a traditional HTP service. Basically, if you send a request to one specific VLLM instance, especially if you are doing conversation, if you're doing a chat and if you're doing agentic coding, it's still a chat basically. There's a lot of exchanges back and forth between you and your server, between your agent and your server. You want to stick for as much time as possible to the same VLLM instance. This might be counterintuitive in a way because for microservices, we know we don't want to hammer the same service on and on because otherwise it will get overloaded. We want to do sort of round robbing or random robbing across the replicas.

But the thing is microservices or service in general, these are usually in a way stateless. The state is usually stored somewhere else and it's not part of your request. I mean, the request can be served independently by any instance. Unfortunately for LLMs, in order for LLMs to do their inference in an efficient way, you want to stick for as much time as possible to the same instance. But at the same time, you cannot stick forever to the same instance because at some point you will reach some limit. You are not the only user of that VLLM instance. You want to serve and distribute the load across your VLLM instances. So there's a balance that you have to strike between staying with the same instance and benefit of the caches, the KV caches, the prefix caches that are in place, the systems that allow you to do inference in an efficient way and lower costs.

But at the same time, you don't want to overload the same instance too much. So you also have to keep this into account. This is not the job for a traditional Kubernetes schedule. And that's where llm-d comes into place. That's what llm-d does. llm-d is not just a router or a scheduler. It's actually a family of projects and they are all meant to give you a set of tools to do distributed inference so that you can leverage all of the GPUs that you have and use it at their maximum as much as possible so you get the best value, the best bang for your bucks because these hardware is expensive whether you loan it or you own it. So you want to use it 100% as much as possible. And that's why we provide scheduler. We have something that we're going to release. I mean, in the open source ecosystem, it's already been released.

We're going to release also as part of product of Red Hat. This is called batch inference. Batch inference is using your cluster even when it's under load. So you can schedule request to do batch processing in the background when your cluster is underused because basically this hardware is so expensive that you want to keep it at 100% all the time. So even when there is no live inference going on, you can schedule batch processing to run when you're sleeping when there's less work to be done live. So that's what llm-d does. It uses your hardware as much as possible so that the money you spend gets you the best value and you do it on your own hardware so you can do inference without leaking data to a third party, which is important these days.

#9970. Barracuda’s email security gateways bitten by make-me-root vulns

Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security Gateway (ESG) products that, when chained, could allow the crims to run commands with root privileges.

“We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations,” the security vendor said in a late Monday night update to its earlier security advisory.

Barracuda declined to answer The Register’s questions, including one about how many organizations have been hit by attackers. A company spokesperson told us that it “worked directly” with the affected businesses “to quickly address the issue. Barracuda acted promptly to remediate the vulnerabilities, releasing patches for affected products.”

The vendor disclosed and fixed the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, last week.

CVE-2026-116606 is a 9.3 CVSS-rated, pre-authentication authorization bypass flaw in ESG. While authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must have access to the administrative user interface.

As Purplecop Security founder Tausif Ahmed said on Tuesday: “If your Email Security Gateway's admin UI is open to the internet, that's the first thing I'd close today.”

CVE-2026-111560 is an 8.6-rated command-injection flaw that affects multiple Barracuda products: its ESG, load balancer (ADC), message archiver (BMA), web application firewall (WAF), WAF control center (WCC), and web security gateway (WSG).

“If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda warned on November 2. At the time, the vendor did not report any active exploitation of either.

We don’t yet know who is responsible for the attacks, or whether the intruders gained root access – but if they did, they could steal data, install backdoors, and take full control of affected systems.

These types of edge-device exploits have been used by Chinese-government spies, and in 2023 the FBI blamed PRC-linked attackers for a series of attacks that targeted Barracuda ESGs to deploy custom malware and maintain access to high-value networks. According to Mandiant, 27 percent of identified affected organizations were government entities.
