#9954. Memory Safety Bugs in Rust Standard Library

By Yechan Bae / November 9, 2026 / 19 min read

Microsoft’s FORGE Lab found several memory safety issues in Rust’s standard library (std and core), including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The research used Hyenas, FORGE’s frontier research version of codename MDASH, an AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system. The findings reveal three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting. Its rich type system and ownership model rule out whole classes of memory-safety issues, but much of the standard library relies on unsafe code underneath its safe APIs. When that code breaks its safety contract, even safe Rust can encounter behavior the language is designed to prevent.

Rust’s memory-safety guarantees are increasingly important as the language becomes part of software that billions of people rely on every day. Billions of people are estimated to interact with Rust-based software or operating systems daily, often without knowing it. Microsoft made Rust a Tier-1 internal language alongside C++, C#, and TypeScript, GitHub rewrote the Copilot agent runtime in Rust, and Bun, Android, the Linux kernel, and Cloudflare are moving code to it as well. Much of this software relies on Rust’s foundational libraries, core and std, and the safety guarantees of the APIs they provide. Bugs in those libraries can have consequences well beyond the code where they originate.

Unsafe Rust has been a long-running interest for us. Our team includes the people behind Rudra, a static analyzer that looked for memory-safety bugs across the Rust ecosystem in 2021. We also write many of our own tools in Rust, so its safety is more than a research topic for us. This year, we took a closer look at the standard library to see what kinds of mistakes still show up in its unsafe code today.

In this post, we share some of the bugs we reported to the Rust issue tracker. We use them to discuss what Rust does and doesn’t guarantee, why writing correct unsafe Rust is so difficult, and why Rust’s safety model still matters even though its memory safety isn’t perfect.

At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we study vulnerabilities in complex software, including the Rust standard library. Our team combines years of experience in vulnerability research with AI-assisted tools that help us investigate code and find bugs that are difficult to uncover through traditional analysis alone.

Some of the bugs in this post were found with help from Hyenas, our research version of codename MDASH. Our researchers investigated the underlying code, reproduced the bugs, assessed their potential security impact, and worked with Rust maintainers to report and fix them.

This post focuses on soundness bugs in the standard library’s unsafe code. Bugs in the compiler itself, such as miscompilations and holes in the type system, are a different topic that we don’t cover here.

A note on open issues. At publication, two of the issues reported by our team remain open. The article also references related issues reported by others and fixes that are still under review. The Rust maintainers triaged and responded to our reports quickly, and we believe maintainers and the contributors working on these issues are doing their best and making the right tradeoffs among the many bugs they handle.

If you’re interested in an open issue, please comment only when you have something genuinely new to contribute, such as new information or an affected real-world use case.

At the lowest level, Rust uses unsafe blocks to work with raw pointers and interact directly with the operating system. Much of the standard library, including Vec and String, is built from small unsafe pieces wrapped in safe APIs. Inside an unsafe block, the programmer takes responsibility for the guarantees the compiler can’t check, and that responsibility extends to the safe API built around it. That API must be sound: no matter how safe code uses it, it must be impossible to trigger undefined behavior.

Upholding that promise is harder than it looks. Consider a function that returns the byte at idx from any type that can be viewed as a byte slice, skipping the redundant bounds check after doing its own:

The hard part of unsafe Rust is knowing what you can trust. The function above looks correct, but it assumes that two calls to as_ref return the same slice. Because S is chosen by the caller, a safe AsRef implementation can return a long slice the first time and an empty one the second, and get reads out of bounds. Unsafe code must be careful with every call it makes, and the bugs we found fall into three patterns of misplaced trust: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Unsafe code often breaks an invariant for a moment and restores it afterward; for example, it may allocate an uninitialized buffer and fill it directly, avoiding redundant writes to zero the memory first. That’s fine as long as the function runs to the end. But many operations in Rust can panic, from out-of-bounds indexing to calls into user-provided code, and by default a panic unwinds: it leaves the function early while still running destructors. Unwinding inside that window becomes an invisible exit that exposes the broken invariant to code that trusts it. Bugs of this kind are called panic safety bugs.

We identified a panic safety issue in MapWindows::clone. Iterator::map_windows, a nightly API, yields overlapping windows of N items. It keeps the current window in a Buffer whose destructor drops the N items starting at start. In Rust 1.97.0, library/core/src/iter/adapters/map_windows.rs defines it as:

Buffer::clone, in the same file, built the new buffer first and filled it afterward:

After line 197, buffer breaks its own invariant: its slots are uninitialized, but its destructor is already armed. The clone() call on line 201 runs the user’s T::clone before the slots are written. If that call panics, unwinding drops buffer and runs drop_in_place on N uninitialized values. Our proof of concept uses only safe code: an element type whose clone always panics, which causes a crash when the destructor accesses uninitialized memory. The fix holds the new buffer in ManuallyDrop until it is fully written, so unwinding leaks the half-built buffer instead of dropping it.

The general lesson is to treat every call to code you don’t control, such as clone, drop, comparisons, closures, and iterator methods, as a possible early exit. Either finish the work that may panic before breaking an invariant, or make the broken state safe to unwind through: hold it in ManuallyDrop, or use a guard whose destructor restores the invariant, like Vec’s internal SetLenOnDrop. The Rustonomicon covers this under exception safety.

The recently stabilized Allocator API shows how hard panic safety is to get right. With std, an allocation failure aborts the process by default instead of unwinding, so much of the standard library’s unsafe code assumes allocation never unwinds. Custom allocators can break that assumption. While the API was being stabilized, we reported one place in BTreeMap::insert that becomes unsound when an allocator unwinds, and others reported more (#159334, #159368, #159370). Fixing them one by one would mean auditing everything that allocates, so the stabilization, shipping in Rust 1.100 on November 12, instead requires implementors never to unwind from the trait’s methods or from drop. The proposal notes that “unwinding out of many allocation-related methods was found to be a pervasive source of unsoundness.”

Unsafe code often calls into code its caller provides: a comparator, a trait implementation, a closure. That code is safe, but safe doesn’t mean correct, and it can return inconsistent or plainly wrong answers. The question is who is responsible when it does. In C++, it’s the caller. std::sort requires its comparator to be a strict weak ordering, and breaking that rule is undefined behavior. With libstdc++, sorting equal elements with <= reads past the end of the vector:

The same comparator passed to Rust’s sort_by is only a logic error. The sort may panic or leave the slice in an unspecified order, but it never causes undefined behavior. The responsibility sits with the unsafe code. The comparator is safe code supplied by the caller, so the unsafe code inside the sort must stay sound no matter what it returns. The same goes for every safe trait a user can implement: comparisons can be inconsistent, an ExactSizeIterator can report a length that doesn’t match the items it yields, and Borrow can return a different value on each call.

Another of our bug reports shows how easy this trust is to miss: str::replace with a custom Pattern can create a non-UTF-8 String. String search APIs accept any type that implements the nightly Pattern trait, and a pattern can describe itself through as_utf8_pattern. str::replace uses that description to take a fast path when replacing one ASCII byte with another. In Rust 1.96.0, the fast path in library/alloc/src/str.rs looked like this:

replace_ascii, in the same file, then rewrites the bytes:

The CharPattern branch on line 272 checks that the character is ASCII, but the StringPattern branch on line 271 assumes a one-byte string pattern must be ASCII. That holds for &str patterns, but StringPattern stored &[u8], and as_utf8_pattern is a safe method any Pattern can implement. In our proof of concept, a custom pattern reports the single byte 0x80, which only appears inside multibyte UTF-8 sequences:

str::replace rewrites the continuation bytes and returns a String that isn’t valid UTF-8, and later string operations that rely on UTF-8 reach undefined behavior. The fix changed StringPattern to hold &str instead of &[u8], so the type itself now guarantees UTF-8.

When unsafe code depends on a property of a user-provided implementation, don’t take it on faith. Call the implementation once and keep the result, validate what it returns, or encode the property in a type that safe code can’t forge, as this fix did. If none of those work, make the trait unsafe so implementors explicitly promise to uphold it.

join shows how easy it is to fix this kind of bug only partway. In 2020, we reported that it trusted Borrow::borrow to return the same string on each call (CVE-2020-36323), and the fix handled strings that shrink between calls. In April 2026, the same function needed another fix: join borrows the first element twice, and if it grows on the second call, the remaining-length calculation underflows into a heap overflow. The earlier fix had never covered that path.

Others reported similar problems in the Pattern API this year. A safe Pattern can hand back a valid searcher built for a different string, and consumers such as strip_prefix_of apply its ranges to the original string unchecked, reading out of bounds (#158265). The same problem turned up in split_once (#165076) after a report that the Searcher contract doesn’t spell out what str::split relies on (#164904). Both bugs are still open.

The first two patterns stay inside Rust code. The third sits at the boundary with the operating system, where unsafe code trusts process-wide state such as signal stacks, memory mappings, and the environment, which other threads, C libraries, or the kernel can touch at any time. These bugs have been hard to find automatically, because a static analyzer would need to model all of that surrounding behavior. AI agents change the picture: they understand enough about the environment the code runs in to make this area practical to search. We started exploring it and found some interesting bugs.

When a thread overflows its stack, Rust prints a clear message and aborts instead of crashing with a bare segmentation fault:

This relies on a few pieces of process-wide state. Each thread’s stack ends in a guard page, an inaccessible region just past the stack’s limit: pthread reserves one for every spawned thread, and on Linux the kernel’s own stack guard plays that role for the main thread. Touching it raises SIGSEGV, and Rust registers a handler for that signal. The handler can’t run on the stack that just overflowed, so Rust also gives each thread an alternate signal stack, a small separate mapping with a guard page of its own, which the kernel switches to when it delivers the signal. The handler checks that the faulting address is inside the guard page, prints the message, and aborts.

We found that calling process::exit from a child thread tears down the main thread’s alternate stack while the main thread is still running. process::exit runs the runtime’s cleanup before calling libc’s exit, and in Rust 1.98.0 that cleanup ends in library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/stack_overflow.rs:

Line 202 passes MAIN_ALTSTACK, the main thread’s alternate stack, to drop_handler:

Line 298 disables the alternate stack of the calling thread, but line 301 unmaps the main thread’s. The code assumes it runs on the main thread, which isn’t true when a child thread calls process::exit. The main thread keeps running until libc’s exit finishes, with its signal stack registration still pointing at unmapped memory. If it overflows its stack in that window, the kernel can’t deliver the signal, and our proof of concept dies with a plain segmentation fault instead of Rust’s message. The bug dates back to 2015, and the fix stops cleaning up the main thread’s alternate stack altogether.

We also checked whether this could become a security issue. In theory, it could lead to code execution: if a writable mapping landed at the old alternate stack’s address, the kernel would deliver the main thread’s next signal onto it, and another thread could overwrite the handler’s frame, such as its return address, while it runs. In practice, the conditions are very tight. Everything has to happen in the brief window before libc’s exit finishes, the new mapping must have exactly the right size to reuse that address, and overwriting the frame takes a second race inside a short handler. For issue #161018, our testing found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions examined, and we assessed practical exploitation as unlikely. This assessment does not automatically apply to the other issues discussed. The issue has more details in its security impact analysis.

Our other report involves the process environment. On Unix, CommandExt::exec replaces the current process with a new program. When the command has its own environment variables, exec points the process-global environ at a new array, calls execvp, and restores environ if execvp fails. In Rust 1.99.0, Command::exec takes the environment lock in library/std/src/sys/process/unix/unix.rs:

Command::do_exec, in the same file, then swaps the environment:

Line 242 takes only the read side of the environment lock, yet line 410 writes the process-global environ; line 409 saves the old value so it can be restored if execvp on line 413 fails. Writing environ under a read lock lets other threads in. A thread calling env::var takes the same read lock and can see variables meant only for the new program, and two failed exec calls racing each other can leave environ pointing at a freed array that a later env::vars_os() reads. Both proofs of concept use only safe Rust. A 2018 fix held an exclusive lock here, but when the environment lock became a read-write lock in 2021, exec kept the read side. A fix that avoids touching environ by calling execve directly is in review.

The environment has caused trouble before. After a discussion that began in 2015, the 2024 edition marked env::set_var as unsafe, because C functions on most Unix platforms read the environment without going through Rust’s lock.

Getting this boundary right is hard, and more problems are still open. While exploring this area, we independently ran into a double free in safe code that process::exit can cause through thread-local destructors. It was reported by someone else (#164243), but it’s worth mentioning here. libc’s exit first runs the calling thread’s thread-local destructors, as C++ requires, and Rust registers its destructors the same way. If a destructor calls process::exit while a thread local is being replaced, libc drops that thread local a second time. A proposed fix switches process::exit to POSIX _exit, which ends the process without running these handlers.

Every unsafe block rests on assumptions about the code around it. The bugs in this post came from three kinds of misplaced trust:

The first two patterns are well studied. Rudra looked for both in 2021, and the standard library was already fixing panic safety bugs in 2015 (CVE-2015-20001). They remain challenging to avoid because any call inside unsafe code might unwind or run code the caller supplied.

What we saw this year was mixed. On the positive side, the nightly process is working. Many reports were caught while the affected APIs were still unstable, and several were fixed by changing the design before stabilization. StringPattern now holds &str instead of &[u8], and Allocator was stabilized with a rule that implementors must not unwind. At the same time, bugs in these patterns still reach stable releases, and their fixes aren’t always complete. join was fixed in 2020 and needed another fix in 2026 for a path the first fix had missed.

The third pattern is different. Its bugs live where Rust meets the layers below it: the kernel, through system calls such as sigaltstack and munmap, and the C library, through process-wide state such as environ and the cleanup that libc’s exit runs. Getting them right takes knowledge that lives outside Rust’s type system, which has made these bugs difficult to find with traditional static analysis. That may also be why they last so long. The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years, and exec has written environ under a read lock since 2021. Unlike our reports in the first two patterns, both affect stable Rust.

Language models already know a great deal about how these interfaces behave, so agentic scanners can check unsafe code against the system it runs on, not just the language. We think this boundary is one of the most promising places for agentic security research, in Rust and beyond.

Rust holds its safe APIs to a stricter standard than C and C++. Safe code must never be able to cause undefined behavior, no matter how it uses an API. In C++, a comparator that breaks std::sort’s ordering requirement causes undefined behavior, while Rust’s sort must stay memory-safe with any Ord implementation. POSIX doesn’t guarantee that setenv is safe to call while another thread reads the environment. That makes memory safety bugs in Rust hard to compare one-to-one with bugs in other languages.

For the same reason, a soundness bug in the standard library isn’t automatically a vulnerability in the programs that use it. Each bug in this post needs an unusual setup to trigger, such as a panic at exactly the wrong moment, a deliberately misbehaving implementation, or calling process::exit from a child thread. It becomes a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way.

Rust’s safety standard is strict and difficult to meet, but it’s also useful. It gives an unambiguous answer to what counts as a soundness bug, so problems can be fixed and prevented once in the library, instead of in every program that uses it. Rust’s safety model strikes the right balance between control, safety, and performance for systems programming, which is why so many projects choose it.

At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we’re exploring how technology such as codename MDASH can help researchers find bugs like the ones in this post at greater scale. Rust’s standard library is one of several foundational open source projects where we’re applying this approach.

This research also extends beyond the lab. It helps inform the development of codename MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender. These findings can also serve as inputs to Microsoft Perception, our new multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work together across broader security workflows. For example, the Web App Pen Test Agent can use codename MDASH findings to help prioritize testing, validate exploitability against live applications, and produce actionable vulnerabilities that downstream agents can use to prioritize and support remediation. This connects AI-powered code analysis with real-world security validation and response, helping security teams move from identifying potential vulnerabilities to understanding and addressing actual risk.

Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs, it’s to identify meaningful issues, turn those findings into actionable research, and improve the safety of foundational software that developers and organizations depend on.

#9953. Ye olde server consolidation has made Cisco push top-of-rack switching to 100G

Newer server processors pack more cores into fewer boxes, creating a need for network speed

Server consolidation has led Cisco to boost the speed of top-of-rack switches to 100G.

The networking giant last week announced the catchily named N9348C8D-H2, a 1U device packing 48 100G SFP-DD ports and eight 400G QSFP-DD uplinks.

At the Cisco Live event in Melbourne, Australia, this week, Cisco’s senior veep for datacenter and internet infrastructure, Kevin Wollenweber, said one reason the company created the device is that modern servers often feature a pair of fast network interface cards.

The twin cards are needed because sixth-gen server processors from Intel and AMD offer dozens, or even hundreds, of physical processor cores and therefore generate a lot of traffic.

The density of computing power those processors provide has led chipmakers and server manufacturers to suggest replacing handfuls of machines running older, power-guzzling Xeons and Epycs with boxes running more efficient sixth-gen chips.

The Register hears it’s not uncommon to achieve 6:1 server consolidation ratios when moving from third- or fourth-generation Xeons or Epycs to current models. Users who make that move can pack many more server cores into the same rack. Power bills go down, but the quantity of data leaving a rack goes up.

Wollenweber said Cisco realized it had “tons” of switches that offer 25G ports but felt it had a gap in its range for non-AI scenarios like server consolidation that produced increased data flows.

The exec admitted that the 100G ports may be overkill for a modest collection of new servers, but argued users recognize it won’t be long before they grow into the excess capacity – perhaps as they use more agentic AI applications.

Cisco sees traffic from AI agents stressing the north-south connections that link organizations to the cloud and also driving much more east-west traffic across internal networks.

At Cisco Live, the company’s execs suggested that network upgrades are therefore an inevitable necessity.

That’s not entirely self-serving, because agents will vastly outnumber humans and constantly create traffic, compared to the flurries of network activity that happen when humans use generative AI or chatbots.

Cisco argues that deploying agents at scale will therefore only be possible on highly automated networks.

“Humans can no longer comprehend the amount of data that we actually have in a network,” Wollenweber told The Register.

Cisco’s Canvas agentic operations platform aims to at least make humans aware when their attention is needed, by detecting problems and offering to make repairs.

Joe Vaccaro, Cisco’s senior vice president and general manager for Network Platform and Assurance, told The Register he believes network administrators don’t feel threatened by suggestions from AI agents when they concern familiar, routine, low-risk tasks that IT pros are confident the agents can handle. Over time, he said, networking pros will learn to trust agents with more complex work. ®

Hot on the heels of the previous two stable kernels, Greg Kroah-Hartman has announced the release of the 7.3.3, 6.18.62, 6.12.116, 6.6.162, 6.1.192, 5.15.225, and 5.10.274 stable kernels. Each one only contains fixes for three use-after-free vulnerabilities announced today by the Xen security team.

Two of the vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to cause a denial of service (DoS) for the entire Xen host machine with possible information leakage (CVE-2026-100080, CVE-2026-100082), and one may allow privilege escalation as well as a DoS of the host machine (CVE-2026-100081). #9951. Go Turns 17

Stories about how and why companies use Go

How Go can help keep you secure by default

A complete introduction to building software with Go

Reference documentation for Go's standard library

Tips for writing clear, performant, and idiomatic Go code

Learn and network with Go developers from around the world

Austin Clements, for the Go team 10 November 2026

Today, November 10th, we celebrate the 17th anniversary of Go’s open source release!

Over the past year, we released Go 1.26 in February and Go 1.27 in August, alongside a steady stream of releases across our golang.org/x libraries and developer tools. Meanwhile, the pace of change across the software industry continues to accelerate, driven by shifting hardware, evolving security threats, and the rapid rise of AI-assisted development and agentic systems.

In a tumultuous time for the industry, Go aims to be a steady hand on the tiller. Our goal is to keep Go grounded in its foundational principles of simplicity, reliability, efficiency, and an unwavering commitment to compatibility, while adapting to modern hardware, production workloads, and developer workflows. Increasingly, our investments serve a dual purpose: what helps human engineers write, understand, and maintain reliable Go code at scale also provides the guardrails and authoritative context that AI coding assistants and agents need to be effective.

In the language itself, Go 1.26 and 1.27 addressed several long-standing restrictions in generics and everyday Go syntax, guided by years of real-world experience. When generics first landed in Go 1.18, methods could not declare their own type parameters, which sometimes forced awkward package-level functions and “inside-out” nested calls. Go 1.27 introduced generic methods on non-interface types (such as the new Rand.N method in math/rand/v2), allowing APIs to stay naturally organized on types and enabling readable method chaining. Together with support for self-referential type constraints in Go 1.26 and broader type inference for generic function values in Go 1.27, generics in Go feel more complete and natural than ever.

Alongside generics, two refinements to value construction make everyday Go code cleaner and more concise. Go 1.26 extended the built-in new function to accept an initial value expression, allowing new(42) or new("go1.26") without the ubiquitous newInt-style helper functions used to populate optional pointer fields in JSON and protocol buffer structs. And in Go 1.27, struct literal keys can refer directly to fields of embedded or nested structs, reducing boilerplate in composite literals.

In the standard library, our focus has been on evolving Go’s “production stack” and eliminating subtle operational traps. Few packages are as central to that as encoding/json, which has been a mainstay of Go since before Go 1.0. While its core model has held up remarkably well for over 15 years, tighter JSON standards and security expectations have turned some of its original defaults into interoperability and security hazards, such as silently accepting invalid UTF-8 or duplicate object keys and matching struct fields case-insensitively. At the same time, its buffered design prevented true streaming and limited performance. Addressing these issues while upholding Go’s compatibility promise for the millions of existing programs that depend on encoding/json meant designing a new major version of the package.

Six years in the making, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages reached general availability in Go 1.27. Driven by Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, and contributors from across the Go community, this modern JSON API brings safer, stricter defaults, flexible caller- and type-specified customization, and up to 10× faster unmarshaling, while cleanly separating high-level semantic marshaling (json/v2) from low-level, reflection-free syntactic streaming (jsontext). Crucially, we didn’t leave existing code behind: the original encoding/json package is now implemented entirely in terms of v2 under the hood. Existing v1 callers get faster unmarshaling simply by upgrading, and packages using v1 and v2 interoperate seamlessly so that the ecosystem can migrate gradually without flag days.

We’ve also brought new production diagnostics to Go’s concurrency primitives. Concurrency is one of Go’s greatest strengths, but goroutines accidentally left blocked on abandoned channels or locks can silently leak memory and CPU in long-running services, and traditional goroutine profiles cannot distinguish leaked goroutines from ones legitimately waiting for work. First previewed in Go 1.26 and now generally available in Go 1.27, the new goroutine leak profiler (goroutineleak in runtime/pprof and /debug/pprof/goroutineleak in net/http/pprof) solves this for production services. Contributed by Vlad Saioc and Uber’s Programming Systems team, building on academic research with Aarhus University and Washington University in St. Louis, the profiler repurposes the garbage collector’s reachability phase to identify goroutines blocked on concurrency primitives that no runnable goroutine can ever reach. That allows it to pinpoint leaks in production with near-zero false positives and zero overhead when not in use.

In net/http, closing an HTTP/1 response body with even a single unread byte—such as a trailing newline left behind by a JSON decoder—previously forced the client to tear down the underlying TCP and TLS connection. Go 1.27’s HTTP transport now automatically drains small unread response bodies in the background on close, turning a widespread latency footgun into up to a 5× speedup for sequential HTTP/1 requests while letting application code stay clean and simple.

These releases also added several notable standard library APIs, including a native uuid package, a generic and type-safe errors.AsType, and an in-memory httptest.NewTestServer designed for virtual-time testing with testing/synctest. Existing packages saw significant speedups as well: io.ReadAll now runs twice as fast while allocating half as much memory, compress/flate compresses faster (speeding up gzip, zip, zlib, and png), and image/jpeg has a faster, more accurate encoder and decoder.

Modern CPUs look very different from the hardware Go first launched on 17 years ago, with wide vector units and deep, non-uniform memory hierarchies. A major focus of our runtime and compiler work is ensuring Go programs make full use of modern silicon, both transparently when you upgrade your toolchain and through new APIs when you need explicit control.

After debuting as an experiment in Go 1.25, the Green Tea garbage collector became the default in Go 1.26. By organizing object marking around contiguous memory spans rather than chasing pointers across the heap, Green Tea aligns with modern CPU memory architectures to reduce garbage collection overhead by 10–40% in real-world workloads—and by an additional ~10% on recent amd64 processors using AVX-512 vector instructions during scanning.

Of course, the runtime shouldn’t be the only part of a Go program that can tap into vector hardware. Without access to Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD) capabilities, compute-intensive software, from cryptography and media processing to data analytics and AI, leaves a significant portion of modern silicon dark. Until recently, the only way to light up that hardware in Go was by writing and maintaining per-architecture assembly. To change that, Go 1.26 and 1.27 introduced two experimental SIMD packages: simd/archsimd, for low-level access to architecture-specific vector instructions on amd64, arm64 (NEON), and WebAssembly (wasm); and simd, a higher-level, width-agnostic API that provides portable, near-assembly performance across architectures with automatic fallback emulation.

We’ve also attacked the cost of memory allocation from multiple angles. The cheapest heap allocation is the one that never happens: in Go 1.26, the compiler began allocating initial slice backing stores on the stack at append sites—even for slices that ultimately escape to the heap—eliminating the flurry of small heap allocations that typically accompany slice growth. And for heap allocations more broadly, Go 1.27 introduced size-specialized memory allocation to speed up allocating the small objects (such as small structs, slices, and strings) that dominate allocator time. Generating dedicated fast-path allocator routines for size classes up to 80 bytes made small allocations up to 30% faster and improved overall performance in allocation-heavy programs. Together with a ~30% reduction in baseline cgo call overhead in Go 1.26, these improvements make Go programs faster and leaner out of the box.

Go’s approach to security spans the entire lifecycle of software: providing safe APIs by design, preparing cryptography for the future, and actively defending the live ecosystem as new threats emerge.

To defend against store-now, decrypt-later attacks and support the industry’s accelerating timelines for quantum readiness, Go has continued expanding its post-quantum cryptography support. Go 1.26 enabled hybrid post-quantum key exchanges (SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024) by default in crypto/tls and added the crypto/hpke package (implementing RFC 9180 Hybrid Public Key Encryption, including post-quantum hybrid KEMs). Go 1.27 followed up with the new crypto/mldsa package, implementing the FIPS 204 post-quantum ML-DSA signature standard and integrating it into crypto/x509 and crypto/tls.

At the same time, we’ve continued hardening the standard library and runtime against subtle classes of vulnerabilities. Most key generation and signing functions across Go’s crypto/... packages now unconditionally draw from a secure system randomness source, closing off a classic footgun where non-cryptographic readers were accidentally passed in. Under the hood, Go 1.26 also added 64-bit heap base address randomization to harden cgo binaries and introduced the experimental runtime/secret package for eagerly erasing sensitive cryptographic temporaries from registers, stack frames, and the heap.

Securing Go deployments also requires rapid vulnerability and incident response in a fast-moving threat landscape. From the Go vulnerability database and govulncheck to our release infrastructure, we’ve invested heavily in ecosystem defense. In October, that preparation was put to the test during the eMudhra certificate key disclosure incident, when eight intermediate TLS and code-signing certificates chaining to a widely trusted root CA were discovered to use trivially weak private keys. Because Linux lacks a uniform OS-level certificate revocation mechanism, Go’s built-in TLS verifier is the frontline defense for millions of Linux services. Within seven and a half hours of initial notification, the Go Security team shipped a targeted block in our first-ever URGENT track security release (Go 1.27.3 and Go 1.26.10) alongside an updated Go vulnerability database entry so govulncheck could flag affected binaries, giving Go users everything they needed to protect their deployments before the weak keys were publicly disclosed the next morning.

Go has always been more than a compiler and standard library: it is an end-to-end platform for software engineering. Over the past year, our work in golang.org/x/tools, the gopls language server, vscode-go, and pkg.go.dev has focused on making that platform even more productive for both human developers and AI coding assistants.

In last fall’s Go Developer Survey, the single biggest challenge developers reported was ensuring their code follows best practices and current Go idioms. As Go evolves while standing by its compatibility promise, older ways of writing code continue to work alongside newer, clearer, or faster alternatives, creating a natural drift in idioms over time. That drift has been compounded by AI coding assistants, which gravitate toward the older patterns that dominate their training data.

Go 1.26 tackled this with a complete overhaul of the go fix command, returning the long-dormant tool to its pre-Go 1.0 roots to apply dozens of automatic modernizers across entire codebases. What gofmt did for stylistic consistency, modernizers aim to do for idiomatic consistency. Available both as instant suggestions in gopls and as bulk, push-button upgrades in go fix, modernizers simplify existing code and help developers discover new language and library features. We now routinely consider whether new language and library proposals should ship with a modernizer of their own. Just as importantly, modernizers give coding agents an immediate way to bring generated code up to date, while helping shift the global corpus of open source Go code so that future models learn modern idioms from the start.

Bespoke modernizers work well for the language and standard library, but a centralized team can never write them for every third-party module in the ecosystem. That’s why Go 1.26 also introduced the annotation-driven source-level inliner, the first step toward a “self-service” paradigm for automated code maintenance. Any package author can now annotate a deprecated function, type, or constant with //go:fix inline, and the inliner will safely migrate callers and references via go fix or in the IDE, carefully handling evaluation order, side effects, and name shadowing.

In the editor, we’ve made four feature-packed releases of gopls over the past year (v0.21.0, v0.22.0, v0.23.0, and v0.24.0). In collaboration with the Dart team, we designed and proposed an open Language Server Protocol (LSP) extension for interactive refactoring, allowing language servers to ask for user input through dynamic, multi-step dialogs in any supporting editor. Now integrated into gopls and vscode-go, interactive refactoring powers customizable struct tag addition and removal, interface implementation (including generic interfaces) with live symbol search, and cross-package declaration moves. Beyond refactoring, gopls also gained generalized package renaming across directories, zero-configuration support for editing Go assembly files, subexpression hover inspection, completions and inlay hints for promoted fields, automatic govulncheck scanning when go.mod dependencies change, and continued enhancements to its built-in Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for AI coding assistants.

Rounding out the developer platform, in May we launched the official pkg.go.dev API and followed up with support for go doc pkg@version in Go 1.27. Previously, developer tools and IDE integrations had to resort to fragile web scraping to query ecosystem metadata. Today, the pkg.go.dev API gives tool authors and AI coding agents a fast, authoritative service for querying module versions, package symbols, importers, and vulnerability data, while go doc pkg@version makes it easy to pull up documentation for any version of any package right from the command line.

On the tooling front, we’re building on the pkg.go.dev API, gopls, and go fix to make Go’s developer tools even more capable for both human developers and coding agents. Following the strong community response to go fix and //go:fix inline, we’re exploring ways to expand self-service static analysis, enabling developers, package maintainers, and organizations to easily integrate custom analyzers and domain-specific best-practice checks directly into their development workflows. We’re also exploring ways to surface richer package health and quality signals on pkg.go.dev and through its API, helping developers and coding agents evaluate and choose trustworthy, reliable dependencies.

In the language and libraries, Go 1.28 will resolve one of Go’s longest-standing language requests by allowing composite literals to omit redundant types whenever the type can be inferred from context, cutting visual noise in deeply nested configurations, API requests, and table-driven tests. And with recent generics refinements and hashing APIs in place, we’ve just accepted a swath of proposals for generic collection APIs—including sets, ordered maps, and more—which will land in golang.org/x/exp over the next few weeks so the community can try them out and share feedback ahead of future standard library inclusion.

Under the hood, we’re working hard to graduate a large subset of the simd and simd/archsimd packages (covering amd64, arm64 NEON, and wasm) in Go 1.28, with further expansions and arm64 scalable vector (SVE) support targeted for Go 1.29. Amid the global RAM crunch, reducing Go’s memory footprint is also one of our major priorities for the coming year.

In the toolchain, Go 1.28 will increase build parallelism by writing compiler export data early and streamline static analysis by decoupling tool export data from the compiler. Looking further out, we’re working to support cgo builds without requiring a C toolchain, and we’re kicking the tires on WebAssembly’s early-stage stack-switching extension, which is already showing promising improvements in Go Wasm performance and binary size.

Finally, ensuring Go stands the test of time means scaling not just our technology, but the open source project itself. Over the past year, some of Go’s most impactful advances, including encoding/json/v2 and the goroutineleak profile, were driven by or built in close partnership with contributors outside Google. To better support our growing ecosystem and contributor base, we’re working to bridge the gap between Go maintainers at Google and our broader community, and to diversify Go’s technical stewardship. That includes restructuring the proposal process to improve throughput, give the community clearer visibility into the process and input into prioritization, and formally involve community contributors in triage and review. Beyond proposals, we are building a clearer contributor ladder to empower proven contributors with greater autonomy, decision-making privileges, and maintenance responsibilities, and opening up maintainer summits and day-to-day communications to trusted contributors from our amazing community.

Seventeen years in, Go is thriving because of the people who use it, build with it, and contribute to it every day. Thank you to everyone in the Go community for being part of this journey, and we wish you all the best in the year ahead!

#9950. Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it? We introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), and applied to a GPT-OSS 120B model compressed to 60B parameters and quantized to MXFP4, it produces a model that beats its own full-precision (bfloat16) version on 7 of 9 benchmarks. The 4-bit model ends up smaller, cheaper to run, and more accurate than the checkpoint it was quantized from. This inverts the usual relationship between a 4-bit model and the 16-bit model it came from.

Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage. The difference between methods is entirely in that last step.

The dominant healing recipe is quantization-aware training (QAT). It inserts fake-quantization operators into the forward pass and keeps fine-tuning the model on a task loss, so the weights learn to tolerate the low-precision representation. In practice this means re-running an already expensive multi-stage post-training process, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, agentic tuning, through a noisier, lower-precision forward pass. It is costly, and as our results show, it can also become unstable if training continues too long past its best point.

An alternative, quantization-aware distillation (QAD), avoids re-running that history. Instead of a task loss, it distills a frozen full-precision teacher directly into the quantized student through a KL-divergence loss on the output logits. This works well when the only change is quantization, because a genuine full-precision version of the exact same model exists to act as teacher. But once a model has gone through structural compression, fewer layers, heads, or neurons, and not just fewer bits, that assumption breaks. There is no independently trained full-precision version of the smaller architecture. The only candidate teacher is the recovered bfloat16 checkpoint, which is itself a distilled approximation of the original model. Distilling from it anchors the quantized student to a degraded target and caps its accuracy at that recovered checkpoint's own ceiling.

So the question of how to heal a model that has been both structurally compressed and quantized was, until now, genuinely open.

QAH removes that ceiling with one change: it distills directly from the original, pre-compression model rather than from the recovered one. Teacher and student do not even share an architecture. The teacher is full-size and full-precision, the student is half the size and running in MXFP4. Because a teacher's output distribution is architecture-agnostic, nothing about the size or shape mismatch prevents the transfer. The student never sees hard labels, only the teacher's output distribution, matched through KL divergence on the logits.

This reframes what the quantization stage is doing. Under QAH it is no longer a lossy postprocessing step applied after healing is finished. It is a second, full pass of distillation against the original teacher, supervision that the bfloat16 checkpoint never received. The 4-bit student is not compensating for information lost to quantization; it is picking up information the earlier recovery stage did not have the time or data to transfer.

There is also a stability benefit that falls out of the loss itself. Because KL distillation ties the student to a fixed teacher distribution, once the student catches up there is no further pressure for it to drift. A cross-entropy task loss, by contrast, keeps pushing the student toward hard labels indefinitely. That difference turns out to matter for both accuracy and training stability, as the comparison below shows.

To make QAH work at long context, where the healing corpus includes documents up to 32k tokens, we reuse the memory-efficient chunked KL-divergence loss from our companion paper on efficient distillation. That loss computes the KL one slice of the sequence at a time and never materializes the full vocabulary-by-sequence grid, which is what makes 32k-token healing fit inside a fixed GPU memory budget. We covered the mechanics of that loss in a previous post.

QAH overview. After structural compression and quantization, capabilities drop sharply. QAH distills from the original model, a frozen teacher whose logits are precomputed offline, rather than from the recovered checkpoint. Source: paper Figure 1.

We applied QAH to a GPT-OSS 120B model, compressed to 60B parameters and recovered in bfloat16, then re-quantized to MXFP4 under QAH. The natural comparison is against that same 60B model's bfloat16 checkpoint, the best full-precision version of this architecture that exists. The QAH model wins on 7 of the 9 benchmarks.

The two benchmarks where QAH trails, MMLU-Pro and SciCode, lose by less than a point and a half. Everywhere else the 4-bit model is ahead of its own 16-bit source, and the largest gains land on exactly the capabilities compression usually damages most: long-context reasoning (+7.4 on AA-LCR) and math (+5.6 on AIME 2025).

The comparison against the original 120B teacher is just as telling. Despite running at half the teacher's parameter count and roughly a quarter of its weight memory, the QAH model surpasses the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench (66.5 vs. 66.0) and comes within 1.6 points on GPQA Diamond (67.4 vs. 69.0). The largest remaining gap against the teacher is on AA-LCR, an extreme long-context benchmark where the capacity lost to compression is intrinsically the hardest to recover.

The 4-bit QAH model matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, and beats the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench. Source: paper Figure 2.

To isolate the effect of the loss function from everything else, we also compared QAH directly against QAT under matched conditions, quantizing a GPT-OSS 9B model to MXFP4 and tracking average performance across MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond as training progresses.

Both methods reach a similar peak, 54.9 for QAH against 54.6 for QAT, so on best-case accuracy they are effectively tied. The difference is in how they get there and what happens afterwards. QAH reaches its peak in about 100 steps, roughly 7 times faster than QAT's 700, and then stays within about two points of that peak for the rest of training. QAT collapses sharply once past its peak, shedding nearly 19 points by step 1,200.

The practical consequence is a real deployment risk difference. A QAT checkpoint needs careful early stopping against a held-out signal to avoid shipping a model that has already started to degrade, whereas a sufficiently trained QAH checkpoint can be served safely because it simply does not drift. This is consistent with the mechanism: KL distillation against a frozen teacher gives the student no incentive to move once it matches the teacher, while a cross-entropy objective keeps pushing on hard labels and eventually erodes capabilities the model inherited from the original.

QAH peaks at 54.9 in roughly 100 steps and holds; QAT reaches 54.6 only around step 700, then loses nearly 19 points by step 1,200. Source: paper Figure 3.

The accuracy story comes paired with the efficiency story that motivated compression in the first place. At 4-bit precision the QAH model uses roughly 4 times less weight memory than the bfloat16 student, and at half the parameter count of the 120B teacher it roughly halves compute per token, which is what lets it run on substantially smaller hardware. For model families that ship in bfloat16 rather than 4-bit, the combined parameter and precision reduction would be closer to 8 times less compute per token.

The takeaway is that a compressed, 4-bit model does not have to be a lower-accuracy version of its full-precision counterpart. With this healing recipe it can be smaller, cheaper to serve, and more accurate at the same time, and it reaches that point in a fraction of the training a QAT recipe would need. Quantization stops being a tax you pay for efficiency and becomes an extra opportunity to teach the model.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making large models smaller and cheaper to run without giving up the capabilities that make them useful. It sits alongside our companion work on efficient distillation, which supplies the long-context training machinery QAH depends on.

Want the full technical details, including the healing pipeline, the chunked KL implementation for long-context healing, and the distributed-training findings? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying compression and healing to your own models.

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as rbtv77 gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

This is a really fascinating take on model compression 🤯🔥. The idea that a 4-bit model can actually outperform the full-precision version turns the usual assumption about quantization completely upside down.... Instead of simply accepting the accuracy loss that comes with compression, QAH seems to show how targeted recovery can bring back—and even improve—important capabilities like reasoning, math, and coding. 🧠⚡

What really caught my attention is the result with the compressed GPT-OSS 120B → 60B model.... Getting a smaller MXFP4 model to beat its own bfloat16 checkpoint on 7 of 9 benchmarks is pretty impressive. 📊🚀 It makes the whole compress-then-heal pipeline feel much more practical for real-world deployment, especially when memory usage and inference costs matter.

I also like the broader implication here.... Quantization doesn't necessarily have to mean sacrificing model quality if the recovery process is designed with the quantized model in mind. 💡🔧 A smaller model that costs less to operate while still delivering stronger benchmark performance could be a huge advantage for teams trying to deploy capable LLMs efficiently.

Definitely an interesting direction for efficient AI deployment.... Turning a heavily compressed 4-bit model into something that can outperform its larger full-precision counterpart is the kind of result that makes you rethink what "compression" actually means. 👏🔥 Really curious to see how far Quantization-Aware Healing can go across other architectures and workloads.... 🚀🧠

Hi there! From how I'm reading this, I think you might have missed a method error in your experiment that invalidates your headline.

The headline comparison looks like it has no control. The bf16 60B got one round of distillation and the MXFP4 60B got that round plus a second round from a better teacher. The obvious missing comparison is to give the bf16 60B the identical second distillation pass in bf16, same data, same steps, same teacher. Without that comparison you cannot separate "QAH is a good recipe" from "we trained one checkpoint longer against a teacher than the other."

Results table labels the teacher "120B teacher (MXFP4)", which is right since gpt-oss-120b ships with MXFP4 MoE weights natively. But the approach section says the teacher is full-size and full-precision, and the title claims the student beats its full-precision original. Those contradict.

Unless I'm wrong, I'd retract this and consdier republishing when you can show the significant difference on the comparable arms without extending one further than the other with more compute.

You're right that the headline table compares checkpoints with unequal training. The 60B bf16 checkpoint got one distillation pass (the recovery); the 60B MXFP4 checkpoint got that pass plus a second one against the 120B teacher. We describe that second pass in the approach section, but we should have been explicit that the table therefore doesn't, on its own, separate "distilling under quantization" from "distilling for longer." We'll add that caveat to the text.

A bit of context on what the paper is: it's an applied case study, not a theoretical claim. The question we set out to answer is the one a deployment team faces: Given a compressed model that has to ship in 4 bits, what's the best way to run the quantization step? The result we stand behind is narrow and reproducible: the shipped 4-bit checkpoint scores above the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, rather than below it, which is the usual outcome of direct post-training quantization. What we shouldn't have leaned into is the stronger causal reading, that quantization itself is "free training", and you're right that the current table doesn't isolate that.

The comparison that would settle it is the one you describe: the bf16 60B given the identical second pass. same data, steps, teacher and, separately, that continued bf16 checkpoint post-training-quantized to MXFP4. The second is really the decision anyone deploying faces: heal under quantization, or quantize afterwards. If we extend this for a revised version, those are the arms we'd add; either way we're flagging them as a limitation of the current version rather than claiming the table resolves the question.

We don't think retraction is the right call. The reported numbers are real and reproducible, and the practical result stands. But we agree the causal framing needs that control, and we'd rather correct it in the open than argue it. Appreciate the push.

#9949. Anthropic tiptoes into MS Office territory

Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data artifact types bring Claude closer to a productivity suite

Anthropic has introduced three new types of artifacts that show the company tiptoeing into the office productivity market long dominated by Microsoft and Google.

On Tuesday, the Claudefather announced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, and promised the imminent arrival of Claude Meetings. These artifact types join existing ones – Docs, Slides, Design, and Motion – to form a nascent Claude-dependent productivity suite.

Anthropic initially used the term artifacts to refer to shareable AI-based interactive tools, like dynamic charts. But the scope of the term has been stretched to cover specific artifact types, which refer to what traditionalists might take to mean files associated with specific hosted applications.

"An artifact is anything Claude makes for you that you'd put in front of someone: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard, or a small interactive tool," the company explains.

The key thing that distinguishes an artifact from a file is that users are meant to interact with artifacts through Claude, rather than storing and transferring them independently. Think of it more as a container or managed object that opens in Claude (via a sharing URL), because artifacts in fact consist of various content types – .txt, .md, .html, .jsx, .svg, .pptx, .docx, .zip, .pdf, and .mp4, among others.

Anthropic's vision of Claude as a container for other applications goes beyond artifacts. The AI biz has also expanded its interactive connectors, which turn Claude into a landlord for other software applications. Its own promotional video for the feature hammers that point home in its title: "Your apps have moved into Claude."

"Starting today, partners can embed their apps directly in Claude, so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, and others without switching tabs," Anthropic said. "Plugins from Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) come with built-in skills, so sellers can prep for a call, accountants can analyze financial data, and HR teams can handle time off and expenses."

In a prior era, those would be fighting words. Tech companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft have worked for years to maintain their positions as platform landlords. Anthropic's invitation to become a Claude tenant ought to set off competition alarm bells. But perhaps with LLMs being able to re-create other people's apps on demand, there's less interest in defending app boundaries as if they were moats to keep out rivals. With AI, the call is coming from inside the house.

Alongside the rollout of Claude Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data, Anthropic is pushing the notion that Claude is useful for people working outside of computation and mathematics, the occupational category that, according to the company's own data, accounts for a larger share of Claude usage than any other.

"Inside Anthropic, non-technical teams are starting to get as much out of Claude as our engineers," the biz insists, hauling out canned testimonials from the likes of Accenture and Datadog.

If Anthropic can demonstrate that there's an untapped market of non-coders who would welcome a Claude subscription, investors in the company's pending IPO will be glad to see it. ®

#9948. [$] Locking down hibernation for the winter

When a computer hibernates, the kernel writes the contents of memory to disk and then shuts the system down. Resuming from hibernation involves reading that data back into memory, and then having the kernel pick up where it left off. Unfortunately, the kernel does not have any way to know that the data it is reading back has not been tampered with, which is why lockdown, an optional kernel feature that attempts to prevent modifications to the running kernel, disables hibernation. Matthew Garrett, who has been working on lockdown for many years, has shared a patch set that aims to fix this problem. His solution must also protect against downgrade attacks (where an attacker reboots the computer with an older kernel version to bypass new protections), which complicates the implementation.

InfoQ Homepage News Google Releases Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics Control, Simulation, and Policy Improvement

Nov 09, 2026 2 min read

Google has released Gemini 4 Argon framing it as a general-purpose physical-reasoning model for robot control, Real2Sim scene construction, multimodal labeling of robot video, and iterative policy improvement, rather than as a single end-effector policy.

In the published prompts, Argon directs a Boston Dynamics Spot through a foot-pedal task after practice in a MuJoCo twin, steers a simpler arm with visual coordinates and HTTP motion primitives, and closes a loop with the Gemini Omni video world model. Real2Sim examples rebuild MuJoCo scenes from teleoperation video; labeling prompts annotate demonstration footage for behavior cloning. Google also reports synthesizing domain-randomized MuJoCo episodes from one RGB photo to fine-tune a vision-language-action policy, citing a rise from 56% to 75% success on the corresponding real setup.

Early practitioner reaction focused on simulation fidelity. Davin YC Dong commented on X:

Google's Argon robotics examples tune simulation twins against contact events as well as visuals. That is the part I'd inspect: a scene can look convincing while its objects behave incorrectly. For manipulation, matching what happens at contact matters as much as matching pixels.

Separately, a developer posting as pulpmatrix argued for source discipline around Video-to-Sim-to-Real claims circulating the same week:

Video-to-Sim-to-Real is real, documented in Google's Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics dev blog (MuJoCo twin, 87% ERQA). Cornhole isn't in it: no paper, no repo, no hit rate, and real throws calibrated the robot first.

Specialized vision-language-action systems such as OpenVLA-class policies, Physical Intelligence's π-family models, and NVIDIA GR00T with Isaac-oriented tooling optimize for action prediction under robot embodiments and typically rely on large teleoperation or simulation corpora. Scene-to-sim and generative world tools, World Labs-style reconstructions, NVIDIA DreamDojo-style action video, and Isaac Sim digital twins, emphasize environment synthesis or video prediction without necessarily owning the full control-and-QC loop shown in Google's prompts. Prior Google work such as Gemini Robotics-ER remains a related line for spatial perception and planning. For architecture reviews, the question is whether one frontier model plus heavy prompt harnesses displaces a pipeline of VLA, simulator, and labeler services.
