#9939. The Open ASR Leaderboard Adds Its First Global South Language

Voice Arena and Hugging Face partner to launch open ASR evaluation for Hindi and Indian English

Benchmarks decide what gets built. A model that scores well on the Open ASR Leaderboard gets adopted and iterated on, while capabilities the leaderboard does not measure tend not to improve. Much of the recent work on the leaderboard has gone into making the evaluation metrics more trustworthy:

All of that makes one number (WER) harder to game. It is still one number. A long line of work has shown that ASR error rates are not evenly distributed across the people using them. Racial disparities in automated speech recognition found commercial systems roughly twice as bad for Black speakers as for white speakers, and Quantifying Bias in Automatic Speech Recognition found further differences by gender, age and accent. None of that is visible on a leaderboard, and not because the leaderboard is hiding it. The test sets it runs on record what was said and almost nothing about who said it.

To address this gap, we introduce two evaluation sets to the Open ASR Leaderboard: Monsoon en-IN and Monsoon hi-IN. Hindi, spoken by more than half a billion people, is the first Indic language on a multilingual tab that currently covers only European languages. Each set is released as a public split, available for self-scoring, and a private split withheld to limit benchmark-specific optimisation. The four splits are speaker-disjoint, comprising 4,888 speakers, with 12 speaker attributes recorded for each.

A test set can only expose a failure mode it varies along. Most benchmarks are built from whatever audio was readily available. Monsoon was built to vary along nine axes: geography, age, gender, vocabulary, devices, acoustic environments, speech type, speech rate, and the existence of multiple valid transcripts for the same audio. Each is a way an aggregate WER can be right on average and wrong for a particular population.

Four splits, two languages, collected through one pipeline.

The data is sourced from unscripted dual-channel spontaneous conversations, with clips segmented from a single channel so that each clip carries one speaker. Along with the fields reported in the table, each clip also records occupation, education, marital status, income band, handset brand, current city and years in the current district.

Five clips from the public Indian English split, with the metadata each one carries:

29-year-old woman, West Tripura, Tripura. Student, samsung SM-G781B.

32-year-old woman, Satna, Madhya Pradesh. Unemployed, samsung SM-E146B.

22-year-old man, Rohtas, Bihar. Student, motorola moto g54 5G.

27-year-old woman, Warangal, Telangana. Unemployed, vivo V2247.

57-year-old man, Puducherry. Private job, Xiaomi M2006C3LI.

The English sets use standard string references, where the leaderboard's normaliser collapses most spelling variation. Hindi has far more of it, and no normaliser can resolve it, because the variants are not a fixed mapping between two conventions. The Hindi sets therefore ship a lattice: for each span of the transcript, a list of the spellings that are accepted as correct.

Monsoon is small measured in hours and large measured in speakers. That is the design, and it is where most of the value sits.

Speaker concentration and diversity beyond the fields above.

Three properties follow, and each is a claim about variance rather than volume.

No voice carries the score: The ten largest contributors account for between 2.8% and 6.8% of total duration, and more than half of all speakers appear exactly once. A result on Monsoon is an average over hundreds of distinct voices, not a small number of talkers recorded at length. Test sets of comparable duration are usually constructed the other way.

No region or handset carries it either: The Indian English public set draws on 428 native districts across 30 states and union territories; the Hindi sets, being a Hindi-belt language, concentrate more tightly but still span 202 and 295 districts. Recordings come from 315 to 582 distinct device models, with no single model exceeding 2.1% of segments in any subset. Corpora collected on standardised hardware overfit to one microphone response; this one cannot.

Indian English here is not one accent: This is English as it is spoken across the country, not the English of one region. All six zones are represented: in the public set, 35% of segments are contributed by southern speakers, 18% from the East, 18% from Central, 16% from the North and 11% from the West. The accent variation that follows from that spread is recorded in the metadata rather than asserted.

Monsoon ships 18 columns per segment, of which 12 are metadata, where most public ASR test sets ship an identifier, a transcript and a duration. Demographic fields are complete or near-complete; contributors consented to this use.

The two languages have different geographic shapes, and the shape is informative. The Hindi sets concentrate in the Hindi belt, with Uttar Pradesh accounting for roughly 40% of speakers, which is what a Hindi corpus sampled by population should look like. The Indian English sets are much flatter: no state exceeds 13%, and a third of speakers come from outside the eight largest. Public and private halves match closely on both.

Indian state boundaries were drawn along linguistic lines, so district and state carry real accent signal, which is why these fields are released rather than summarised away. Analysis of this kind has been reported at scale for Indian ASR: district-level error rates spanning roughly 4% to 44%, with underrepresented regions well behind the Hindi belt and the metros, plus disaggregation by audio quality, speaking rate, utterance duration, gender, age and device. Those runs were on a closed benchmark. Monsoon makes the same class of analysis possible on a public leaderboard test set.

Broad geographic coverage requires recruitment across hundreds of districts rather than longer sessions from fewer speakers, and distributed recruitment at this scale introduces failure modes that a smaller collection does not face: contributors gaming the task, played-back audio submitted as live speech, and inattentive annotation. Each is addressed by an explicit check.

Recruitment and recording: Contributors were recruited through the Voice Arena community, a global digital platform whose reach extends into the rural and semi-urban districts that speech corpora rarely cover. Pairs then recorded two-person conversations over a peer-to-peer interface, dual-channel, on assigned everyday topics. Contributors used their own handsets and their own connections. Many of those are low-end devices on unstable bandwidth, which is why that condition is present in the released audio rather than filtered out of it. Prospective contributors completed a language proficiency screening before being granted recording access, were compensated, and provided informed consent covering use in training and distribution. A per-speaker duration cap, calibrated per language to the population size and geographic distribution of its speakers, prevented a small number of prolific contributors from dominating a language or region; more than half of the speakers in these sets contribute exactly one segment.

Elicitation: Eliciting spontaneous speech at scale presents its own difficulty, as contributors tend to produce short and sparse responses without structured guidance. Each conversation was therefore seeded with an open-ended narrative cue and progressively revealed follow-up questions, spanning domains including travel, healthcare, agriculture, education and digital services, guiding the exchange toward extended description without scripting it. Candidate topics were generated with large language models, then reviewed and localised by native-speaker linguists.

Quality control: Every recording passed a set of gating checks prior to transcription. The spoken language was verified against the assigned language using language identification models trained on human-annotated data across more than 30 languages. Speaker gender was confirmed against the self-reported label using a dedicated classifier, applied as corroboration of the self-report rather than as a replacement for it. A further model distinguished genuine spontaneous conversation from pre-recorded or played-back audio. Signal-to-noise ratio estimation removed recordings degraded beyond intelligibility, while natural environmental background noise was deliberately preserved so that the acoustic realism of in-the-wild speech is retained. Recordings clearing these checks were segmented by voice activity detection, split at two seconds of continuous silence or at a fifteen-second soft cap closed at the next detected silence. Segmentation was applied independently per channel, so every segment is single-speaker and single-channel. Segments then passed a DNSMOS P.808 check.

Transcription: Reference transcripts are human work. A first draft was generated by internal ASR models trained on in-domain data, none of which appear on any public leaderboard, so no system evaluated on these sets contributed to the references it is scored against. Every subsequent stage was performed by native-speaking linguists under a five-level protocol built on a strict separation of labour, in which each correction round is followed by an independent verification round performed by a different annotator, so no linguist audits their own output. A linguist first corrects the draft segment by segment against the acoustic signal; a second re-verifies it and flags residual disagreements. Subsequent levels iterate this cycle with fresh annotators, progressively resolving ambiguous phonetic realisations, code-switching boundaries, named entities, and orthographic consistency across spelling variants. Numerals are written as words, so that the transcript corresponds directly to what was spoken. Segments still flagged at the final level were returned for re-transcription before admission. Annotator behaviour was monitored automatically throughout, flagging submissions containing characters outside the target script, unnatural character or word repetitions, and unusually low or high edit counts.

What follows is one example, run on the public Indian English split, to show the kind of evaluation the metadata makes possible. It is not the finding the sets exist to deliver; it is an illustration of what becomes answerable once every clip carries a speaker.

Eight models on the leaderboard land between 4.81 and 4.99 WER on this set. That is 0.18 points from best to worst, inside what five hours can resolve. Ranked on the corpus, they are the same model.

Grouping speakers by region tells a different story. Each speaker's native district is rolled up to its zonal council, the Ministry of Home Affairs grouping of Indian states, giving five well-sampled zones. openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo varies by 0.46 points across them. mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507, fourteen hundredths of a point behind it on the corpus, varies by 1.68, running 4.38 in the Central zone against 6.06 in the East. Two systems that are indistinguishable on the leaderboard differ almost fourfold in how much their accuracy depends on where the speaker is from.

Which zone is hardest is not fixed either. ibm-granite/granite-speech-3.3-2b is worst in the North, microsoft/VibeVoice-ASR-HF in the South, mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507 in the East. If a single region were simply harder to transcribe, every model would rank the zones the same way. They do not, which points at the models rather than the audio.

Region is one of twelve recorded attributes, and the zones above are a coarse rollup of 428 districts. The same breakdown runs on age, education, occupation and handset, and the released files carry everything needed to reproduce it. None of it is available for a test set that records only what was said.

English orthographic variation is bounded. British against American spelling, punctuation, casing, digits against words: a normaliser can map most of it to a single form, and the leaderboard's does. Hindi is not bounded in the same way. Everyday speech is heavily code-mixed, English-origin words have no settled Devanagari spelling, and compound forms are written joined or separated according to preference. A single phrase can have ten or more valid written forms, and no fixed mapping collapses them, because there is no canonical side to map to.

Scored with a single reference, WER rewards a system for producing the spelling the annotator happened to choose. Two systems that recognised the audio equally well can differ by several points on orthography alone.

The Hindi sets therefore ship a lattice: for each span of the transcript, the set of written forms accepted as correct. Building it is manual work. Candidate variants are drawn from multiple ASR transcripts of the same audio and expanded with language models, then native-speaker linguists decide which are valid for that utterance and prune the rest, so only forms consistent with what was said are admitted.

Thus, for Hindi we report the Orthographically-Informed Word Error Rate (OIWER), introduced by AI4Bharat, instead of WER. A hypothesis is aligned against the accepted set at each span, so any admitted form counts as correct and only genuine recognition errors are charged.

To quantify the effect, the same hypotheses were scored twice. Flattening each lattice to its first variant per span yields a single string reference of the kind a conventional benchmark provides; any of the admitted variants would serve equally well, and a different choice would yield a different reference. Scored against the flattened reference, error rates rise for every system, and they do not rise uniformly. Rankings change as a consequence. The figure below shows two pairs of systems that reverse order between the two references: under a single reference a system is rewarded in part for reproducing the annotator's orthography, whereas the lattice scores only recognition.

We also open source our implementation, voi-oiwer, so every result on these sets can be reproduced directly.

For the private splits, get your model on the Open ASR Leaderboard and the Hugging Face team will run the evaluation. As before, the process for adding a model to the leaderboard takes place on the Open ASR Leaderboard GitHub:

Indian-English joins the main leaderboard as Voice Arena Monsoon, in the default column set rather than as an opt-in toggle, so it contributes to the headline Average WER for every model. The private split feeds the aggregated Private (conversational) column alongside Appen and DataoceanAI data. The public and private Hindi appears in the Multilingual tab, where a model is ranked only if it supports every selected language, making that column a like-for-like comparison. Alternative, select "Hindi" from the "Language dataset breakdown" dropdown menu.

Hindi is a sharp case of a general problem. Any language written more than one way, spoken by people a benchmark has not sampled, carries both of the failures described here. These sets do not fix them. What they add is a way to see them: a test set on a leaderboard the field already watches, carrying enough about each speaker and each reference that a difference between two systems can be traced to who was talking and how they write it, instead of disappearing into one number.

These four sets are part of Monsoon, Voice Arena's broader dataset initiative for the Global South.

As such, we made the difficult decision to begin the process of transitioning all of our repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. If this is your idea, then I can understand your pov about (L)GPL and free software in general.

There are many projects with BSD/MIT licences that are successful and alive and some of them (like LLVM) have even significantly eroded their GPL competition.

Specifically, in LLVM's case, this is precisely because many companies have their internal forks and closed versions of LLVM and only give back the patches which doesn't affect their position regarding to their closed source versions, and can work with others' patches.

In other words, LLVM is one of the *ium projects (e.g. VSCode / VSCodium, Chrome/Chromium) as I call it. For example, IIRC, Intel moved their compiler suite under LLVM, but that version is not open source, either.

GCC suite is specifically designed at software level and licensed that way to prevent this.

Put in other terms, many projects are licensed with MIT to allow their developers to be hired by a company to create a career over that piece of code, and spread in software ecosystem to create a dependency to the developer responsible for the code.

Lastly, because of these dynamics, MIT is about developer freedom and GPL is about user freedom. I personally care about user freedom way more than developer freedom.

IIRC, Intel moved their compiler suite under LLVM, but that version is not open source, either.

IIUC, only the frontend is LLVM; the codegen backend is still whatever secret sauce Intel had before. Similar with all of the other LLVM-frontended compilers (IBM's compiler is also there now).

Most proprietary LLVM forks have custom (or at least somewhat tweaked) backends, but I'm familiar with several that also use custom frontends -- ie to maintain cmdline compatibility with older proprietary toolchains (And/or interop with snowflake file formats), integration into license managers, etc.

There seems to be some confusion as to why they've made this disruptive effort to relicense and I can guess, I have no particular knowledge of the situation, that their objection is to someone making a sloproom clone using their source code, but claiming the result under a different, proprietary, license as their own, and they believe that switching to the GPL gives them a lever to sue and put a stop to it. I think the reference to monetisation may refer to people who make money from LLMs. The models would be useless without the open source training data they use, and yet the code they make probably doesn't breach copyright. So you can make an argument that some of the value captured in token sales is due to the open code used for training data. On the other hand, there are good models which are open weight, meaning they can't be making any money from that training data, in the same way that you can't make much profit from a selling a GPL binary because anyone could build the source code. There is approximately infinite competition. Neither licence assign the author's copyright to anyone else. Both require attribution.

You want to: 1. Encourage open source development and create a community around the project 2. Have the project able to be used by the maximum number of others, including yourself, in any future software you want to write. 3. And, yes, explicitly including use in closed source products, potentially with unreleased downstream private changes. 4. Allow contributors to the open source version to get hired by companies working on said closed source product. With a common expectation being that there will also be upstream work done on company time. A community of people working on a bsd/mit licensed project often has this shape. So, what threatens it? Companies using it in closed source will not usually eliminate the upstream community, but instead helps fund it. So that's totally fine! Of course, there have been cases where a company takes over a project so thoroughly, and stops contributing upstream at all, ultimately causing the original project to die. That is a bad outcome. NOT because of the private use, but because of the death of the upstream community. And when a project is forked/relicensed into a GPL version, that is the same impact: the BSD licensed community for the project may become dead. All previous contributors to the BSD code then, suddenly, have a dead codebase on their hands. The desired restriction here really is: "use this software however you want, as long as you don't destroy the bsd-licensed upstream community". But I think that is really not realistically _possible_ to require via licensing, only to encourage via social factors.

The license requires: > The above copyright notice and this permission notice shall be included in all copies or substantial portions of the Software. The GPLv2 is quite a bit wordier, but it's basically the same idea: > [...] provided that you conspicuously and appropriately publish on each copy an appropriate copyright notice and disclaimer of warranty; keep intact all the notices that refer to this License and to the absence of any warranty [...] Neither license prevents rebranding (in my opinion it's a real weakness of free software licenses). Both require minimal attribution in the form of a copyright notice, but not more. Neither prevents aggressive monetization. I guess the GPL makes it easier to prove that some downstream is in fact based on the project, if they comply with the license and publish source code. But what are you going to do once you prove that? Issue a takedown? For what license violation? When it comes to LLM rewrites, perhaps the GPL is a bit clearer about applying to "a work based on the Program" even if it does not contain (as MIT puts it) "substantial portions of the Software". But I'm skeptical that there's a real legal difference. The main difference the GPL makes, of course, is that the Asahi project could theoretically incorporate changes from downstream back into the project. That is the GPL's reason for existing. But in this case, the Asahi project describes the downstream code as "lazily rewritten", as using "LLM assistance" (which the Asahi project bans), and as being prematurely-released copies of their "in-development" code. It really doesn't sound like they have any interest in using it. So I'm somewhat mystified what the GPL is supposed to accomplish. That said, I have no firsthand knowledge of the downstreams they're talking about.

When it comes to LLM rewrites, perhaps the GPL is a bit clearer about applying to "a work based on the Program" even if it does not contain (as MIT puts it) "substantial portions of the Software". But I'm skeptical that there's a real legal difference. The main difference the GPL makes, of course, is that the Asahi project could theoretically incorporate changes from downstream back into the project. That is the GPL's reason for existing. But in this case, the Asahi project describes the downstream code as "lazily rewritten", as using "LLM assistance" (which the Asahi project bans), and as being prematurely-released copies of their "in-development" code. It really doesn't sound like they have any interest in using it. So I'm somewhat mystified what the GPL is supposed to accomplish. That said, I have no firsthand knowledge of the downstreams they're talking about.

Modern Free Software licences now try to extend their grasp beyond copyright, and imho that is a BIG mistake. Neither patents, nor branding, are anything to do with copyright. And blocking re-branding would pretty much kill Free Software! If you can't rebrand then either (a) the only person able to distribute is the guy who originally wrote the project, or (b) anybody can modify the project but they have to keep the original name, and therefore they sink the project's reputation. Branding is your guarantee of "the genuine article". You NEED branding. You NEED trademarks. And you NEED to allow people to protect their reputation. Forcing people to remove your branding/trademarks from their derivative works is just normal honest business - it's NOT removing them that's dishonest. Cheers, Wol

I've seen some people go with MIT or BSD and then get annoyed at somebody building a proprietary project on top or not giving back, and this always confused me. If you see that as a problem, then use something stronger. It's weird for me to choose something permissive then expect people (and especially amoral organizations) to abide by some code of niceness. IMO if you expect people to reciprocate it's best to make it upfront and explicit.

IMO if you expect people to reciprocate it's best to make it upfront and explicit.

Does MIT allow forking without attribution? No, not it does not. You have to say that you are using code based on the MIT license. The requirement to attribute copyright reveals the original authors and the existance of the original project code. Does it allow you to "monetize without giving back"? Well, let's talk about that. The MIT license allows you to sell compiled binaries. So, "yes" to monetizing. The GPL also allows this. No difference. BOTH licenses require you to disclose whose code you are using because you have to attribute copyright to them. So your ability to monetize can be held in check by the "consumers" ability to compare what you are selling with the "free" alternative. In other words, you can only really "monetize" the value of what you provide above and beyond the MIT code you are using. If you are not adding any value, a "rational" consumer can choose the free alternative. The choice of GPL vs MIT does not really make much difference in terms of competing with forks that do not add any value. If you are just going to recompile the code and sell it, there is not that much difference between MIT and GPL really. If you are a fork, the GPL requires you to directly distribute the source code yourself. MIT does not require that. But MIT requires you to reveal that the MIT project (and code) exists so that people can go get it themselves from somebody else that is distributing it. In my view, there is not much difference when we are talking about just blanket copying a project and redistributing it or even trying to sell it. So, I must say, the concerns made by Asahi about low quality, low effort competition or peope trying to take their work to obscure origin or to restribute without attribution do not seem to be addressed at all by the change in license from MIT to GPL? So, what about "giving back"? This is where MIT and GPL do differ. The risk of permissive licenses is that the original project may lose popularity in head-to-head competition with rivals that are making changes and adding value that would make people choose the fork over the original. Whether this is ok or not is up to the original author of the code. Choosing MIT says that you are ok with this. If you are not, don't choose MIT. But be honest that your concern is more about popularity than it is about "freedom". Because it is only the stuff that your competitors are offering and you are not that puts you at a disadvantage. The GPL makes it harder for forks to compete. It does this by making it harder for them to add value on top of the project that will make them more attractive than the original project. It does not make it any harder for them to use the original code. See above. However, the "fork" has to make its "improvements" available to the orignal project as well. If those changes are valuable, the original project can incorporate them too. So, let's be clear. The choice of license between MIT and GPL is not really about the code you are placing under an Open Source license. That code is equally free and available to all in either case. The MIT code is perhaps even more "free" if we view the "permissive" nature as freedom. Both licenses require the code that already exists to be available and both licenses require that the users of the software know that the code is avaialble. The difference between the licenses comes into play when a fork adds changes on top of the original project. In GPL projects, those changes also have to be made available in source code form to both the users of the software and to the original source code project. With a permissive license like MIT, those changes do NOT have to be shared. The example given about WINE is instructive. The issue then was that CodeWeavers, a commercial WINE backer, did not like that Cedega (a competitor to CodeWeavers) was selling "improved" versions of WINE but not making their changes available to WINE and to CodeWeavers. It was not about the MIT code. It was about the "not MIT" code. As Asahi is non-commercial, it is less clear to me what damages they are trying to protect against here. Selling low-quality derivatives without attribution is no harder under either license. If that is what poeple are doing, they may well continue to do so, GPL or no GPL. What this change may protect against is to insulate Asahi from competition that actually IS adding value that they are not. But that is not the way they are framing it. A key consideration is that the users and the engineers may disagree on what "value" is. In particular, consider AI assissted changes on top of the original Asahi project. Users may like these changes and prefer the fork. There may be "value" in the eyes of users. But the Asahi devs may see these changes as "low value" if they think the code is low value or low effort (or low ethics depending on your view on AI). But how does a switch to GPL impact this case? If users are going to be attracted to forks that based on "AI slop" in the view of the Ashai devs, does the GPL help them? Are they going to incorporate these changes into Asahi? If not, how does the GPL help them? It may not. Perhaps what they are hoping for is to trap lazy competitors. If I make a "low effort" Ashai clone with additional AI features addded, I may be too lazy or too disorganized to comply with the GPL. The fact that I do not share my changes may make it easier for Asahi as a GPL violation is a clear-cut thing to try to enforce. But what is the remedy? If a low-effort fork pushes code to GitHub, does that change anything? We will see. Anwway, Asahi is an awesome project. They are doing amazing work and a lot of WORK. They can of course choose the license that suits them. My statements are questions are not meant to be negative towards the Asahi project in any way.

It was not about the MIT code. It was about the "not MIT" code. As Asahi is non-commercial, it is less clear to me what damages they are trying to protect against here. Selling low-quality derivatives without attribution is no harder under either license. If that is what poeple are doing, they may well continue to do so, GPL or no GPL. What this change may protect against is to insulate Asahi from competition that actually IS adding value that they are not. But that is not the way they are framing it. A key consideration is that the users and the engineers may disagree on what "value" is. In particular, consider AI assissted changes on top of the original Asahi project. Users may like these changes and prefer the fork. There may be "value" in the eyes of users. But the Asahi devs may see these changes as "low value" if they think the code is low value or low effort (or low ethics depending on your view on AI). But how does a switch to GPL impact this case? If users are going to be attracted to forks that based on "AI slop" in the view of the Ashai devs, does the GPL help them? Are they going to incorporate these changes into Asahi? If not, how does the GPL help them? It may not. Perhaps what they are hoping for is to trap lazy competitors. If I make a "low effort" Ashai clone with additional AI features addded, I may be too lazy or too disorganized to comply with the GPL. The fact that I do not share my changes may make it easier for Asahi as a GPL violation is a clear-cut thing to try to enforce. But what is the remedy? If a low-effort fork pushes code to GitHub, does that change anything? We will see. Anwway, Asahi is an awesome project. They are doing amazing work and a lot of WORK. They can of course choose the license that suits them. My statements are questions are not meant to be negative towards the Asahi project in any way.

So, I must say, the concerns made by Asahi about low quality, low effort competition or peope trying to take their work to obscure origin or to restribute without attribution do not seem to be addressed at all by the change in license from MIT to GPL? So, what about "giving back"? This is where MIT and GPL do differ. The risk of permissive licenses is that the original project may lose popularity in head-to-head competition with rivals that are making changes and adding value that would make people choose the fork over the original. Whether this is ok or not is up to the original author of the code. Choosing MIT says that you are ok with this. If you are not, don't choose MIT. But be honest that your concern is more about popularity than it is about "freedom". Because it is only the stuff that your competitors are offering and you are not that puts you at a disadvantage. The GPL makes it harder for forks to compete. It does this by making it harder for them to add value on top of the project that will make them more attractive than the original project. It does not make it any harder for them to use the original code. See above. However, the "fork" has to make its "improvements" available to the orignal project as well. If those changes are valuable, the original project can incorporate them too. So, let's be clear. The choice of license between MIT and GPL is not really about the code you are placing under an Open Source license. That code is equally free and available to all in either case. No, MIT license do not require to disclose your code, it only mandates to preserve attribution and the legal notice. But if you change just the 10% of the code and leave the remaining 90% unchanged then you can keep all the source private as long as you give attribution of the remaining part.

If you leave 90% of MIT code unchanged, you have to tell me who write it. Which means you have disclosed it to me. I can go get it. That is my point. You can keep your copy private but the public code does not disappear and you have to make me aware of it. The Open Source code does not go anywhere. I can still use it. I can still study it. I can still modify it. All you can keep private are your 10% of changes. In my view, "you can keep all the source private" leads people to totally misunderstand what has happened. When many people talk of "stealing the code", they act like the original Open Source code has somehow disappeared or become less open. It has not.

In my view, "you can keep all the source private" leads people to totally misunderstand what has happened. When many people talk of "stealing the code", they act like the original Open Source code has somehow disappeared or become less open. It has not.

I've looked at the MIT license text, and I don't see a useful attribution requirement; if I tell you that some part of the code in my product is © 2026 Meta Platforms Inc, and used under the MIT license, how do you go from that to the code I used?

I don't have to tell you how much of my code is from the original, just provide the copyright notice and the MIT license text. And that means that you've got fun ahead of you working out which bits are likely to come from one of the 185 repositories Meta publish on GitHub, and which bits are mine; noting, of course, that it's possible that it's code that Meta no longer publishes on GitHub for whatever reason.

I don't think the second part is true. Yes GPL requires providing source code to those who receive binaries but it does not, according to my understanding, require providing the code to the original project. Of course it also disallows forbidding recipients of the binary and source from providing the source to others. So if a commercial "imprroved" Ashai were made under the GPL Ashai would not automatically get the modifications. But anyonoe who purchased a copy of it would get the source code and would be allowed to share it with Ashai.

So if a commercial "imprroved" Ashai were made under the GPL Ashai would not automatically get the modifications. But anyonoe who purchased a copy of it would get the source code and would be allowed to share it with Ashai.

1. Work with a qualified lawyer (aka specializes in software licensing ) on what the problem is and what the solutions could be 2. Follow the lawyer’s advice on how to relicense things. 3. Work with the lawyer on how to announce and describe the issue. There can be specific reasons why a specific license is seen as 'stronger' in different countries or court systems to get the effects you are wanting. [Attribution can mean different things in different countries and some court systems may like X license over Y license for some obscure reason that the lawyers can make clear.] This is probably something that should be on the list early in any project. Even if you are going to select MIT-0 or BSD-0 , getting an idea of why you are doing this and what you can expect as benefits or trouble is good.

#9937. GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

The supply chain attack campaign's shift toward developer endpoints and cloud access signals what could be next for the cybercrime outfit.

A new wave of GhostAction attacks has largely failed, but this supply chain campaign operator is well-positioned to cause more chaos down the line.

GhostAction, an ongoing campaign in which attackers target GitHub by compromising developer accounts and injecting GitHub Actions workflow files into repositories.

Workflows tell GitHub Actions what code to execute when events occur (such as when a commit is pushed or a pull request is opened); these malicious workflows rely on GitHub's high trust in these files (by design), seizing repository secrets, package publishing tokens, GitHub personal access tokens, credentials embedded in source code, and much more.

The idea is that an initial compromise could be leveraged into more compromises and access points across repositories, CI/CD systems, and cloud environments, not unlike many supply chain worms observed in the wild lately, albeit functioning differently.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

The campaign was first documented last year, and attackers continue to deploy GhostAction against organizations. What has changed is an apparent escalation of the technique beginning this month. During an earlier Oct. 8-12 wave, attackers pushed the security-audit.yml workflow into roughly 30,000 repositories, using compromised accounts to distribute credential-stealing code at scale. But GitGuardian on Oct. 27 published research highlighting further escalation. GitGuardian's Gaetan Ferry wrote that between Oct. 13 and 21, GhostAction's operator "pushed 72,000 commits to 23,000 public repositories," noting that 8,000 of them were new targets.

During this latest wave of the campaign, GitGuardian observed that once a developer account is compromised, the operator would deploy different payloads depending on which runner the repositories were hosted on. Runners are the systems that execute GitHub Actions workflows. Many organizations use GitHub-hosted runners, while others configure self-hosted runners that run inside their own environments.

These payloads include one called "seven workflows," which searches GitHub runner repositories and wikis for credentials including AI-provider API keys; the "Security-audit.yml" file seen in earlier GhostAction attacks that searches GitHub-hosted source code and Git history for credentials; self-hosted runner payloads targeting self-hosted CI runners; a payload targeting GitHub runners and AWS-requesting GitHub OIDC tokens (in order to assume AWS roles and achieve cloud account access); and the font stealer payload, which is the most notable workflow payload seen in recent attacks, due to its provenance.

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

The font stealer family installs a Node.js credential stealer on local developer machines, disguised as a VS Code task. The technique appears to be copied from PolinRider, a campaign that hides obfuscated loaders in developer repositories to steal credentials and has been associated with North Korea. The attacker also added PolinRider loaders between Oct. 22 and 26 to repositories already impacted by GhostAction. Ferry says that out of the five payloads, only the PolinRider-styled local stealer had a chance to successfully run, but GitGuardian has no evidence that any run actually occurred.

GitGuardian could not assess whether there was overlap between GhostAction and PolinRider, but hypothesized that GhostAction's operator possibly copied a public PolinRider launcher in order to target an overlapping set of victims.

Jenn Gile, cofounder of OpenSourceMalware (which previously covered the GhostAction attacks this month and detected signs of the PolinRider copycat a few weeks ago), tells Dark Reading that the PolinRider clone illustrates some of the inner workings of the GhostAction group.

"What we're seeing looks like imitation, not evolution. The fake-font technique in GhostAction is a copy of what DPRK's PolinRider campaign has been using nearly all of 2026," she says in an email. "The multiple payloads are real, but they're variations on a theme (five workflow versions over about ten days in one repo we examined), not a new capability. Historically, we might have called this evolution because it took real skill to figure out. But this looks a lot like an LLM helping the threat actor test different variants."

Related:Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

All of that said, GitHub identified and prevented execution of the malicious workflows, GitGuardian noted. However, importantly, the attackers still demonstrated persistent access to nearly 1,800 compromised accounts, many of which had already been used in earlier GhostAction activity; "1,382 of the 1,792 compromised accounts had already been used on Oct. 8, so the same stolen tokens keep working," according to Ferry.

Ferry tells Dark Reading that the campaign has been "highly ineffective on the malicious workflows side." But even if there's no sign this wave succeeded, the nature of the payloads (such as the one aimed at gaining cloud access) also shows where the attackers may intend to pivot next, toward internal networks where there are fewer platform-level protections that could thwart their efforts.

"We expect new waves to appear in the near future, with revised payloads," he explains. "This 'fail early and adapt fast' strategy has already been observed for this threat actor."

Given that targeted accounts or repositories remain compromised, repo owners should look for and delete the files that GitGuardian lists in the IoC section of the blog, on every branch. And, if signs of compromise are detected, users should revoke the account's tokens across the board and rotate every credential committed in the affected repository or its history, as well as every Actions secret and wiki credential.

#9936. Introducing @huggingface/kernels: 200+ WebGPU Kernels for Local AI

One of our biggest goals on the WebAI team at Hugging Face is to make browser inference as fast and as user-friendly as possible. Getting there is a multi-layer effort: models need browser-friendly representations, runtimes need to build efficient execution plans, and the individual GPU operations at the bottom of the stack need to make the most of many different devices and browser implementations.

Today, we are releasing the first layer of that effort: @huggingface/kernels, a minimal library for loading and running optimized WebGPU kernels from the Hugging Face Hub, together with an initial collection of 207 kernels at huggingface.co/webgpu-kernels.

The collection covers operations used across a wide variety of machine learning architectures and workloads. More importantly, each kernel is published as a complete, versioned package: its interface, shader templates, correctness cases, benchmark cases, and usage instructions all live together on the Hub.

We are also launching Fleet, an in-browser GPU benchmarking and testing suite that runs and scores the kernels on your hardware. Beyond the results for your own machine, Fleet gives the community a way to contribute performance and correctness evidence from devices we could never cover in a conventional test lab. With your consent, every run adds private evidence that can help us find failures (incorrect results, pathologically slow cases, etc.), improve kernel variants, and make better optimization decisions across real-world hardware.

A model running in the browser eventually becomes a sequence of GPU operations: matrix multiplications, normalizations, convolutions, attention primitives, quantization operations, data-layout transformations, and many more. WebGPU makes these operations available across modern browsers through a portable API, while WGSL provides a common language for the shaders that execute them.

Portability, however, does not automatically mean performance. Two shaders can implement the same operation and produce the same output while behaving completely differently across different accelerators. Workgroup sizes, memory access patterns, vectorization, data types, and fusion strategies can all affect performance. The best choice can also change with the input shape, device, browser, and available WebGPU features.

This is why kernels form a foundational layer of fast browser inference. Higher-level runtimes can only be as efficient as the operations they dispatch. By making those operations individually discoverable, testable, benchmarkable, and versioned, we can improve the foundation independently while keeping a stable contract for the layers above it.

Each kernel in the collection has its own repository and kernel card. The card documents the operation's semantics, inputs, outputs, attributes, supported data types, source files, and a ready-to-run @huggingface/kernels example.

For example, ai.onnx.Add implements elementwise addition with multidirectional broadcasting. It is one of the simplest operations in a neural network, used everywhere from residual connections to adding a bias. Its card documents the two inputs, the broadcasted output shape, supported data types, and the variants available for different shapes and devices.

Behind the card, the repository contains the artifacts needed to understand and evaluate the implementation:

This structure turns a shader into a reusable software artifact. The interface is inspectable without reading WGSL, correctness and performance cases travel with the implementation, and published versions can be loaded explicitly rather than depending on an unversioned file URL. Our kernels can also serve as reference implementations for developers building custom WebGPU kernels or integrating these operations into their own runtimes.

Running these kernels requires a browser with WebGPU support. WebGPU availability depends on the browser, operating system, GPU, and driver. You can check for it in JavaScript with "gpu" in navigator.

@huggingface/kernels provides the bridge between a kernel repository and your application. Call getKernel with a Hub repository ID and a contract version, then invoke the returned function with typed input data and tensor shapes. Here is a small bias-add example:

The second input is broadcast across the first dimension, producing an output with shape [2, 3]. The loader derives that output shape and logical data type from the manifest contract and the inputs, then allocates c automatically.

Addition on six floats is deliberately the smallest possible demo. At this size, the GPU round trip costs far more than the math. The point is the call pattern: it stays exactly the same for the heavyweight operations where optimized kernels actually pay off, such as matrix multiplication (ai.onnx.MatMul). Only the repository ID and the inputs change.

Even this elementary operation illustrates why kernels need variants. Equal-shape addition can use a direct vectorized path, while broadcasted inputs need different indexing logic. The published Add kernel includes variants for equal shapes, vectorized broadcasting, scalar processing, and general broadcasting. The runtime can select an implementation that fits the current call and device without changing the application-facing API.

The version: 1 option selects version 1 of the published kernel contract. It is separate from an ONNX opset, an operator's since_version, or a model revision. Keeping those concepts separate lets applications depend on a stable JavaScript-facing contract while kernel implementations evolve behind it.

So, how much of a difference do optimized kernels actually make? We put our collection head-to-head with ORT WebGPU on an Apple M4 GPU, using ONNX Runtime Web 1.30.0-dev.20260826-b1f76d586a. We started with 1,756 test cases across all 207 operations and kept the 809 cases where both sides produced matching outputs and reliable timings.

Across those comparisons, our kernels were 2.57x faster by geometric mean and 1.90x faster at the median, with 629 wins, 176 losses, and 4 ties. Here is a closer look at four familiar operations:

Some individual wins were much bigger. A particularly difficult bilinear Einsum case (i,ij,j with size 4096) ran in 0.136 ms with our kernel versus 1,396 ms with ORT WebGPU: more than 10,000x faster. A row-wise CumSum over [256, 4096] was 301x faster, at 0.016 ms versus 4.784 ms. These are unusual cases rather than the speedups you should expect everywhere, but they show how much a specialized kernel can help when a general implementation hits a slow path.

We timed the work done on the GPU itself, leaving out setup such as loading kernels, creating sessions, uploading inputs, compiling shaders, and reading outputs back. Very short workloads are naturally harder to measure, and small cases can benefit from the GPU cache, so these numbers are best read as a useful comparison rather than a promise for every application.

They are also results for individual operations, not complete models. Exact performance will change across GPUs and browsers, which is why Fleet is so important for building a broader picture.

We are also working with the ONNX Runtime team to upstream these improvements so they can benefit the broader ONNX Runtime Web ecosystem.

WebGPU performance varies across GPUs, browsers, and drivers, so results from one machine only tell part of the story. Fleet lets anyone run correctness and performance checks in the browser and see how the kernels behave on their hardware.

With consent, each run privately contributes evidence that helps us spot device-specific failures, compare variants, and improve selection rules. The goal is simple: use broad, real-world coverage to make the kernels faster and more reliable for everyone.

The initial 207 kernels are a starting point, not the end state. Publishing kernels independently on the Hub gives us a common place to inspect contracts, compare implementations, reproduce correctness checks, and improve performance without embedding every shader directly into every runtime.

The collection is also part of the Hub's broader kernel ecosystem: on the Kernels page, the WebGPU kernels sit alongside kernels for CUDA, ROCm, Metal, and other platforms, and can be filtered, sorted, and explored like any other artifact on the Hub.

This is the low-level foundation for the next steps in our browser inference stack. We are excited to connect these kernels to higher-level model tooling, continue expanding operation coverage, and make fast local inference easier to use across the WebAI ecosystem.

Explore the WebGPU kernel collection, try @huggingface/kernels, and join the Fleet to contribute evidence from your device and help us make the kernels better for everyone.

The Fleet part may matter as much as the kernels. The 809 comparable cases on an M4 are useful, but browser, driver and device variance is where WebGPU tends to get painful. Will Fleet eventually expose per-device distributions, or is the plan to use the runs only for aggregate selection rules?

In an automated build system, I could see per device kernels, made more interesting by fusion of ops.

The area that obviously needs more attention are the 947 tests that did not result in reliable output. This could be the test, it could be that the ORT WebGPU is wrong, or the new kernel is wrong, or the test harness had issues, hard to know from the outside. Perhaps the Fleet thing is meant to improve this.

Very excited to see such attention at making WebGPU first class in ML!

@sroussey Agreed—the excluded 947 need a taxonomy before the 2.57× summary can travel. I'd want counts by operation and device for unsupported, ORT mismatch, new-kernel mismatch, and harness/timeout, with raw failing cases downloadable. Then Fleet can optimize only within a proven-correct compatibility envelope; fusion and per-device tuning become much safer.

Excellent! This will help our WebAI community continue developing highly optimized solutions. Many thanks @Xenova and @nico-martin for the great work you have been doing.

#9935. Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Researchers can't quite explain why cyber threats look so different in Italy compared with everywhere else.

To read this article in Italian, click here!

Italy is suffering from a disproportionately large number of cyberattacks, new data suggests. Not only that: The kinds of attacks hitting organizations in the country are vastly different from those hitting other places. Researchers have a triad of theories as to why.

It's true that certain regions and countries face greater cyber-risk thanks to economic, military, and political factors. Israel is a magnet for hacktivists and regional, state-aligned advanced persistent threats (APTs). Brazil's unique history makes it a hive of banking Trojans. The United States economy will always draw the most attention from scammers. It isn't so obvious, though, why Italy is such a popular mark for cybercriminals.

"One of the main reasons why we decided to look into the Italian threat landscape is because Italy kept appearing at the top of our stats in our monthly internal reports," says Gianluca Tiepolo, cybercrime analyst at Intel471. In a report shared exclusively with Dark Reading ahead of its release, Intel471 found that Italy is a total outlier in the global cyber threat landscape. Organizations there are being compromised at a rate beyond what one would reasonably expect, based on the country's size, economy, and politics. And exploits against vulnerabilities and Web infrastructure are far more common in Italy than elsewhere.

Related:L’Italia è afflitta da vulnerabilità informatiche, senza una causa chiara

"We wanted to understand what was driving those stats," Tiepolo says. In the end, though, the data paints a nearly inexplicable picture of what's going on in the land of pasta and Chianti.

Italy is the 25th largest country in the world but, according to this new data, its organizations make up about 7% of all initial access data sold on cybercriminal forums. That's second only to the United States (30%) globally. Italy also ranks fourth among countries most targeted by ransomware.

Far stranger still are the types of cyber intrusions affecting organizations in Italy. According to the new data, initial access brokers (IABs) obtained their initial foothold through vulnerabilities in 57% of cases. Credentials only explained 23% of cases. Meanwhile, IABs have been selling access to victim-owned Web infrastructure in 49% of cases, with remote access and remote desktop tools making up 26% of cases.

So what? Maybe those figures don't pop off the page. Now, though, let's compare them with Intel471's own data from its 2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook report:

Globally in 2025, IABs targeted remote access and remote desktop tools 67% of the time — 41% more often, relatively, than in Italy. Meanwhile, Web infrastructure — by far the most at-risk asset in Italy — represented such a small fraction of Intel471's global data that it didn't even bother to cite it in their report.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

In the same vein, according to the company's global data, credential-based attacks are eight times more common in general than any other type of attack today. It found that 49% of IAB listings advertised credentials as the attack type, compared to 23% in the Italian-specific data. And guffaw-ingly, whereas in Italy they represent around 57% of all attacks, exploited vulnerabilities showed up in only 6.5% of cases globally.

Though cybersecurity data reporting can be interpreted in different ways depending on the circumstance, Italy does seem like a kind of cyber-risk unicorn, Tiepolo says, adding that Italy has been falling behind on cyber readiness for a long time now.

"I'm Italian," he says. "I've been working with a lot of different Italian clients. What I can say is that Italy is probably slightly behind other European countries, simply based on security technology [adoption]. For example, endpoint detection and response (EDR) technologies became popular in Italy around 2020–2021. Before 2020, most Italian companies didn't use EDR technology. So maybe historically, Italy is a bit behind in actually investing in cybersecurity products and technologies."

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

Also, opportunistic cybercriminals are exploiting known, widespread, and often quite old vulnerabilities en masse to scoop up more victims in Italy than in other countries. "The data we saw last week from PHP2Shell, I think, validates this assessment. Italy is the country in Europe with the largest number of PHP 4, 5, and 7 versions, which are end-of-life," Tiepolo notes.

"A full 90% of initial access offers for Italy are what we call 'wholesale' offers," he posits. "They're not offers that are targeting Italy specifically, but simply exploiting vulnerabilities. Our assessment is that Italy is probably slower than other countries in patching their systems."

Another, related possibility is that Italy finds itself victim to a kind of cyber vulnerability network effect. The logic goes something like this: If certain technologies are especially common in a country like Italy, and organizations are slow to address vulnerabilities in those technologies, then that country becomes an attractive economy of scale.

As Intel471 wrote in its report, "Once an actor develops an effective exploitation method, the actor can apply that method to additional exposed systems without conducting a separate, extensive reconnaissance effort against each organization. This reduces the effort required to compromise businesses whose size or profile might otherwise offer limited incentive for a dedicated intrusion."

Researchers couldn't say exactly which technologies, vulnerabilities, or exploitations this theory might refer to, but noted that it does fold into the finding that 90% of initial access offerings to Italian organizations online are sold in bulk.

Without co-signing Intel471's data or conclusions specifically, representatives from the Milan-based cybersecurity firm Cleafy tell Dark Reading that they've observed broadly similar patterns.

"Our threat research does point to a related pattern: attackers reusing tools, infrastructure and techniques to scale campaigns across Italian banking targets," the company wrote via email. It pointed to cases such as the drIBAN Web injection kit, which attackers used to exploit the Certified Electronic Mail (PEC) system used widely across Italy. Cases like drIBAN "don't establish that Italy has a disproportionately large initial-access market, but they do illustrate how reusable attack techniques and infrastructure can help cybercriminals scale operations across multiple targets."

There is one other, potentially significant contributing factor to why Italy looks so different from other countries in cyberattack datasets: its prevalence of small businesses.

Most businesses everywhere are small, but, at least in comparison to other advanced economies, it's especially the case in Italy. A May 2024 "data snapshot for Italy" by McKinsey found that "MSMEs" — micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises — contributed roughly 10% more to Italy's economy and employment compared to their relative share in other advanced economies. And last March, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) published a report that cited that 99.9% of Italian firms in 2023 were SMEs, and 94.8% were micro-enterprises.

"Italy has a lot of small and medium-sized companies," Tiepolo says. "One of the things that came out from the data — especially the extortion data — is that these groups are [disproportionately] targeting small- and medium-sized businesses. So this could be one of the reasons [Italy stands out] in comparison to other countries that have more large companies."

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.
