#9890. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

#9889. PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Organizations in the region face growing cyberattacks from the known India-linked threat group, which leverages legitimate Windows functionality in three distinct attack chains.

A known South Asian cyber-espionage group has been targeting organizations across the region with attacks designed to compromise Windows systems, establish persistence, and give attackers remote control over infected machines using custom malware.

The attacks, attributed "with high confidence" to the South Asian threat group known as Bitter (aka TA397), involve three distinct infection chains and demonstrate the group's expanding malware capabilities, according to new research from FortiGuard Labs published today.

Bitter, one of several threat groups linked to India, has been active since at least 2013 and has historically targeted government, energy, and engineering organizations. The group is known for using tailored attack campaigns to gain persistent access to victim networks, collect information, and maintain remote control over compromised systems.

At the center of the latest threat campaign is PapRAT, a custom remote access Trojan (RAT) that gives attackers extensive control over compromised Windows systems, including the ability to execute commands, manipulate files, capture screenshots, and download additional payloads, according to FortiGuard Labs.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

"This campaign illustrates how Bitter combines native Windows tools with custom malware to establish and maintain access to targeted systems," Cara Lin, a FortiGuard Labs threat researcher, wrote in the post.

Bitter has recently revamped PapRAT from a C++ code base to Rust, expanding its functionality in the process from eight commands to 11, according to the report. Additional capabilities in the latest version include PowerShell execution, a sleep directive, and a clean-exit command.

"PapRAT's C++ and Rust implementations indicate continued investment in Bitter's toolset," Lin wrote.

Indeed, attackers have increasingly adopted Rust for malware development for various reasons, including its cross-platform development capabilities and potential evasion advantages.

The latest updates to PapRAT also underscore the importance of certain defensive measures, including "monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures," Lin wrote.

Researchers observed three distinct attack chains being used by Bitter, all of which exploit legitimate Windows functionality to disguise malicious behavior.

These tactics demonstrate "how advanced cyberespionage operations deliberately abuse native system tools to evade traditional endpoint detection," notes Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

The first attack chain uses a malicious LNK file that abuses the native Windows ftp.exe utility to execute scripts and create scheduled tasks that maintain contact with the attackers' command-and-control (C2) server.

The second uses a VHDX disk image containing an LNK file that opens a decoy spreadsheet while silently launching an MSI installer to deploy PapRAT.

The third attack begins with a URL shortcut that retrieves an LNK file through WebDAV, leading to an MSI installer that deploys PapRAT. In this chain, PapRAT also delivers WmRAT, a secondary implant previously documented by other researchers, according to FortiGuard Labs.

"By co-opting native Windows utilities like ftp.exe and scheduled tasks to establish initial command-and-control communication, threat actors operate within trusted administrative channels before deploying custom malware," Barney observes. "When an intrusion leverages trusted system processes, signature-based controls simply have nothing to alert on."

This so-called "hybrid tradecraft," which combines legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware, requires organizations to focus on strict privilege boundaries and identity security rather than relying on endpoint signatures alone as part of a comprehensive defense strategy, Barney says.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

To defend against these attacks, organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages, Lin recommended in the post.

"Combining user awareness with controls that detect suspicious execution chains and outbound C2 traffic can help limit exposure to campaigns that blend legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware," she wrote.

The third attack chain is particularly problematic for defenders because removing PapRAT from compromised systems may not eliminate the attacker's access, observes Jason Soroko, senior fellow at Sectigo.

This means defenders need to look deeper into their systems "to check what else was installed and identify scripts and scheduled tasks that could keep fetching commands," he says. A comprehensive recovery effort must look beyond the file that triggered the original alert to identify any additional payloads, persistence mechanisms, or other components of the compromise.

She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. #9887. Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

The latest "Digital Defense Report" identifies government agencies as prime targets for AI attacks, but it doesn't mention that they are broadly being targeted through Microsoft bugs.

AI is changing cybersecurity. The hope is that software will eventually ship with fewer vulnerabilities, while the expectation in the meantime is that vendors will issue eye-popping volumes of software patches as a result of using AI to identify flaws in existing products. Software customers will increasingly use AI to more effectively and efficiently protect their networks. These promising developments will take time to unfold, as vendors and their customers learn how to incorporate AI into their software development and cybersecurity risk management workflows.

Attackers, meanwhile, are already using AI to generate novel attacks and orchestrate increasingly complex and large-scale hacking campaigns. AI is already enabling criminal groups to achieve hacking successes normally reserved for patient, highly resourced nation-state threat actors. And nation-state threat actors are using AI to increase the scale and sophistication of their cyber operations. The threat level is rising at an alarming rate.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

Microsoft flagged the impacts of AI on cybersecurity in its recently released "2026 Digital Defense Report." Among its findings, it assessed that government agencies and services were the most affected by cyber threats and frequently targeted for nation-state activity.

Microsoft's report has a major blind spot, however: the impact of legacy software, especially its own, on organizations' cyber-risk. Legacy software will remain the substrate of organizations' attack surface for the foreseeable future. Vendors need to up their security game, and their customers need to demand better security from their vendors, particularly as AI heightens the threat landscape.

For example, with an 85% market share, Microsoft is the most dominant player in the US public sector productivity software market. Its products are therefore a prime target for state-sponsored groups seeking access to US government agencies and the data and secrets they are charged with protecting. So we should expect attackers to prize vulnerabilities in Microsoft's products and devote a substantial proportion of their hacking efforts to these popular products.

But there is more to the story than Microsoft's sheer prevalence in federal IT. Microsoft's grip on the federal IT market exposes the US government to a disproportionate share of cyber vulnerabilities. According to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Microsoft accounts for nearly 16% of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) so far this year — the most of any company. Microsoft accounts for nearly 23% of known exploited vulnerabilities from November 2021 (when CISA began tracking KEVs) to October 2026.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

By comparison, the next-highest vendor, Cisco, is responsible for approximately 7% in 2026 and 6% total, less than half of Microsoft's share.

Some agencies even rely on Microsoft as their single software vendor. This isn't particularly surprising — Microsoft has a track record of locking customers into its ecosystem by bundling its cloud computing offerings with office and security products (bundling is one area of focus of the Federal Trade Commission’s ongoing antitrust investigation into Microsoft) and then making it too difficult or costly for customers to switch vendors.

In 2023, the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) discontinued its Data Loss Prevention program after moving to bundle security tools into a sole-source Microsoft enterprise license. The move reportedly put 18 million veterans' personal records at risk of leakage. The VA has now moved to reverse course by seeking alternatives to Microsoft, having recognized the consequences of a Microsoft monoculture. Lesson learned.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

Microsoft's Digital Defense Report identifies how frequently government agencies are affected by cyber threats and targeted for nation-state activity. Microsoft knows this firsthand. Since 2023, Chinese state-sponsored actors have compromised Microsoft products in at least two significant instances, accessing over two dozen US government agencies' emails in one attack and compromising at least seven agencies in another in July 2025.

Russian state-backed actors have also exploited Microsoft's weak security at least three times since 2020, including the infamous SolarWinds attack and an operation to exfiltrate emails between Microsoft personnel and government agencies. US government officials and advisory bodies have concluded that these breaches were preventable and caused by Microsoft's negligence. The reach and severity of breaches will only grow as China, Russia, and other nation-state threat actors become AI-native and AI tools become increasingly sophisticated.

Microsoft deserves some credit for using AI to evaluate products it has already deployed: its record-setting Patch Tuesday count of 974 vulnerabilities disclosed last month is no doubt the result of using AI to identify flaws. But that's not good enough.

All software vendors, including Microsoft, should invest more in the security of their products before they are released, even if it comes at the expense of slowing the rollout of new product features. And they should all be transparent to customers about these processes to enable customers to make more informed purchasing decisions. Otherwise, Microsoft's "2027 Digital Defense Report" will paint an even darker picture of the threat environment.

Director of the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance, Stanford University

Andrew Grotto founded and directs the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance at Stanford University's Center for International Security and Cooperation. He serves as the faculty lead for the Cyber Policy and Security specialization in Stanford’s master’s in international policy program, where he teaches courses on cyber policy and economic statecraft. He is also a visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution. Previously, he was senior advisor to the Secretary of Commerce for technology policy during the Obama administration and Senior Director for Cyber Policy on the National Security Council in the Obama and Trump administrations. He advises technology companies on digital risks, including companies that compete with Microsoft.

#9885. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

#9883. The hardest tarball

Personal and work related blogof Harmen Stoppels.

Open source software developerat Stoppels Consultingin Zürich, Switzerland.

Find me on GitHubor send me an email atfirstname[at]lastname.ch

Here is a curiosity: an archive that can be constructed using a single GNU tar invocation, that is extracted in 8 distinct ways depending on what tool you use.

It creates an archive hardest.tar from three files file ./file empty in sequence, where file is repeated so that GNU tar stores the second one as a hard link, and empty is empty. Exploiting the unique path of the second entry, the hard link is renamed to cafÃ©. This triggers tar to create a pax header to store the file name as UTF-8. We add a size=512 record to the pax header, which overrides the default size=0 from the hard link. The value 512 is not a coincidence: it is exactly the size of a tar header.

Visually, this archive has the following structure, with two basic interpretations based on whether a hard link can have a size or not.

Now, POSIX says that data blocks for a hard link “may be included” in pax archives, but the implications of this are not entirely clear. So the 512 bytes after the hard link are its data, and not the header of empty as we archived it? How can a hard link have different contents from its previous counterpart file?

This archive gives by far the richest and most surprising results I've encountered so far when extracting it with well-known tar utilities and libraries. The results below were produced using the latest releases of all packages at the time of writing.

This group is reasonable in principle: they ignore the size on the hard link, and extract file, its hard link cafÃ©, and empty.

This is the system tar utility of macOS, which is closer to POSIX in spirit regarding the concept of size on hard links, and writes the 512 bytes into the hard link. The end result is that file now contains the tar header of empty.

This group agrees with bsdtar that the 512 bytes are data of the hard link, but doesn't write them into the hard link. Instead, they skip forward over the data, and you are left with just file and cafÃ©, without empty.

This is where you begin to need more imagination. Because cafÃ© contains data, a separate file is created that contains the header of empty as data, while file keeps its original contents.

Makes cafÃ© a separate, empty file, and also extracts empty. Why not?

Does not extract cafÃ© at all, but to make up for it, it creates an empty directory PaxHeaders next to file and empty.

R has an entirely different approach: it extracts empty with 512 null bytes. It mistakenly applies the size to empty instead of the hard link, and those 512 bytes are from an end-of-archive marker.

Haskell's tar would be exactly like GNU tar, if only it did not have string decoding issues, which turn the file cafÃ© into cafÃÂ© on disk (in the year 2026, this is not a rendering quirk of your browser).

These implementations reject the tarball. I believe this is the best thing you can do, even if it's technically not POSIX-compliant.

This tarball is one of 134 tricky tarballs that I'm collecting and categorizing in my test suite haampie/tar-minefield, developed since the last post. Its website https://stoppels.ch/tar features a big table that shows how implementations deal with all these cases, as well as detailed info per test case. A variant from the tarball of this post is included as a test case.

If you'd like to discuss this, send me an email at firstname[at]lastname.ch.

#9882. One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

The record theft shows how weak system separation, inadequate controls, and untested attack possibilities can turn one breach into systemic loss.

Last week's $6.3 billion breach at Binance underscores why effective security often depends not just on what an organization's controls are designed to block, but also on what they are configured to allow.

Details from Binance's disclosures thus far show that a threat actor, whom the FBI has identified as North Korea's TraderTraitor group, compromised a developer's laptop to access an internal service container with the permissions to initiate withdrawal requests.

Using that access as a starting point, the attackers exploited additional points of compromise and an Ethereum account-delegation mechanism to gain transaction approval authority over a hot wallet. And in around 20 minutes, the threat actors drained billions of dollars in assets.

In the process, the attackers appear to have bypassed Binance's normal approval controls. The company itself has said there's no evidence the attackers used any leaked wallet keys to carry out the massive theft.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

"Binance's initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to an employee as the starting point. Its subsequent investigation has identified additional points of breach, showing the incident went beyond one device," the cryptocurrency exchange noted.

The incident, at least based on available details so far, has raised questions about whether Binance had sufficient independent safeguards to prevent a compromised system from approving and executing unauthorized withdrawals.

"At a minimum, a platform holding digital assets should have multiple layers of security so no single compromise, such as a hacked employee laptop, can authorize a transfer," says Tim Rawlins, senior adviser and director of security at NCC Group. "Those layers need to be independent of one another."

Funds, for instance, should be separated across hot and cold wallets to limit the impact of a compromise. Developers and administrators should have privileged access workstations to ensure systems they used for critical operations are separate from those they use for other activities such as email and Web browsing, he says. Also critical is 24/7 monitoring for anomalous behavior to help detect compromised endpoints and suspicious activity before attackers can exploit privileged access.

The focus should be on identifying single points of compromise, such as components or privileged roles whose compromise could give an attacker control over funds. "Protecting private keys is only part of the challenge. The systems that request and approve their use must also be secured. A properly secured system has layered, independent controls, hot/cold separation, and has been through threat modelling and end-to-end security testing," Rawlins says.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

For now, much remains unclear about exactly how the unauthorized transactions occurred and what safeguards Binance had in place to protect against them. Following the attack, the cryptocurrency exchange moved quickly to freeze some $3 billion. It has also claimed to have replenished — though not recovered — approximately 95% of the affected assets, meaning it has used its own funds to replace the stolen assets.

Cryptocurrency exchanges face many of the same threats as traditional financial institutions. But unlike banks and other financial institutions, which have long been subject to regulations governing operational risk and security, crypto exchanges have not yet faced the same level of oversight, making them a popular target for attackers.

John Bruggeman, vCISO at IT services firm CBTS, says large cryptocurrenct exchanges like Binance have to know that they are constantly being targeted by threat actors. In addition to controls that protect the perimeter or authenticate users, these companies also need to know what trusted identities and systems can do, verify high-impact actions, and prevent one compromised component from becoming a path to valuable assets.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

That means segregation of duties, management of private keys that authorize transfers, limits on the size of a transfer, MFA on the use of the private key monitoring, alerting for large transfers, and endpoint detection on all employee devices, Bruggeman says.

Also key is user behavior analysis for all users. Architecturally, organizations like Binance should have custody mechanisms for protecting the cryptocurrency and wallets themselves, transaction controls on how to move the cryptocurrency, some kind of rate limits on withdrawals, identity and access controls, and segregation of duties so no one user can initiate and also finalize a transfer, Bruggeman says.

The Binance breach is an important reminder of why all organizations need to test the path that attackers can potentially take after gaining initial access to an environment and not assume that individual controls, each working as they should, are sufficient protection, analysts said. "The entry point and the damage can sit very far apart, so stop grading your security by how well the front door holds," says Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at Secure.com.

The traditional approach to security is to check whether a request is valid. It almost never checks whether the action behind it should happen, he says. Available information suggests the attackers used Binance's own signing system to sign the transfers, so they looked valid on the way out. It was the "correct math, wrong decision," Ahmed says.

Security has to move from proving identity to governing consequences, he says. That means putting a human approval gate in front of any action that moves money or data, with limits that count across every system at once. "And test the whole route from laptop to payout, not each box on its own," Ahmed advises.

The Binance attack scenario can play out in any enterprise, too. "Swap out the withdrawal service for a payment system, a customer database, or a deployment pipeline, and this is an ordinary enterprise breach," he says. "A clean report from every tool you own tells you nothing about whether someone can walk from a laptop to the money, because no single tool is asked that question."

Robert Coles, senior manager of threat intelligence security at Black Duck, says the broader takeaway for organizations isn't really about cryptocurrency or the attack on Binance itself. Rather, it's about the blast radius, or what happens after initial break-in. It's one thing, he says, for an attacker to gain initial access. But turning that into a theft of billions of dollars is another entirely.

"Every organization has critical systems and privileged accounts where a compromise can have a much bigger impact," Coles says. "We spend a lot of time asking how we keep attackers out. We should spend just as much time asking, ‘If they do get in, what stops them next?'"

Security teams must assume something eventually will get compromised and make sure that one compromise doesn't become a catastrophic business event, Coles noted.

The Binance breach, the biggest ever by magnitude, is by no means the first to affect a major cryptocurrency exchange. In February 2025, Bybit lost approximately $1.5 billion in cryptocurrency after attackers manipulated a transaction approval process involving an Ethereum cold wallet. In May 2019, Binance itself lost 7,000 bitcoin after attackers obtained user API keys and two-factor authentication codes to bypass existing security checks. In October this year, attackers compromised a third-party script on Polymarket's website and used it to move funds from some user wallets.

North Korean threat actors have been especially aggressive in targeting crypto exchanges and wallets in general and account for 76% of all the money that traders have reported as stolen so far in 2026. In six of the past nine years, groups from the cash-strapped nation have accounted for at least one-third of all reported cryptocurrency theft.

InfoQ Homepage News Pinterest and Intel Take Open-Source Profiling to Internet Scale

Nov 10, 2026 3 min read

Pinterest has partnered with Intel to extend gProfiler, an open-source continuous profiler that provides production performance visibility across an internet-scale fleet of infrastructure.

Pinterest claims it operates hundreds of thousands of instances supporting 640 million monthly active users, with services written in Java, Python, C++, Go, and Node.js. At that scale, even a small efficiency improvement can have significant infrastructure and cost implications. The challenge was that engineers were using separate tools such as perf, async-profiler, and py-spy, producing fragmented profiles that were difficult to correlate across languages and machines.

Rather than building another proprietary profiling platform, Pinterest worked with Intel to extend gProfiler and contribute those capabilities back to the open-source project. The collaboration adds dynamic profiling, hardware-level telemetry, wall-time profiling, and performance-counter flame graphs, while also hardening the system for large production fleets.

gProfiler acts as an orchestration layer over several existing profilers. It combines system-wide perf data with runtime-specific tools such as async-profiler for Java and eBPF-based profiling for Python, producing a unified flame graph across the processes running on a host.

This is important for modern services where application execution crosses multiple layers. A Java application may spend time inside the JVM, native libraries, or the Linux kernel, while a Python service can involve interpreter, native, and kernel activity. Instead of requiring engineers to select and manually correlate separate profilers, gProfiler combines those views.

The agent discovers processes, starts the appropriate profilers, merges their stack traces, and uploads the resulting profile without requiring application code changes.

The new capability allows engineers to select services, hosts, or clusters and trigger profiling remotely through the UI or API. Agents normally remain dormant, consuming less than 1% CPU and 100 MB of memory, and receive profiling instructions through periodic heartbeats. You can change profiling frequency, duration, and the profilers used without redeploying the agent.

This effectively turns profiling into an operational capability rather than something that requires engineers to gain shell access to individual machines.

Integration with Intel PerfSpect allows gProfiler to collect hardware-level information such as cache behaviour, memory bandwidth, and CPU stalls. Pinterest also added PMC flame graphs, which correlate functions with hardware performance events such as cache misses and branch mispredictions.

Another addition is wall-time profiling. CPU profiling shows where processor time is being spent, but a service can still be slow while consuming relatively little CPU because threads are waiting on I/O, locks, or remote procedure calls. Wall-time profiling makes those waiting periods visible.

The gProfiler architecture separates collection from analysis. Agents run on individual hosts, while gProfiler Performance Studio aggregates and visualises the resulting profiles.

Profiles are stored in S3, passed through SQS for asynchronous indexing, and stored in ClickHouse for analytical queries. A React frontend provides flame-graph exploration, while aggregated data allows engineers to compare profiles across hosts, services, and time periods.

Pinterest and Intel also hardened the platform for production, addressing issues involving agent resource consumption, disk usage, and multi-terabyte ingestion before deploying it across the fleet.

gProfiler sits in an increasingly crowded continuous-profiling landscape. Parca and Grafana Pyroscope use eBPF and related sampling technologies to provide fleet-wide profiling, while commercial platforms such as Datadog offer continuous profiling alongside broader observability capabilities.

The distinction with gProfiler is its emphasis on system-wide, multi-runtime profiling and open-source extensibility. Rather than replacing tools such as perf or async-profiler, it orchestrates them. It also adds hardware-level profiling through Intel's tooling.

Intel's VTune provides much deeper processor and application performance analysis, but it was designed primarily as a performance-engineering tool rather than a cloud-native fleet profiler. Pinterest specifically notes that this difference influenced the decision to build on gProfiler rather than adapt VTune for its environment.

At small scale, profiling is usually something an engineer enables when a performance problem appears. At Pinterest's scale, the cost of waiting for engineers to reproduce problems or manually profile machines becomes too high. Continuous profiling provides a baseline, while dynamic profiling allows teams to investigate specific anomalies when they occur.

By combining runtime profiles, system behaviour, and hardware performance data under an open-source platform, Pinterest is effectively making profiling another layer of production observability.

#9880. Welcome RL Environments to the hub

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it."

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

#9877. 3AM Affiliate Embraces AI-Like Loops in European School Attack

Evidence suggests a model may have generated and revised commands during the ransom gang's breach, though researchers stopped short of claiming full automation.

A 3AM ransomware attack targeting a UK school estate may provide an early look at how cybercriminals could use AI as a force multiplier rather than a replacement for human operators.

Bitdefender today published research concerning a "hybrid AI ransomware attack" observed in the wild, attributing certain actions taken to human or agentic elements. On the surface, the attack is fairly straightforward. As a blog post explained, a 3AM ransomware affiliate attacked a school in the UK, "then used ordinary Windows tools to build domain trusts and reach other schools."

Attackers stole backup credentials, created rogue domain-admin accounts, established trusts between previously separate Active Directory domains, moved between schools, stole data, and deployed 3AM ransomware. In other words, the attack largely followed a familiar ransomware playbook, despite Bitdefender's claims that AI helped execute parts of the operation.

Related:'AdFection' Turns Ad Impressions Into Zero-Click Spyware Delivery

Where the attack got more interesting was how, as the security vendor argued, it didn't fit neatly into pre-existing buckets for attacks involving AI. It wasn't exactly an AI-generated attack where the malware was fully or largely created by a large language model (LLM); it wasn't exactly an AI-assisted attack where human engineers built the tools while using AI to speed up work; and it wasn't exactly an AI-operated attack where the LLM orchestrates actions and runs the show, as it were.

In this case, Bitdefender argued an AI system appeared to handle repetitive command generation and troubleshooting while a human operator made high-level decisions.

Many elements of the attack were ordinary for ransomware, such as significant use of living-off-the-land (LOTL) techniques, where attackers abuse tools already present on the victim's machine rather than relying on malware — in this case PowerShell, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), reg, netsh, rundll32, and other domain and scheduling utilities preinstalled on Windows. The attacker also used "an Impacket-style remote-execution tool," as well as Mimikatz and a previously published Veeam script.

But despite the attack's ordinary nature, Bitdefender assessed that several things suggest the use of an agentic loop, the control structure that makes an AI agent work. Certain actions appeared to be taken by a program rather than a human operator.

"The commands carry the usual tells of a model: a call to the backup software's web interface (Veeam, a widely used enterprise backup product) on a port and with a login method that do not match the vendor’s documentation, a mistake typical of writing from memory rather than from the manual (Veeam REST API authorization), along with confirmation files, self-labeled output and numbered revisions of the same script," the blog post read. "The retries behave like a loop too."

Related:Biomemory Launches DNA Shield, First Commercial Product Built on Its Molecular IT Platform

In another example, researchers assessed that the time taken between PowerShell command attempts was shorter than a human would take if issuing them by hand, but longer than if an LLM was orchestrating by itself. The longer time taken between individual tasks but the shorter time between retries "is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries."

Bitdefender caveated its findings by noting that it was unable to access the machine the attacker worked from, so it couldn't document anything tangible involving the AI model itself. The research acts as an argument that this attack behaves like a human operating alongside an agent, which is a working model defenders may wish to plan around.

With that in mind, Martin Zugec, technical solutions director at Bitdefender, tells Dark Reading that "a hybrid model is more reasonable for financially motivated cybercriminals, technically and economically, than a fully autonomous attack."

Related:Foul Language: WordlistLoader Disguises Malware as Ordinary Text

But even as a one-off, the situation is notable because the primary victim was an organization in a critical sector, and Bitdefender's anecdote suggests the affiliate may have used an AI agent to scale the attack by handling repetitive troubleshooting and command generation, although the report stops short of showing AI-enabled capabilities the attacker otherwise lacked.

Moreover, other similar institutions could fall in the crosshairs. "From a domain controller it enumerated trust relationships between domains and searched SYSVOL (the shared folder where Active Directory stores logon scripts, readable by any domain user) for the names and subnets of other schools," according to the research blog post.

The good news is that because much of this attack followed the typical ransomware playbook, the defender recommendations that stop regular ransomware would also stop the attack described in this research.

Zugec adds that agentic loops are noisy from an indicator standpoint, as many of their actions are repetitive and brute force in nature. "An agentic loop doesn’t make an attack quiet; it makes it repetitive: the same command re-run, small tweaks, numbered scripts and probe files left on disk. Even the quickest retries took 40 seconds or more. 'Machine speed' is mostly a marketing phrase about very expensive incidents; in real attacks, especially with local models, we expect this slower and noisier pattern. Speed isn't the giveaway; repetition is."

The vendor recommends focusing on prevention: Keep admin credentials of different domains separate, treat backups as a possible target, restrict remote execution and administrative shares to known management hosts, block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them, and put endpoint security tooling on every machine.

"Prefer controls that work regardless of volume and speed," the blog post read, "because they stop an action the first time and the hundredth."

#9875. Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

The tower is square in plan at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H company logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines)

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines)

Our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

#9874. LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise

Cybercriminals have turned reselling cloud access to LLMs into a lucrative business model, with some victims paying as much as $1 million in resource consumption before access was revoked.

Cybercriminals have created a thriving business model out of stealing cloud access to commercial large language models (LLMs) and reselling it to paying customers, with the resource cost for victims reaching high as $1 million before access to their LLM was revoked.

The practice, called LLMjacking, has been around almost as long as LLMs themselves. However, now it's become an illicit enterprise on the underground market, providing a lucrative source of revenue for cybercriminals while victims are left to absorb the high cost of model usage, according to a report published Monday by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant.

LLMjacking can create a massive spike in computing resources in a matter of hours, differentiating it from its more well-known cousin, cryptojacking, which gradually consumes resources. This has made it an attractive revenue stream for "a diverse set of financially motivated threat clusters operating out of multiple regions globally," Google researchers shared in the report.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

"Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 USD in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million USD before access was revoked," they wrote.

The report details how attackers gain initial access to LLMs and achieve persistence on targeted networks, and describes the service model around LLMjacking that has become a lucrative endeavor for cybercriminals.

To gain initial access to an organization's LLM, attackers typically identify publicly exposed LLM endpoints or obtain valid LLM application programming interface (API) keys, according to Google.

"The dominant initial access vector has been exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens — including identity and access management (IAM) credentials, service account keys, GitHub personal access tokens (PATs), and active session tokens — which threat actors leverage to establish an initial foothold into target organizations' infrastructure," the researchers wrote.

Some attackers also deliberately keep their initial activity quiet to gain access to an organization's LLM, according to Google. The researchers observed the use of minimal API requests, sometimes containing just one output token, to validate stolen credentials without generating significant consumption.

This sneaky way to gain and then sell access to the LLM could mean organizations are giving up valuable resources without even knowing, while the attacker is cashing in, notes Nick Tausek, lead security automation architect at agentic AI firm Swimlane.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

"By the time someone asks why the cloud bill has exploded, the attacker may already have paying customers," he says. "Selling stolen model access gives criminals a reason to keep that access working for as long as possible, which makes the quiet activity before the spending spike especially important."

This notably represents a detection challenge for organizations that need to identify early indicators of compromised identities, unauthorized permissions, and suspicious access to AI services rather than just look for unusual consumption, he says.

The report outlines several examples of how attackers compromised and LLMjacked organizations, demonstrating that there is not just one route to take for successfully and illicitly gaining access to an LLM.

In the middle of the year, for example, a threat cluster tracked as UNC6993 compromised a cloud instance through a misconfigured service account key and used it to grant further access to an LLM API. Attackers also hosted a session hijacking page mimicking an application portal to join a group of LLM users.

"This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multifactor authentication (MFA) controls," the researchers explained.

Related:Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

In another instance, a threat actor gained initial entry by combining a stolen personal access token (PAT) to access private code repositories and a suspected Web application vulnerability in a package running within a containerized cloud environment.

Similarly, a different threat actor used compromised cloud federation tokens to programmatically generate new access keys that allowed the attacker to bypass MFA protections, according to Google.

Once access to an LLM has been gained, it then needs to be sold for attackers to make money. The key to this part of the LLMjacking business model is what is called an LLM Mixer, which is an underground service that turns stolen access to commercial AI models into a subscription business, according to Google. These services aggregate compromised credentials, route customer requests through victim environments, and offer access to premium models at prices significantly below legitimate market rates.

As the researchers describe it, LLM mixers act as illicit middlemen, allowing cybercriminals to resell access to compromised enterprise LLM accounts without their customers needing their own legitimate API credentials or cloud infrastructure.

"In one investigation, GTIG observed two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure, demonstrating the sophisticated specialization emerging in this space," the researchers wrote.

Indeed, LLM Mixers are an important part of the emerging LLMjacking ecosystem because they provide the monetization layer that makes stealing enterprise AI access financially attractive.

Since LLMjacking relies on victims being unaware for as long as possible, the key to not getting dinged with a huge resource-consumption bill is to catch on as quickly as possible to the intrusion.

To do this, defenders should prioritize IAM and supply chain security, two of the most common pathways for gaining access to and abusing cloud services, according to Google.

Other best practices for preventing LLMjacking in a cloud environment include good credential hygiene by using a centralized secrets-management platform; least privilege by ensuring users and service accounts only possess the permissions necessary for their specific role and required tasks; and code monitoring by automating secret scanning within codebases such as GitHub and GitLab.

Routine configuration audits, rate limiting, network allow listing, budget alerts, and MFA are also good defense strategies, according to Google.

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.
