#9837. Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

A operação, que contou com o uso de inteligência artificial, utilizou e-mails falsos, documentos governamentais falsificados e a criação de uma organização local para atacar escolas no Peru e no Equador, entre outras ações.

This translation was generated with our internal AI tool.

Uma operação de influência sediada na Rússia enviou e-mails se passando por autoridades educacionais do Peru e do Equador, levando algumas escolas a realizar eventos que os operadores então utilizaram para alimentar controvérsias, de acordo com um relatório divulgado pela OpenAI.

A operação de “fachada falsa”, apelidada de “Dark Clark,” utilizou uma combinação de planejamento baseado em IA e relatórios, além de técnicas mais tradicionais, para convencer administradores escolares a celebrar um “Dia Nacional da Diversidade Cultural e Linguística” em 21 de maio e a destacar três figuras políticas ucranianas, que foram então usadas para tentar semear divisão, afirmou a OpenAI em uma análise do uso operacional de seus modelos de IA. Em outras campanhas, como as direcionadas à Argentina e à Bolívia, as operações russas pareciam ter como objetivo influenciar a política local.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

Os supostos operadores russos utilizaram IA para tornar seu fluxo de trabalho mais eficiente, redigindo relatórios internos sobre suas atividades e, em alguns casos, criando conteúdo para suas campanhas, informou a empresa.

“A IA pode conferir a essas operações de fachada maior escala, eficiência, fluência linguística e capacidade editorial”, afirmou a OpenAI em sua análise. “Os operadores podem usar essas vantagens para explorar vítimas desavisadas, como funcionários ou editores, e divulgar seu conteúdo para públicos que não têm ideia de quem está por trás disso, nem quais são suas motivações.”

A América Latina tornou-se um palco cibernético de espionagem e operações de influência na disputa entre as principais potências globais, tornando-se a região mais atacada ciberneticamente no mundo. Atores conhecidos ligados à China tiveram como alvo tanto a Venezuela quanto o Panamá no início deste ano para obter informações sobre a política na região e proteger os interesses petrolíferos do país. A Rússia expandiu suas operações de inteligência cibernética e desinformação, principalmente para frustrar os esforços dos EUA na região, de acordo com um relatório da RAND de 2026.

“A Rússia também mantém capacidades cibernéticas para realizar invasões direcionadas e desinformação com o objetivo de semear divisão política, perturbar a percepção da situação e enfraquecer as mensagens dos EUA em situações de crise”, afirmou o relatório da RAND.

A operação russa parece estar ligada a uma entidade conhecida como “Politology” ou “La Compania”, que tem vínculos com o falecido oligarca russo Yevgeniy Prigozhin, com o objetivo de influenciar a política global, de acordo com a análise da OpenAI. Os relatórios fornecidos ao modelo de IA continham informações detalhadas sobre as operações do grupo, incluindo detalhes sobre trabalhos anteriores que os ligavam aos grupos de Prigozhin.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

O ataque de desinformação contra escolas em Lima, no Peru, foi uma das campanhas descritas pelos atacantes. Ao elaborar uma diretiva com aparência oficial para os administradores escolares, citando um fictício “Dia da Diversidade Cultural e Linguística”, eles solicitaram que os alunos participassem de atividades de 10 a 15 minutos para aprender sobre três figuras políticas ucranianas. Posteriormente, os operadores instruíram os administradores a enviar fotos do evento.

A OpenAI investigou os eventos e encontrou detalhes que corroboravam as alegações dos operadores, disse Ben Nimmo, pesquisador-chefe da equipe de inteligência e investigações da OpenAI, à Dark Reading. O Ministério da Educação do Peru emitiu uma carta oficial (em espanhol) dois meses depois, mencionando a diretiva e informando que a embaixada da Ucrânia havia identificado a fraude em sua própria carta, datada de 25 de maio.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

“Nunca se deve acreditar em um agente de ameaças pelo que ele diz, certo?”, diz Nimmo. “ Para cada alegação, buscamos evidências na internet que a corroborassem. Para algumas das alegações que eles fizeram, simplesmente não conseguimos encontrar evidências. Talvez tenham sido removidas, talvez estivessem em lugares que não seriam encontrados por meio de uma busca em fontes abertas, talvez nunca tenham acontecido.”

Uma diretiva fraudulenta enviada às escolas de Lima, no Peru, por supostos agentes de desinformação russos. Fonte: Ministério da Educação do Peru (traduzido pelo Claude Opus 5.5)

Como a operação resultou em um político na Polônia citando os eventos, a OpenAI classificou o sucesso com nota 5 na Escala de Impacto de Operações de Influência de seis pontos.

Os operadores russos usaram técnicas semelhantes para induzir escolas no Equador a realizar uma cerimônia de juramento de lealdade ao presidente Daniel Noboa e a Erik Prince, ex-chefe da empresa militar privada Blackwater, afirmou a OpenAI em sua análise. Algumas escolas seguiram a orientação, o que levou a cobertura jornalística e uma denúncia oficial por parte do Ministro da Educação.

Os operadores alegaram ter conduzido com sucesso outras operações de influência das quais a OpenAI não conseguiu encontrar evidências, incluindo a divulgação de uma história de que uma influenciadora brasileira nas redes sociais teria sido traficada para a Ucrânia e a disseminação de um trecho de áudio que alegava que bancos bolivianos pretendiam limitar saques em dinheiro. Os operadores também, ocasionalmente, pediam ao ChatGPT para encontrar incidentes regionais pelos quais pudessem assumir o crédito, diz Nimmo.

Os operadores russos criaram uma chamada “plataforma de pesquisa”, denominada Social Research Center, que contratava funcionários regionais para criar conteúdo local, sem que eles soubessem que a organização fazia parte de uma iniciativa de desinformação.

Embora as operações tivessem como alvo a América Latina, a intenção era prejudicar as relações entre a Ucrânia e o resto do mundo, afirma Nimmo, da OpenAI.

“A maneira como eu encaro essa operação como um todo é que ela gira em torno da Ucrânia”, diz ele. “Trata-se de fazer a Ucrânia parecer mal.”

De modo geral, o uso da IA não abriu novos caminhos para ataques nem criou novas oportunidades de desinformação, mas a tecnologia fez com que as traduções para o idioma nativo soassem mais naturais, permitiu que os operadores assumissem papéis específicos com mais facilidade e simplificou o fluxo de trabalho da operação, afirma Nimmo.

“Se você pensar na Agência de Pesquisa na Internet e no inglês desleixado deles, acho que a IA realmente oferece uma vantagem incremental”, diz ele. “Mas não tenho a impressão de que o uso do nosso modelo tenha sido o fator decisivo. De certa forma, o manual de táticas era muito, muito tradicional.”

#9836. TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

#9835. Data Privacy Is Becoming the Deciding Factor in Enterprise AI Adoption

Writing about inference and open source models.

Writing about inference and open source models.

Writing about inference and open source models.

One agent task can involve multiple models, and each call can send customer records, contracts, or source code to a different vendor. That’s definitely something agent developers should take into account from the start.

Lucky for you, this article will show you how the data flows, compare main deployment options, and offer you a checklist to help you prepare for your next security review.

To put it bluntly, adoption is outpacing control. Here’s what’s happening, in a nutshell:

86.9% of companies delayed AI deployments because security and governance weren’t ready, not because of budget or internal support.

69% said security concerns are slowing agent adoption down, and 83% named data leakage as the barrier.

Shadow AI incidents (staff using unapproved AI tools) more than doubled, from 20% to 43%, and they cost more than the year before.

About three quarters of organizations have an AI governance body, but only 12% call it mature. The State of AI 2026: Security Insights CISOs Need to Know +5

The EU AI Act deadline for high-risk systems has been extended, but the rules still apply. To be specific, under the Digital Omnibus on AI, stand-alone high-risk systems listed in Annex III (hiring tools, credit scoring, education) must now comply by December 2, 2027 instead of August 2, 2026.

In its contract review agent walkthrough, Superlinked describes a review process that involves ten model calls. These include triage, vision, Optical Character Recognition (OCR), embeddings, reranking, entity extraction, text-to-SQL, risk reasoning, orchestration, and a safety guardrail. In a typical stack, these calls may involve several different vendor accounts.

Here’s where data leaves your system when a typical agent runs:

Embedding documents for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Your entire document store passes through the provider.

Sensitive passages leave your infrastructure on every search.

These are often the most sensitive files you own.

Data the user never typed ends up in a prompt.

Your observability tools now store copies too.

Before comparing the options, you need to understand what large providers actually keep by default:

Abuse monitoring logs are kept for up to 30 days.

Available only after OpenAI approves the request.

Inputs and outputs are deleted within 30 days, except when longer retention is required, such as with Usage Policy enforcement or legal compliance.

Available by agreement, although some models still require limited data retention and review.

Neither provider is careless with their customers’ data. OpenAI, for instance, states that API data hasn’t been used for training since March 2023 unless you opt in explicitly.

Sensitive steps locally, the rest with the provider

You manage capacity, upgrades, and incidents

Low-volume work, frontier reasoning, small teams

Regulated data, air-gapped networks, steady volume

Reliance on an external processor whose policies can change

Security becomes your responsibility entirely

A routing layer required that you need to build and test

For most teams, I’d recommend the hybrid approach as the most practical choice. Each call is routed based on the data it handles:

Personally Identifiable Information (PII) redaction

Inside your boundary before anything else

Many open-model servers (vLLM, SIE, and others) expose OpenAI-compatible endpoints. That means the router can be as small as:

But code is the easy part. The real challenge is deciding what really counts as has_sensitive_data. (•_•)

Here’s a checklist you can use prior to your security review:

Self-hosting doesn’t automatically make your data more private. In fact, a misconfigured cluster with open logs can be less secure than a well-governed API with ZDR.

A hosted API is still the right call when:

Superlinked’s SIE vs. OpenAI comparison makes a similar point. When you self-host, you take responsibility for protecting the data. There’s no provider running the controls for you.

It all boils down to this: pick the option your team can manage properly.

If the checklist above has got you thinking, “We need to self-host the sensitive steps, but we don’t want to build or maintain a model-serving platform,” well then, SIE (Superlinked Inference Engine) is the right fit for you.

SIE is an open-source inference server that runs encoders, rerankers, entity extractors, and generation models on your own infrastructure. You can run it on anything, from a laptop to a production Kubernetes cluster. It supports 100+ open models through four primitives: Encode, Score, Extract, and Generate.

If you want to test models before setting up a cluster, SIE Serverless offers a hosted version with SOC 2 Type 2 and US or EU data residency. However, keep in mind it’s still a hosted processor, so test it with non-sensitive data and move sensitive workloads to your own cloud. If you want help running it in your own cloud, take a look at Native Inference.

Both say API data isn’t used for training by default, but they can keep inputs for up to 30 days unless you have a zero data retention agreement.

No. Self-hosting moves responsibility for access, logging, and retention to your team, so it’s only as private as your setup.

Usually yes, as long as you redact sensitive data first, use zero retention where eligible, and send only the minimum context.

Best Inference Servers for Running Open-Source Models in Production

#9834. UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Britain's new Labour-led government is making a concerted push to get ahead of the AI risks to its national networks and the industrial complex.

At various levels of the United Kingdom government, officials are warning about the threat of cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure.

His Majesty's Government broadcast its cybersecurity agenda on Nov. 3, releasing a variety of policy papers, an annual report from its lead cybersecurity agency, and related announcements pertaining to the security of small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs), supply chain vendors, critical national infrastructure (CNI), and more. These items all followed from an updated Autumn Budget 2026, released last week, which provisioned nearly two hundred billion pounds for AI-driven government cybersecurity projects.

Amid all of the practical policy updates, the headline quote of the day came from the state's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which assessed that it's "highly likely that between now and 2028, AI‑powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI." It also labeled "highly likely" the prospect that "China, Russia, and other nation states will routinely use AI cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals" in the country.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

In a new report, Manchester-based NCC Group polled Members of Parliament (MPs) about the state of the UK's CNI cybersecurity posture. About half (51%) of MPs reported that their areas of the country are "not keeping pace" with the threats to its infrastructure. Only 22% expressed confidence in their country's posture. Asked about the nation's ability to fight off a major attack against its CNI, 47% believe that it's unprepared, whereas 41% feel it is.

The survey data is best read as aspirational, not prescriptive. There's little evidence that the UK is less prepared than other nations in addressing threats to its critical infrastructure, or that politicians would be able to tell one way or the other. Leaders are simply aware of the magnitude of what faces them.

"The challenge isn't a lack of government action; it's proof that action translates into resilience," says Katharina Sommer, head of government affairs at NCC Group. "There's still no tested blueprint for coordinating cyber response effectively across government and industry, and that’s not a problem unique to the UK. The test for critical infrastructure operators is whether they can demonstrate, before an attack hits, that they can sustain essential services, recover quickly and maintain public confidence," which remains an open question.

A clearer message came through on Nov. 3, from the experts at the NCSC. Using a scale in which "likely" accords with roughly 55% to 75% odds, "highly likely" with 80% to 90% odds, and "almost certain" approaching 100%, it bet that it is:

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

Likely that threat actors will use AI cyber tools to needle vulnerabilities in CNI

Highly likely that nation-states will use AI to increase the speed and sophistication of their cyberattacks, in service of their geopolitical goals in the UK; in particular, the agency identified China as the foremost player in terms of intent and capability to hit CNI and other strategic targets

Almost certain that "many systems will remain vulnerable" to AI-empowered attacks

The NCSC also drew out some future scenarios. Optimistically, it acknowledged that AI-driven cyber threat development might slow, allowing a window of time for the UK to catch up with the problem. Pessimistically, it painted a picture in which AI threats totally outpace the UK's ability to keep up.

"The situation is likely to be worse than is currently known, with many variables and unknowns still to be discovered," according to the report.

The message out of the UK government on Tuesday was, more or less: we're trying to get ahead of this.

In a policy paper, the government acknowledged that 2018's Network and Information Systems (NIS) Regulations — the UK's only multisector cybersecurity law — is "out of date and insufficient to tackle the threats we face." In a speech announcing its Annual Review 2026, NCSC CEO Richard Horne called the law built to replace NIS 2018 — November 2025's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill — "a vital step forward." The updated bill brings data centers, managed service providers (MSPs), and specific "critical suppliers" into the fold, and introduces stricter breach reporting requirements and hefty fines for negligence.

Related:UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

In a separate policy paper concerning the same bill, the government stated its intention to introduce a new vendor risk management framework focused specifically on the "national security risks posed by vendors" connected to essential service providers. And in yet a third, related paper, the government described how the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will be used to account for agentic "loss of control" incidents, in the fashion of this summer's AI industry lab leaks. Projected future measures include:

Security and resilience requirements to prevent loss of control incidents

Empowering ministers to perform postmortems

The bill is currently passing through Parliament.

Besides this one bill, the UK government also announced £2.4 billion in subsidies to help micro-, small, and medium-sized businesses attain "Cyber Essentials" certifications. All of this week's announcements come on the heels of an Autumn Budget last week, which arranged for tens of billions of pounds each to fund, among other things:

A National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, for vulnerability discovery across the country, including CNI

A National Cyber Shield, for training AI agents to automate cyber defense

A separate National Agentic Security Unit for fighting rogue AI agents

"Increasing the funding and focus on cybersecurity to help keep the UK secure is very welcome," says Jack Chapman, senior vice president of threat intelligence for KnowBe4. At the same time, he adds, "the main challenge I see is scale."

"£154 million for cyber-defenses is a good step," he believes, "but the NCSC estimates cyberattacks cost UK organizations £14.7 billion a year."

Dark Reading asked cybersecurity experts what governments like the UK's need to do to prevent future worst-case scenarios. They consistently emphasized the same point:

"AI did not create new weaknesses; it revealed them. Most incidents still start through the same familiar routes, such as phishing, stolen credentials, and the traditional kill chain paths attackers have relied on for years. The key to stopping these threats is, surprisingly, not exciting: it's the fundamentals," Chapman argues.

The fundamentals for Graham Taylor CBE, director of defense strategy for Northern Europe at OPSWAT, start with protecting the edge. "Too many critical sites rely on firewalls and VPNs for connections that only need to send data one way. Where a facility only exports monitoring data, a hardware-enforced data diode removes the return path entirely, so neither a human attacker nor AI can use that link to send commands into the facility," he says.

Jacob Krell, Suzu Labs senior director for secure AI solutions and cybersecurity, emphasizes network segmentation "built like a boat." AI is going to make the perimeter easier to breach, he says, "and it cuts the time to objective once an attacker is inside. Critical infrastructure is notoriously vulnerable here because operators are hesitant to patch and test systems, and their caution is rational; a bad update takes a plant offline. So the perimeter fails more often and the interior offers nothing to slow lateral movement."

John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, tosses out a less conventional suggestion for fighting off AI threats to CNI. "If AI gives attackers the ability to do a tremendous amount of work very quickly, defenders have an opportunity to present them with large numbers of decoys to investigate," he says. "We need creative ways to make those decoys look realistic and dynamic. The more time attacking AI agents spend interacting with decoys, the less time they spend attacking real systems."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9833. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#9832. ShinyHunters Extorted Boeing Spin-off Prior to Arrests

A teenager from Amman, Jordan suspected of leading the prolific data theft and extortion group ShinyHunters has been detained and is reportedly cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the hacking gang. KrebsOnSecurity has learned that the suspect, who uses the hacker handle “Rey,” was detained as ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting a business unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing, which manufactures the fleet of planes used by the employer of Rey’s father — Royal Jordanian Airlines.

The logo for Jeppesen ForeFlight, a business unit divested last year by the aerospace firm Boeing.

On October 3, Reuters cited three unnamed sources saying a suspected ShinyHunters member in Amman named Saif Al-din Khader was detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI. KrebsOnSecurity identified Rey as Khader in a November 2025 profile, in which the young man admitted working with multiple ransomware groups.

Rey was featured again in a September 28 exclusive about the Dutch police arresting 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by ShinyHunters. The story noted that immediately following the Dutchman’s arrest on the evening of September 15, Rey assumed control over the ShinyHunters brand and boasted publicly about stealing highly sensitive data from the FBI and extorting the ransomware group Cl0p.

Rey taunted both the FBI and Cl0p with memes posted to his longtime account on Twitter/X, while simultaneously including images of the avatar used by Van Der Stap’s former hacker alias “Umbreon” in an apparent attempt to frame the Dutchman for both hacks.

A taunting meme uploaded to Twitter/X by Rey on Sept. 22. A giant sized version of the Pokemon character Umbreon can be seen in the bottom left.

As noted in our September 28 report, ShinyHunters gained access to the FBI site and other victims by exploiting a vulnerability (CVE-2026-35273) in PeopleSoft, a software-as-a-service platform from the tech giant Oracle that is broadly used by companies to manage hiring and human resources, benefits and payroll. Oracle quickly issued a fix for CVE-2026-35273, which ShinyHunters first began exploiting as a zero-day in June, and at the time Mandiant released web application firewall rules intended for organizations that couldn’t apply the security update quickly enough.

ShinyHunters told BleepingComputer in June that the original goal behind exploiting the PeopleSoft vulnerability was to breach the FBI’s own PeopleSoft database, but the hackers said those attacks were unsuccessful for some reason. In recent weeks, however, ShinyHunters turned to a well-known URL-encoding trick to bypass Mandiant’s suggested web application firewall rules.

In a report released Sept. 25, security experts at Mandiant and the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed that ShinyHunters had mass-exploited the PeopleSoft vulnerability to steal data from dozens of systems across a range of industries, including higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government.

Reuters reported October 5 that the FBI has removed a contractor at Accenture over their failure to patch the FBI recruitment website hacked by ShinyHunters, which exposed sensitive data on more than 5,000 FBI personnel, including each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

According to two sources familiar with the ShinyHunters investigation, a navigation and digital aviation unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing was among the victims that ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting when Rey was apprehended by Jordanian authorities.

Those sources said the FBI’s investigation into ShinyHunters gained renewed urgency with the group’s attempted extortion of the former Boeing unit, which allegedly included the theft of sensitive information that sources said could pose operational safety and security risks.

In a brief statement shared with KrebsOnSecurity, Boeing acknowledged the extortion attempts by ShinyHunters, and said the incident concerned data stolen from Jeppesen ForeFlight, a subsidiary that Boeing sold in November 2025 to the private equity firm Thoma Bravo for $10.55 billion.

“We are aware of claims by a threat actor regarding data allegedly associated with Boeing and our former subsidiary Jeppesen ForeFlight,” a Boeing spokesperson shared. “We are actively reviewing the matter with the Jeppesen ForeFlight team.”

A spokesperson for Jeppesen ForeFlight shared a written statement in response to questions, saying the company has seen no impact on their end. “Based on our investigation to date into this claim and proactive security posture, there was no impact to our operations or products.”

Rey’s alleged involvement in attempting to extort the former Boeing unit is noteworthy because there is strong evidence that his father works for Royal Jordanian Airlines, which is mostly controlled by the Jordanian government and operates its long-haul fleet on passenger planes built by Boeing. Rey claimed on Telegram in early 2025 that his father was an airline pilot, although that could not be independently confirmed.

However, as noted in our November 2025 profile of Rey, his family’s shared computer was at one point compromised by password-stealing malware, and the data collected by that malware clearly shows Rey’s father used the same credentials to log in at multiple online portals for Royal Jordanian Airlines employees.

Royal Jordanian Airlines has not yet responded to a request for comment. In advance of our September 28 story, KrebsOnSecurity once again emailed Rey’s father to seek comment and update him on his son’s alleged activities. Neither of the Khaders have responded. But just hours after that request was sent, Rey began deleting his various social media accounts, including the Twitter/X account he previously used to taunt the FBI, Cl0p, and other ShinyHunters victims.

Rey may have nixed many of his social media profiles, but his cybersecurity blog on GitHub somehow escaped the purge, and it shows that Rey was fixated on the leaders of the Cl0p ransomware group. In March 2026, Rey’s blog featured a lengthy post that identified two Russian men as the core developers and hackers behind Cl0p.

Rey’s blog on GitHub. This post doxes two Russian men as the core operators behind Cl0p, one of the oldest and most established ransomware groups still in operation today.

Meanwhile, news outlets in the Netherlands reported explosive new allegations leveled at Van der Stap, whose supposed personal transformation from convicted to reformed hacker has been widely covered in the tech news media. The Dutch daily RTL reported on Sept. 29 that investigators suspect Van der Stap tried to orchestrate at least two murders. According to RTL, the murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for these attacks.

Van der Stap was released from prison after serving the better part of a four year sentence for data theft and extortion activity that prosecutors said netted between €1.5 million and €2.7 million. In an interview with KrebsOnSecurity on September 9, Van der Stap described his new role as “offensive security lead” at the Dutch cybersecurity company Neo Security, saying the job involved probing client networks for security vulnerabilities.

Neo Security’s owner Benjamin Korper told Reuters he has hired an outside firm to investigate whether Van der Stap had hacked Neo Security or its customers, but that so far investigators have found no evidence he acted against his employer or clients. Korper said Dutch forensic investigators visited his office on September 15, the night Van der ⁠Stap was arrested in a dramatic police raid that reportedly involved flash bang grenades.

A screenshot of a Sept 16 story by the Dutch news outlet at5.nl, describing a police raid on Van Der Stap’s residence that reportedly used flash-bang grenades.

Prior to his first arrest in 2023, Van der Stap was working as a software engineer at the Amsterdam-based cybersecurity startup Hadrian, while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) — even as he was hacking into and extorting a number of large organizations.

When asked in a recent interview why anyone should believe the word of a self-described “reformed” cybercriminal who had so casually deceived countless friends, co-workers and journalists for years, Van der Stap replied that his work spoke for itself and there was nothing he could say that would convince his worst critics.

“You can throw a bunch of nice words at someone, but you can’t convince them if they don’t want to be convinced,” Van der Stap told KrebsOnSecurity on Sept. 9. “I’m doing what I can to repay victims, and that’s all I can do. If someone doesn’t want to believe me, then that’s on them.”

Cybercriminals aligned with ShinyHunters have been responsible for dozens of data breaches involving billions of stolen records, and breaches claimed by the group stretch back to at least 2019. But experts say the people recently operating behind the ShinyHunters name are not the same core members that populated the group in its early days, most of whom are French citizens who have been arrested (if not also imprisoned) on at least one prior occasion for alleged cybercrime activity.

More to the point, ShinyHunters has become something of a franchise. Think the Dread Pirate Roberts character in the 1980s cult movie classic “The Princess Bride,” only succession by death is replaced with succession by arrest, and there can be multiple simultaneous Dread Pirate Robertses. Sources close to the investigation say the FBI is focusing on a remaining handful of cybercriminal freelancers or affiliates who have been feeding the group stolen credentials to various software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms used by major companies in exchange for a cut of any data ransoms later paid by victims.

In the days after the news broke of Van der Stap’s arrest, a cybercrime-focused chat server on Telegram that was allegedly operated by Rey erupted with hot takes, with most participants heaping ridicule on the teenage hacker after he publicly backed down from threats against the FBI and Cl0p, and again when the ShinyHunters’s darknet website suddenly went offline. Several commentators accused Rey of resurrecting the ShinyHunters brand after its core members were rounded up in France, and making a mockery of the group’s name and reputation ever since.

“He bought the old forum PGP key and used it to make new Breachforum websites and Telegram channels larping as ShinyHunters to ransom companies and then sell the used data or resell his forum when he goes broke,” one member recounted.

A relatively new Telegram channel called “The Battle” has been doxing and needling Rey and other alleged ShinyHunters members for several weeks, and it has gained a considerable readership among the cybercrime communities operating on Telegram. One of the coordinators of that harassment campaign repeatedly portrayed Rey as clueless greenhorn who sought to ride the coattails of a cybercriminal brand that has long enjoyed a reputation for ruthlessly selling or publishing data stolen from victim companies who refuse to give in to extortion demands.

“Rey (Saif Al-Din Khader) made a serious mistake when he started pretending to be a member of ShinyHunters,” wrote the administrators of The Battle server on Telegram. “That group had already been dismantled, with many of its members either arrested or imprisoned, yet Rey still chose to use its name while carrying out his crimes. We’re aware of claims that [Rey] caused over $200 million in damages and helped around 5–6 friend groups in the community make money by using Shiny Hunters group aliases to negotiate deals for a 25–30% cut over the past few months.”

In an interview with The Register, ShinyHunters claimed they hacked the FBI to counter the agency’s narrative in a May 2026 alert that advised victims against paying a ransom to the group, which came off looking unprofessional and capricious in the FBI’s advisory.

A flash notice on ShinyHunters released by the FBI on May 15, 2026.

The public notice warned the group has been known to pursue a number of different victim harassment strategies, from sending threatening text messages and phone calls to victims and their family members to in some cases swatting victims. The FBI warned ShinyHunters members “may also falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist.”

The hackers told The Register their attack on the FBI “demonstrated our technical capabilities and directly refuted the misinformation disseminated by the FBI, journalists, and industry researchers.” At the same time, the group’s leaders seemed to acknowledge that the FBI’s warning materially harmed their prospects for convincing victims to pay, saying “this was fundamentally a public relations and marketing initiative for our business.”

This entry was posted on Wednesday 7th of October 2026 09:48 AM

She probably runs around in a bad fur coat and goggles, whipping an umbrella around and ▶️ing Lourde.

The part of this story that should worry defenders most is the access path, not the arrests. ShinyHunters mass-exploited a PeopleSoft vulnerability for which Mandiant had already published WAF mitigations — and bypassed them with a URL-encoding trick. That’s a published mitigation that organizations simply didn’t implement, and it ended up exposing the FBI’s own recruitment data plus 70 organizations. It undercuts the common excuse that “we couldn’t have known.” The gap wasn’t threat intelligence, it was execution.

#9831. Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Europe's supermarket freezer hacks show how security issues can cascade across an industry, disrupting supply chains at scale.

The recent refrigerator hacks wreaking havoc across European supermarkets is a lesson in how shared weaknesses in operational technology (OT) can spread across a whole supply chain.

On the night of Oct. 11, an attacker reportedly compromised refrigeration controls used by hundreds of French supermarkets, triggering extended defrost cycles in refrigerators and freezers across the country. The incident caused millions of euros in damage across roughly 700 affected stores in France alone, spoiling food, damaging equipment, and even reportedly starting some fires in the process.

The technology leveraged in these attacks included Danfoss refrigeration controllers, as well as Dixell and Copeland XWEB systems. It's unclear how the threat actor gained access to these systems.

However, the Danfoss controllers at the center of this campaign ran Internet-accessible Web servers. Many were accessible using default login credentials: "admin" as the username and the current date as the password. CERT-FR made a number of recommendations in an advisory to affected supermarkets, such as changing default passwords, factory resetting compromised equipment, and updating firmware. Though to that last point, Danfoss told AFP that many of the attacks involved legacy products that no longer receive updates.

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

France's Cyber Crisis Coordination Center (C4) on Nov. 9 published a five page report attributing the series of attacks on Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and specifically on the IRGC's Shahid Shoostari and Shahid Kaveh cyber-offensive units.

France's Ministry of Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement that the country will propose to its European partners new sanctions against the Iranian entities and individuals allegedly involved in the cyberattack, adding that France reserves the right to take additional proportionate measures to respond to the attacks.

What stands out about the French supermarket attacks is how a shared weakness in refrigeration infrastructure appears to have enabled disruption across hundreds of stores. While investigators have not publicly confirmed the initial access vector, the incident raises questions about the risks created when organizations rely on similar technologies, deployment models, and remote-access practices.

Chris St. Myers, director of SentinelLABS, says evidence suggests a common exposure problem, rather than market concentration, may have facilitated this issue.

"CERT-FR confirmed that the French compromises involved Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers, along with Copeland and Dixell XWEB systems. These technologies are deployed across many retail environments, often with similar remote access requirements and configurations," St. Meyers says. "That creates opportunities for attackers to reuse the same techniques across otherwise unrelated organizations."

Related:EU Grocers Pay a Steep Price for Unpatched Fridge Firmware

Thomas Plank, CEO of industrial security firm Tributech, similarly diagnosed common exposure as a core issue behind the attacks.

"What's concentrated is the setup. Across chains and countries, it's the same model: remote-management controllers reachable from the internet, often on out-of-support firmware, maintained by a small number of contractors who look after hundreds of stores from one place," Plank tells Dark Reading. "When everyone runs the same risky pattern through the same few channels, one way in reaches many retailers at once, across borders, overnight. That's why this looks like a campaign rather than a string of unlucky stores."

It's highly unusual and hardly precedented for a cyberattack to have such a significant impact on the food supply chain, but it's not the only incident like it in recent memory.

A similar attack hit refrigeration and freezer systems in stores across other countries at the beginning of November, including Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden. Around the same time, attackers targeted the refrigeration of three blood banks operated by the national French Blood Establishment, though the attack was stopped before blood plasma was damaged.

Related:Taiwan Bullet Train Hack Highlights Cybersecurity Gaps in Rail Systems

For as alarming and impactful these incidents may seem, supply chain targeting has become more common in recent years with 2021's Colonial Pipeline attack, Iran's recent targeting of fuel monitoring systems around the US, and 2024's Change Healthcare incident.

The danger is clear, especially in the context of a supermarket. Piotr Buliński, chief technology officer (CTO) of Internet of Things (IoT) device management firm Qbee, says a supermarket chain runs thousands of small, unattended OT systems between refrigeration, HVAC, and building management. "Each one is 'just a few controllers,' so nobody treats them as critical infrastructure," he says. "Yet when they fail, the damage is immediate and physical."

These incidents remind us once again about the importance of securing critical infrastructure.

Updating OT systems is a challenging task in their own right because of the downtime often required. Much of the critical technology holding up industrial processes is intended to operate for years (if not decades) on end, while the organizations relying on OT can often include those too under-resourced to have dedicated security staff, like municipalities, or indeed, supermarkets.

Even as these problems have gotten a little easier to address over the years and many dedicated firms have risen to address these challenges, organizations still struggle to secure OT.

St. Meyers believes retail OT has historically received less security attention than traditional industrial environments, despite carrying many of the same underlying risks. He says this is possibly in part because refrigeration, HVAC, and building management systems are "often deployed and maintained outside the traditional IT security organization," despite being OT.

Plank agrees. He says one solution for retailers is to verify commands at the device level against engineering limits, as "no freezer should ever accept a command to go to 50°C, whoever sends it and whatever channel it arrives on," referencing the extreme temperatures some targeted equipment reached during the attacks.

For organizations outside the sphere of influence that want to learn from what happened here, there are several lessons: Don't use default passwords, take inventory of where and how industrial technologies are internet accessible, remove internet exposure wherever possible, and make sure all points of access are secured.

Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat research at Sophos, tells Dark Reading that generally, this incident should be seen as a warning to retailers. "Industrial systems, from energy production to water management to food refrigeration, must be secured," he says, "and at a minimum not accessible to malicious hackers via the Internet."

This story was updated at 2:20 p.m. ET on Nov. 9 to reflect France's accusations against Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

#9830. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#9828. FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm

Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.

The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.

One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.

An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.

According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.

[Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].

“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.

Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”

The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.

Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.

“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”

Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.

ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.

Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.

This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.

This entry was posted on Friday 9th of October 2026 08:17 PM

Arresting the *founder* rather than the negotiation firm itself is the detail that should worry operators the most. Individual accountability for running a negotiation service is essentially untested — the practice is legal in most jurisdictions as long as the customer is the victim of the incident rather than the perpetrator, and there’s no licensing or registration regime for it.

That gap means an arrest is a signal, not a fix. Expect more of these services to move offshore or rebrand under new ownership, and expect the tooling that makes them profitable (leak-site monitoring, initial-access-broker contact lists, automated follow-up) to keep scaling regardless of who gets charged.

The part I don’t see covered: how much of the value in this business is the *list* rather than the negotiation. If the negotiation contact itself is worth little to a criminal group — the customer already knows they’re breached — then arresting the negotiator mostly removes a service fee, not a capability. The durable asset is the broker/leak-site relationship feeding targets in.

What this arrest will do regardless is chill the negotiation industry: firms will start asking counsel to review every engagement letter, and some will quietly exit the business. One practical takeaway for defenders: this is another reminder to treat your IR retainer and negotiation playbooks as legal-adjacent documents. Worth adding to the discussion of the FBI negotiation-company arrests: the practical gap most defenders have is not awareness of ShinyHunters, it is visibility into what the group actually does to get in.

Across the intrusions we have analyzed, the initial-access and exfiltration chain is unusually consistent and entirely built on commodity tooling:

– Remote access and support tools installed as a foothold (ScreenConnect, Screenovate, AnyDesk, Rclone) rather than exploiting a novel vulnerability. – Multi-week dwell times, so presence-based detection rarely triggers early. – Data staged out in chunks sized to stay under typical DLP alerting thresholds — a full customer or employee dataset rarely needs to leave in one transfer to be useful to the extortion side.

The practical consequence is that alerting on named malware is largely beside the point for this group; alerting on the *tools* and on small repetitive outbound flows is what actually catches the chain.

#9827. AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

Security records are increasingly being used by vendors to train their models, creating new risks for enterprises.

Traditionally, security incident records have served a singular, very important purpose: to document what the organization observed, decided, and did. Closure notes, rule text, false-positive dispositions, and the reason why an alert was dropped are treated by security teams as records contained in the ticket queue. For organizations to reconstruct their decisions and, crucially, be accountable for them later, all of this evidence must be retained.

To be sure, security automation is anything but new. For years, SOAR platforms have executed playbooks, closed alerts, and recorded dispositions. They run a rule that customers wrote. The change is what happens to the record afterward, as a portion of the evidence has an alternate destination for a different purpose. Once incident records are ingested into a security AI system with permission to capture data for model building or validation, this evidence can become data the vendor uses for model development and validation.

Related:AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

A sufficiently large collection of prompts and related records can offer more than a glimpse into which signals are treated by the organization as meaningful, which detections are suppressed, what analysts mark as benign, and where it misses something.

A single closure is a comparatively harmless note. A series, however, presents a map; suppressing the same class of alerts delineates boundaries of concern. The rationales for closures indicate acceptable levels of PowerShell noise or failed logins that warrant a ticket. Tuning decisions encode which signals the team stops trusting and when. The contents of the ticket do not need to be accessed by an external party for it to understand the pattern, which is the sensitive portion.

This isn't about reconstructing an AI incident; that's a logging decision. Nor is it about prompt injection, or the familiar case of a vendor training on customer chat logs. The problem is what happens when ordinary security records acquire a second use.

Microsoft Security Copilot provides an option for the owner to allow Microsoft to capture and human-review Security Copilot data to enhance and validate Microsoft's security-specific model, which is built on the Azure OpenAI foundation model. The data captured for model improvement can include whatever Microsoft plug-ins and Security Copilot agents have used while interacting with the product. The documentation states that this data is not used to train the foundation model and is not shared with OpenAI. A second setting controls the capture of data for the purpose of product-performance reviews.

Related:People Are Getting Weird About AI

The default for each setting depends on the method of provisioning the workspace. With the exception of Microsoft 365 E5 and E7 auto-provisioning, data sharing is enabled by default. The customer that enabled the setting has made an intentional decision, but the customer that has not viewed the settings page may not know which default applies. Using the service and allowing a vendor to capture data for model development or validation are different decisions, and Microsoft has already made them separable.

The archive had one job: namely, to help the organization reconstruct and defend its own decisions. Now the same records may be held by a vendor for model development or validation, which in turn creates new risks. A vendor breach puts the records outside the customer's network, while a legal demand can expose them without the customer's control. The retention rules and access controls were built for an archive the organization controlled, but they were not built for a second copy elsewhere.

An auditable record has to preserve more than the final decision. It has to distinguish what the organization knew, what the analyst decided, what the system was given, and what the system recommended. Otherwise, the model's observation effectively becomes the decision. Counsel asking what the organization knew at the time of the incident will not be satisfied by this. An auditor asking why the detections were tuned down should not be met with the closure rationale that also appears in the evidence stream.

Related:What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

This belongs in the procurement contract. A vendor's use of customer security records to provide a service does not by itself authorize their use for model improvement, and evidence retention and model development are different things that should require separate permission. Rule content, closure notes, and ticket text should not be covered by a generic AI clause. If the vendor wants the data for model improvement, then this should be an explicit, revocable choice.

Until these uses are formally separated, the archive has two functions. One of them continues, as expected, to be operated by the organization. The other turns all the evidence into the vendor's resource.

Gerald Mako has more than a decade of experience advising European and Asian governments on artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and technology strategy. His work focuses on AI governance, cyber resilience, and the security challenges created by increasingly autonomous systems.

Chief Information Security Officer, Cobham Satcom

Lemuel Valdez has led cybersecurity and security transformation across private equity portfolios, government, and critical infrastructure environments. He has advised and supported more than 20 PE-backed companies on cyber risk, due diligence, incident response, security architecture, and regulatory compliance.

#9826. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.
