#9800. AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

A command in Claude Code inadvertently saves files with credentials and other sensitive data to public Git repositories, creating security gaps for organizations.

AI coding assistants may inadvertently be leaking thousands of secrets to GitHub public repositories, making what seem like routine interactions between developers and these tools a gaping enterprise security risk.

Research from security firm Apiiro found 2,539 credentials across nearly 2,000 public GitHub repositories, with secrets such as database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens, and SSH root logins among the exposed data, according to a recent report published online. Apiiro tracked some of the leaked data to Claude Code, which was, unbeknownst to users, copying secrets to a hidden file and committing them with the rest of the developer's code.

Among specific secrets leaked were "a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key, a production Azure Postgres password, a Square production token, and the owner password of a medical-records database," Apiiro researchers Shmulik Cohen and Matan Giladi wrote in the post.

Related:People Are Getting Weird About AI

Most of the secrets belong to individual developers across 63 organizations, "from student groups to startups, software agencies, and established vendors," they wrote.

The issue stems from how coding assistants — Claude Code, in a specific case that the researchers examined — carry out certain commands. "Ask Claude Code to check a database or call an API, and the command it proposes carries the secret from your config file," the researchers explained.

The tool will ask the user before running the command and, if the choice is "Yes, and don't ask again," then "it saves that exact command, secret included, to .claude/settings.local.json inside the project folder," according to the report.

"Nothing in the repo marks that file as private, so it gets committed with the rest of the code," the researchers explained.

The fact that a routine development task creates a security exposure is dangerous for organizations, especially because these AI coding tools are supposed to be helpful, not harmful, notes Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing for database security firm Liquibase.

“A developer approves a command to save time, the AI agent retains credentials as part of that approval, and those credentials can eventually end up in a public repository," he observes via email. "Nobody intended to expose them, but the workflow made it possible."

In the case of Claude Code, Apiiro examined 104,185 publicly accessible copies of .claude/settings.local.json on GitHub, finding that 1,122 files contained real secrets. The researchers identified 1,379 distinct secrets in those files alone, including 636 provider-specific keys and 743 passwords or tokens associated with public hosts.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

Claude Code is not being overtly careless; it does try to protect files when it creates its .claude/settings.local.json file inside a Git repository, the researchers noted. The tool does this by adding the file to the developer's global Git ignore list, which tells Git to ignore the file on that particular developer's machine. This prevents it from being included in routine commits.

However, the protection is not built into the development project itself, and the "ignore" rule does not travel with the repository when it is cloned onto another machine, the researchers noted. "The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it," they wrote.

Moreover, Claude Code itself was sometimes responsible for committing the exposed files. In 539 of the 1,105 repositories containing real secrets that the researchers investigated, a commit co-authored by Claude Code had modified the affected settings file.

The action that exposes these secrets while using Claude Code appears to be a "dead zone" of sorts for developers using AI coding assistants, so they likely have no idea that they've just exposed a secret, observes Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of AI penetration testing firm BreachLock.

Related:What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

"A 'don't ask again' prompt is a decision to write a credential into a file, and many developers clicking it likely don't know that file exists," he says. "Once it lands in a repository, it sits in a place many secret scanners were never built to check, which appears to be why some of these leaks slipped through."

Apiiro contacted Anthropic about the issue before publishing the findings. After their publication, Boris Cherny, Anthropic's head of Claude Code, said in public comments that although Claude Code historically has not done secrets scrubbing, the company is looking into what it can do to prevent the secrets exposure described by Apiiro, according to Apiiro's report.

Those approaches may be to make sure auto mode catches the exposure, or to build in basic secrets scanning, among other ideas that Anthropic will prototype "to understand the tradeoffs" before shipping something with its next version of Claude Code, Cherny said.

Indeed, the leakage exposes how Claude Code's protection relies heavily on a developer-specific Git setting rather than a safeguard built into the project or the AI coding tool itself, exposing a gap that can turn an ordinary command approval into a persistent credential leak.

To avoid this, Apiiro recommends that developers rotate every credential a file has ever held, and open all fields and delete every rule containing a secret, even if a file was never committed to a project. Meanwhile, security teams should treat all AI agent folders as secret-bearing on laptops as well as in repos, and add them to pre-commit and secret scanning, including history.

"As AI agents become more involved in software development, organizations need to recognize that source code isn't the only thing they need to secure," McCurdy observes. "Agent configuration files, transcripts, and execution histories can contain sensitive information, and traditional security checks may not catch everything."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9799. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9798. redalpine Closes Oversubscribed $250M Fund to Back the Science Defining the Next Decade

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

European technology is in its strongest run in years. Startups across the continent raised €68.4 billion in the first nine months of 2026, already more than in all of 2025, with the full year on course to finish about 31% higher. AI companies drew €44.1 billion of that total, nearly two-thirds of all European deal value.

The fastest-rising part of the market is deeptech, the category of companies built on scientific or engineering breakthroughs such as fusion energy, robotics and AI-designed drugs. It drew a record $20.3 billion in 2025, or 32% of all European venture capital, while VC-backed European deeptech companies are now valued at about $690 billion. Capital is flowing back into the funds that back these companies from day one, as European VC funds raised $14.9 billion in the first nine months of 2026, close to the total for all of 2025.

AI's share of European VC deal value has nearly quadrupled in a decade, rising from 9.3% in 2015 to 35.5% in 2025. Deeptech has grown alongside it, taking a record 32% of European venture capital in 2025, more than double its share a decade earlier. Dealroom's 2026 report found the fastest growth in compute infrastructure, with strong gains in defence, computational biology and chemistry, space, robotics and energy.

Europe's research base is the engine behind that growth. The continent is home to 30% of the world's leading deeptech universities and produces twice as many science and engineering graduates as the United States, while Paris, Cambridge, London, Munich, Stockholm and Zurich rank among the world's top deeptech hubs. That talent gives early-stage investors a deep pipeline of scientist founders, which is the pipeline redalpine has drawn on since 2006.

European tech funding reached €27.8 billion in the third quarter of 2026 across 732 deals, up 32.4% on a year earlier and more than two and a half times the €11 billion raised in the same quarter of 2024. Five rounds passed €1 billion in the quarter, led by Mistral AI's €3 billion raise along with large rounds for Nscale, Helsing and Quantum Systems, while more than 2,630 investors took part in deals.

Crunchbase data points the same way, with European startup funding up 77% year on year to about $25 billion in the third quarter, while AI companies took a record 75% share at $18.8 billion. Deal value for the first nine months of 2026 has already passed the €66.2 billion invested in all of 2025, a year in which later-stage rounds of Series D and beyond grew 45.2% as European companies scaled further at home.

The money is also returning to new funds. European venture funds raised $14.9 billion in the first nine months of 2026, close to the $15.5 billion raised across all of 2025, with large closes such as EQT's €5 billion Scaleup Europe Fund. Limited partners, the pension funds, insurers, development banks and family offices that commit money to venture funds, are backing specialists with a record in AI and science, which is the group redalpine belongs to.

Beyond AI, PitchBook data shows billions moving into the hardest technology categories in the first nine months of 2026, with €10 billion for cleantech, €9.1 billion for advanced manufacturing, €8.7 billion for robotics and drones and €3.5 billion for space technology. These categories can overlap, since a robotics company may also be an AI company. Each one is growing as industry, governments and investors look for European suppliers of critical technology.

Those are the fields where redalpine already invests, from fusion energy at Proxima Fusion to robotics at Enact Intelligence, AI biology at Helical and Basecamp Research and AI for critical systems at Arlequin AI. Every one of the large late-stage rounds in these sectors started with a Seed investor able to judge the science, which is the stage RAC VIII is built to lead.

The fund's limited partners include returning and new investors such as Aviva Investors, the asset management arm of the UK insurer Aviva, the private markets firm Flexstone Partners and KfW, Germany's state-owned development bank. Entrepreneurs, executives with deep domain expertise and business owners also invested, giving redalpine a network of operators who can support portfolio companies directly.

That mix of investors reflects a broader push to keep more of the value created by European technology companies with European savers, including pension funds. Aviva Investors has said it sees the partnership as a way to gain access to high-growth UK and European start-ups for the long-term benefit of pension investors.

RAC VIII will invest in about 20 early-stage companies across Europe, primarily leading or co-leading Seed and Series A rounds with initial tickets of $1 million to $15 million. A Seed round is usually a company's first institutional funding, raised to build a product and prove the technology works, while a Series A funds the move from early traction to a scalable business. Spread across about 20 companies, the fund has roughly $12.5 million of capital per company before fees, which leaves room for follow-on investment.

Selection is strict. redalpine screens more than 5,000 companies each year, while its early-stage funds make five to ten new investments a year, so only about 0.1% to 0.2% of the companies it reviews receive a first cheque (our arithmetic). Half of redalpine's investment team are trained scientists, including biologists, physicists and engineers, who can assess complex technology before there is a product or customer data to judge.

The first three RAC VIII companies show where the fund is headed. Enact Intelligence, a Swiss startup led by co-founder and chief executive Manuel Yves Galliker, formerly of Physical Intelligence, is building force intelligence for robotics, which lets robots sense force and touch through their own actuators so they can handle objects more precisely than with cameras alone. Enact raised a $30 million pre-seed round in October 2026 with redalpine, Notion Capital and Firstminute Capital, along with angel investors Arthur Mensch of Mistral, Yann LeCun and Thomas Wolf of Hugging Face.

Helical, founded in Luxembourg and based in London, is building a virtual AI lab that turns the outputs of biological foundation models into reproducible drug discovery decisions. redalpine led its $10 million Seed round in April 2026. Helical says it already works in production with several of the world's top 20 pharmaceutical companies, with public collaborations that include Pfizer and Tanabe Pharma America.

Arlequin AI, a Paris company founded in 2024, is developing a new AI architecture called topological neural networks that learns from both data points and the relationships between them, with uses in security, defence, fraud detection and critical systems. redalpine co-led its €28 million Series A in September 2026 alongside OTB Ventures, with the Defence Innovation Fund of Bpifrance also taking part.

redalpine's portfolio includes some of Europe's most valuable technology companies. Mistral AI, the Paris AI model developer, closed a €3 billion Series D at a post-money valuation above €21 billion in September 2026, led by Samsung Electronics. N26, the Berlin digital bank, is one of the firm's best-known fintech investments, while Basecamp Research, a London company designing medicines with its EDEN biological foundation model, raised a $140 million Series C in September 2026 with NVIDIA and Anthropic's Anthology Fund taking part.

Proxima Fusion shows redalpine's early-stage model at work. The Munich company, spun out of the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in 2023 to build stellarator fusion power plants, raised its Seed round with redalpine as lead before closing a €130 million Series A in June 2025, the largest private fusion round in Europe at the time, taking its total funding to more than €185 million.

Across the portfolio, companies backed by RAC VII have raised over $1.1 billion in total funding since that fund closed in 2024, about 5.5 times the size of the fund itself (our arithmetic). Twelve portfolio companies have exited since 2023, giving redalpine's investors realized returns alongside a growing set of private companies valued in the billions.

redalpine was founded in Zurich in 2006 by software entrepreneur Peter Niederhauser and molecular biologist Michael Sidler, who started the firm on the view that the most important companies would emerge where software and science meet. It invested in fusion energy, AI, robotics and biotechnology before those fields became established venture themes. The firm has since opened offices in Zug, Berlin and London and built a presence in Silicon Valley.

Over two decades redalpine has backed more than 100 companies, which have gone on to create over 10,000 jobs and raise more than $3 billion. It began as a single early-stage fund and has grown into a multi-stage platform that can back founders from Seed to IPO, including the Summit Fund, an evergreen vehicle that invests in redalpine's early-stage funds, follows on in their strongest companies and buys into later-stage category leaders.

General Partner Sebastian Becker argues that AI is levelling the playing field between regions, which shifts the advantage to whoever understands the underlying science and the hardest problems best. In redalpine's view that has always been Europe's strength. The firm says it is seeing a new generation of ambitious founders determined to build world-leading technology companies from Europe.

The firm also sees a change in European confidence among the institutions that fund venture. Partner Rafael Hubatschek has described institutional investors as putting real conviction behind European technology, which fits the mix of returning and new limited partners in RAC VIII. A platform that can back a company from its first round to later growth stages lets redalpine keep supporting founders as they grow into global category leaders.

RAC VIII starts investing with three companies already in the portfolio and room for about 17 more over the coming years, in a market where AI and deeptech take a growing share of European venture capital. The fund's focus on force intelligence for robotics, AI for drug discovery and new AI architectures for critical systems places it in the categories that drew the largest rounds of 2026.

European venture investment is on course for its best year since 2022, while the share flowing to AI and deeptech keeps rising. A specialist with two decades of history, a scientist-led team and a growing base of European institutional investors is well placed to lead those rounds. The firm's past funds backed Mistral AI, Proxima Fusion and N26, while RAC VIII gives redalpine $250 million to find the next generation of European technology leaders.

#9797. How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

Cloud Range's free 28-question OT Cyber Readiness Assessment helps organizations identify gaps in operational technology (OT) incident response.

Cloud Range introduces a 28-question OT Cyber Readiness Assessment to help organizations identify gaps in preparedness for cyberattacks affecting operational technology.

The assessment covers seven critical areas, from OT asset visibility and IT/OT coordination to incident detection, response, recovery, and readiness validation.

Recent OT cybersecurity research reinforces the importance of preparing IT, security, OT, and engineering teams to investigate and respond to attacks that can disrupt physical operations.

NASHVILLE, Tenn., Nov. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Cyberattacks affecting operational technology (OT) can disrupt production, equipment, and essential services, resulting in consequences that extend beyond disruptions to traditional IT systems. To help organizations evaluate their preparedness, Cloud Range today introduced the Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment, a free, 28-question resource designed to identify potential gaps in OT incident response preparedness.

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

The assessment provides a practical starting point for IT, security, OT, and engineering teams to evaluate how well they understand their environments, coordinate responsibilities, and prepare to detect, investigate, respond to, and recover from cyber incidents affecting industrial operations.

“Organizations can have incident response plans, security tools, and experienced teams in place without knowing how effectively those capabilities will work together when an attack affects operations,” said Debbie Gordon, CEO of Cloud Range. “The first step is understanding where teams are prepared, where they may be relying on assumptions, and where further validation is needed. The stakes are different in OT because decisions made during a cyber incident can have direct operational consequences.”

Recent research illustrates the scale of cyber threats facing industrial organizations. The Dragos 2026 OT Cybersecurity Year in Review reports that approximately 3,300 industrial organizations were affected by ransomware in 2025.

Palo Alto Networks’ 2026 State of Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity Report found that 59% of surveyed critical infrastructure organizations experienced a significant security breach in the past year. The research also found that 74% had not fully integrated IT and OT security operations, highlighting the importance of coordinated incident response.

The report also identifies operational consequences of cybersecurity incidents, including safety concerns, unplanned downtime, production disruptions, and financial losses.

Related:Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Together, these findings underscore a central challenge for organizations operating OT and industrial control systems (ICS): preventing attacks is important, but so is understanding whether teams can recognize, investigate, and respond quickly and effectively when incidents occur.

An attack does not have to originate within an OT network to affect industrial operations. Compromises involving enterprise IT systems, third-party access, supply chains, or interconnected infrastructure can create consequences for production environments and critical services.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment examines seven areas that influence an organization's ability to prepare for and respond to cyberattacks affecting OT environments:

Know Your Environment: Understand critical OT assets, systems, dependencies, and connections between IT and OT environments.

Know Your Threats and Stakes: Recognize relevant cyber threats and their potential impact on operations, equipment, and safety.

Bridge IT and OT: Establish shared responsibilities, communication, and decision-making across IT, security, OT, and engineering teams.

Detect and Investigate: Identify suspicious activity, investigate threats, and determine their potential operational consequences.

Respond Without Making It Worse: Make coordinated incident response decisions that account for production continuity, equipment, and safety.

Recover and Maintain Resilience: Understand recovery priorities, system dependencies, and procedures for restoring critical operations.

Prove Readiness Before It Matters: Validate response capabilities through realistic cyberattack simulations and measurable performance.

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

Each area includes three questions, with responses of Ready, Developing, or Unsure.

Rather than assigning a numerical score, the assessment helps organizations identify gaps, uncertainties, and areas requiring further attention. IT, security, OT, and engineering teams can complete it independently and compare their responses to uncover differences in understanding, unclear responsibilities, or differing assumptions about preparedness.

Why OT Incident Response Preparedness Requires Cross-Functional Coordination

OT environments present distinct incident response challenges because cyber decisions can affect physical equipment, industrial processes, production availability, and potentially safety.

Actions that may be appropriate in an enterprise IT environment, such as isolating a system or shutting down a device, can require additional operational evaluation when industrial systems are involved.

Effective OT incident response therefore depends on coordination among teams with different responsibilities and expertise.

IT and security personnel may focus on identifying malicious activity, containing threats, and investigating compromised systems. OT and engineering personnel understand process dependencies, equipment limitations, and the operational consequences of response decisions.

Both perspectives are essential. The integration gap identified in the Palo Alto Networks research reinforces the importance of shared understanding, clear responsibilities, and coordinated decision-making across IT, security, OT, and engineering teams.

Understanding how to assess OT cyber readiness across these functions helps organizations identify where their procedures, communication, and decision-making may require further attention.

The assessment is intended to support those conversations before an actual incident demands coordinated action.

An assessment can help organizations identify preparedness gaps, but it cannot establish how effectively teams will perform during a real cyber incident.

That requires opportunities to investigate attacks, make decisions, coordinate across functions, and evaluate the results in realistic environments.

Cloud Range helps organizations strengthen critical infrastructure cyber readiness, realistic cloud-based OT/ICS, IT, cloud, and hybrid environments where teams can investigate cyber threats, coordinate incident response, and measure performance. Its critical infrastructure cybersecurity and readiness programs help organizations prepare for attacks that may disrupt industrial processes, equipment, and essential services.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Range supports flat and Purdue-model industrial network architectures, allowing teams to investigate how connectivity, segmentation, and system dependencies influence attack progression and response. Hardware-in-the-loop capabilities can also connect physical OT laboratory equipment to the cyber range for cyber-physical security validation.

Through OT cyberattack simulations and adversary emulation, teams can investigate ransomware, supply-chain compromise, credential theft, lateral movement, and threats affecting industrial systems.

Performance metrics highlight how teams improve in detecting threats, investigating activity, coordinating decisions, and improving incident response over time.

Across Cloud Range customer engagements, measured improvements have included reductions of up to 66% in mean time to detect and improvements of up to 30% in overall incident response time. These results reflect broader cyber readiness programs and are not specific to OT environments.

As IT and OT environments become more interconnected, organizations face growing pressure to understand both their cybersecurity exposure and their ability to respond to incidents with operational consequences.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment provides a structured way to evaluate preparedness across seven critical areas. Organizations can use the findings to prioritize improvements and identify where realistic attack-based validation can provide stronger evidence of readiness.

The objective is not simply to have an incident response plan. It is to build confidence that the people, processes, and technologies involved can work together when an attack affects operations.

Cloud Range is the leader in Cyber Readiness and Validation, helping organizations continuously measure and improve how people, processes, and AI perform under real-world attack conditions. As the creator of the industry's first full-service, cloud-based cyber range, Cloud Range provides realistic IT, OT/ICS, and cloud environments where organizations can safely train, test, validate, measure, and benchmark cyber readiness across people, processes, and AI agents.

Used by enterprise organizations, government agencies, higher education institutions, critical infrastructure organizations, and managed security service providers (MSSPs), Cloud Range helps organizations strengthen cyber readiness through live-fire cyberattack simulations, objective performance measurement, expert guidance, continuous readiness programs, and AI validation.

Cloud Range has received multiple industry awards recognizing innovation and leadership in cyber readiness, cyber defense, and cybersecurity excellence and has been recognized by leading analyst and research organizations for its contributions to cyber readiness, cyber ranges, AI validation, and modern security operations. Learn more at cloudrangecyber.com.

#9796. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9795. Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

#9794. Checkmarx Appoints Kobi Sivilya as Chief Information Security Officer

Sivilya brings deep cybersecurity and technology leadership to Checkmarx as AI transforms software development.

MOUNTAIN VIEW, CA — November 5, 2026 — Checkmarx, the leader in agentic application security, today announced the appointment of Kobi Sivilya as Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) and Chief Information Officer (CIO). In this dual role, Sivilya will oversee the company’s security, IT and business applications, supporting Checkmarx’s global operations and continued growth.

Sivilya will lead Checkmarx’s corporate security and IT functions, aligning security, technology and business applications with the company’s strategic priorities. He will also help advance Checkmarx’s mission to secure modern application development.

“Kobi brings more than 20 years of experience across cybersecurity and technology, with deep security expertise and practical IT leadership,” said Sandeep Johri, CEO at Checkmarx. “AI is changing how software gets built and attacked, and we need his leadership to keep Checkmarx secure as we protect our customers.”

Related:Risks & Rewards: How AI Is Redefining the CISO's Role

Prior to joining Checkmarx, Sivilya served as CISO and VP of IT at Outbrain, where he led the company’s security and enterprise technology functions. He also served as VP of Security Engineering at Fireblocks, where he helped build and lead security engineering for a blockchain platform that protects digital assets for leading financial institutions in a highly targeted environment.

“As AI accelerates software development, organizations need technology and security capabilities that can evolve alongside it,” said Kobi Sivilya, CISO and CIO at Checkmarx. “My focus will be on ensuring our internal technology and security functions support the way our teams work today while positioning the business to adapt to what comes next.”

About Checkmarx Checkmarx makes security inseparable from how software is built. The foundation is decades of accumulated threat intelligence used to secure trillions of lines of code each year. Checkmarx One now pairs that foundation with frontier AI-powered reasoning, unifying architectures to lead the category in detection accuracy. Checkmarx Assist agents prevent, prioritize, and fix vulnerabilities across software and the AI supply chain, so enterprises never have to trade speed for certainty. The combined result is the Checkmarx One platform, giving enterprises comprehensive application security: capturing risk, eliminating vulnerabilities, and unifying governance. Follow Checkmarx on LinkedIn, YouTube and X.

#9793. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9792. Software Project Rescue: When to Stabilize, Refactor, or Rebuild

Your booking API stops syncing. Statuses are wrong, pricing doesn’t match, and the team isn’t sure whether to patch it, refactor the integration layer, or question whether the architecture can support another provider at all. According to research published by Stripe, developers spend nearly a third of their time dealing with technical debt and bad code – time that isn’t going toward new features, stability, or growth.

This is one of the most common situations in software product development: something is clearly wrong, but the right response – fix, stabilize, or rebuild – isn’t obvious. That’s what this article is about.

The clearest signal isn't a specific bug or a single failed release. It's a pattern – development becoming progressively harder, slower, and more unpredictable over time.

Common situations that lead to a rescue engagement:

A fix goes out, and something unrelated stops working. The team spends more time investigating incidents than building features. Nobody is confident that a deployment will go smoothly.т

The demo works. Users can complete the main flow. But edge cases fail unpredictably, error handling is missing, and the product behaves differently under real load than it did in testing. The gap between "it works" and "it's ready for real users" is wider than it appeared.

APIs are connected, but data doesn't sync correctly. Booking status doesn't match between systems. A pricing update in one place doesn't reflect somewhere else. The integrations aren't broken – they're just not coordinated. Adding another one makes everything less stable.

The team used AI to move fast – and it worked, until it didn't. The codebase has features that function but aren't understood. Changes in one area break things in another. Developers avoid touching the AI-generated parts because they can't predict the consequences. According to a 2024 GitHub survey on AI in software development, over 60% of developers now use AI coding tools – but production reliability remains a separate challenge from generation speed.

A previous agency, freelancer, or internal team left a product that works but can't be explained. Documentation is missing or wrong. The integration logic is unclear. The new team is afraid to change anything.

Traffic increased, providers were added, users grew – and the architecture that was fine at the beginning is now the bottleneck. Sync jobs time out, API rate limits are hit during peak usage, and performance degrades in ways that weren't visible before.

If any of these sound familiar, the product isn't failing – it's telling you that its current state can't support where it needs to go.

Rescue is not one thing. It's a category of structured interventions – each addressing a specific situation. Understanding which type applies to your product is what determines the scope, timeline, and cost of the engagement.

APIs are connected, but something is wrong with how they work together. Data gets lost between systems. Booking status doesn't propagate. Pricing shows differently across the flow. Adding a new provider broke the ones already running. Integration rescue maps how data actually moves between systems – not how it was intended to move – identifies where it breaks, and rebuilds the parts that aren't coordinating correctly. This is the most contained rescue type: the product doesn't need to be rebuilt, just the connections between its parts. For products with multiple API integrations, this often means building a shared integration layer that didn't exist before – one place where all external connections are managed, monitored, and isolated from each other.

The product works in testing. It breaks with real users. Bookings fail silently, statuses don't update, and users complete a flow that doesn't actually register on the other side. This type of rescue identifies the specific failure modes that only surface under real conditions – webhook handling, race conditions, edge cases in cancellation and modification flows – and fixes them without rebuilding the entire product.

The product was built quickly with AI assistance – Cursor, Claude Code, or similar tools. It demonstrated well. In production, edge cases fail, the architecture has gaps nobody fully understands, and the team is reluctant to change anything the AI generated because they can't predict what it will affect. AI code stabilization isn't about rewriting what the AI produced. It's about taking ownership of it: understanding what it does, filling the gaps in error handling and architecture, and making it safe to develop further.

A previous team handed over a product that works but can't be explained. Documentation is incomplete. Some integrations are unclear. The new team is afraid to touch anything. Post-handover recovery starts with mapping what exists – what each part of the product does, what the integrations connect to, and which areas are stable versus fragile. From there, the most critical gaps are filled: missing documentation, unclear ownership, and the parts of the codebase that need to be understood before they can be safely changed.

Every deployment is an event. The team is nervous before it goes out. Something unexpected happens more often than not. Hot fixes follow releases regularly. Release stabilization addresses why deployments are unpredictable – usually a combination of no visibility into what changed, no separation between stable and fragile parts of the codebase, and no rollback plan.

When something is clearly wrong with a product, the instinct is often to propose a full rebuild. It feels clean. It feels like starting fresh without the baggage.

Most of the time, a full rebuild is the wrong answer – not because it's impossible, but because it's slower, riskier, and more expensive than it looks. Existing products contain years of business logic, edge cases, and data that can't be replicated by starting over. As HackerNoon has covered in depth in pieces on technical debt, deferred structural work compounds in ways that aren't always visible until they become critical. A rebuild that takes six months to produce something equivalent to what already exists is rarely the right investment.

The right intervention depends on what's actually broken.

Stabilization is the right answer when the product's core architecture is sound but specific areas are fragile – a sync job that fails silently, an integration that breaks under certain conditions, a flow that works in testing and fails in production. Stabilization fixes those specific areas without touching what works. It's the fastest path to a safer product and the starting point for most rescue engagements.

Refactoring is the right answer when the structure of the code – not just specific bugs – is what makes development slow and risky. Modules that are too tightly coupled, logic that lives in the wrong layer, architecture decisions made early that don't fit where the product is now. Refactoring restructures without rebuilding – the product keeps running while the internal structure improves.

A full rebuild is justified when the existing codebase genuinely cannot support what the product needs to do next. Not "it's messy" or "we'd build it differently now" – those are almost always arguments for refactoring, not a rebuild. A rebuild makes sense when the technology is no longer viable, when the architecture is fundamentally incompatible with the product's requirements, or when the accumulated technical debt has made the codebase more expensive to maintain than to replace.

The practical test: if the product can be made safe to develop with targeted fixes, stabilization or refactoring is the answer. If it genuinely can't – if the architecture itself is the blocker – then a rebuild conversation is warranted.

Rescue engagements follow the same sequence regardless of which type applies.

Audit first. Before any code changes, map what exists: what's stable, what's fragile, what's blocking development, and what the highest-risk areas are. This is what determines the scope – not assumptions made before looking at the actual product.

Fix what affects users and revenue first. Not every problem needs to be solved at once. The first phase addresses the issues that are causing real impact: flows that fail, integrations that lose data, releases that create incidents. Everything else is prioritized based on risk and effort.

Stabilize, then improve. The goal of software project rescue isn't a perfect codebase – it's a product that's safe to develop. Once the critical areas are stable, refactoring and improvement can happen incrementally, without the pressure of firefighting.

Hand over with clarity. The end of a rescue engagement should leave the team with a clear picture of what changed, what to monitor, and what to address next. Not a black box – a product the team can own.

We talked a lot about the process, so here is a direct example from ASD Team’s work:

One platform connected three AI services – a language model, a text-to-speech provider, and an AI avatar tool – to turn user text into finished videos. Each service worked correctly in isolation. Together, they couldn’t complete a single video reliably.

The problem wasn’t the AI calls. It was the handoffs between them. The language model returned output that was too large and unstructured for the text-to-speech service, which needed a short script and a delivery tone. Nothing in the system performed that translation – the integrations existed, but the connection layer between them didn’t.

The team mapped each handoff, built the missing orchestration layer, removed workarounds that had accumulated around the gaps, and replaced providers that proved unstable once the full sequence ran end-to-end. The result of software project rescue services was a pipeline that completed consistently for every request.

The right time to start is before the situation becomes critical – not after a production incident forces the decision.

If development is getting slower, releases feel riskier, or specific parts of the product are avoided because nobody is confident about what changing them will affect – those are the signals. Waiting until something breaks completely doesn't make the engagement easier. It makes it more urgent, more expensive, and more disruptive.

The goal of rescue isn't a perfect codebase. It's a product that's safe to develop – where the team understands what's stable, what's fragile, and what to watch. That's the state from which normal development can resume.

This article was published under HackerNoon's Business Blogging program.

#9791. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

#9790. F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

New AI Harms Taxonomy traces how harm moves through AI systems, from misleading chatbot answers to compromised autonomous agents, and identifies where defenses can intervene.

LOS ANGELES (November 10, 2026) — AI now shapes how we search, communicate, decide and run our digital lives. But when it goes wrong, how does it actually hurt people? F-Secure’s new AI Harms Taxonomy maps 26 distinct harms to consumers, tracing the path each one takes to reach a person. The result is a clear view of where protections can step in, and who is in the best position to help.

Developed by Dr. Megan Squire, Principal Threat Intelligence Researcher at F-Secure, the taxonomy tackles a blind spot in how AI risk is discussed. Most frameworks list what could potentially go wrong, but stop short of connecting those harms to the systems and companies that could prevent them. F-Secure’s research goes further by mapping every layer between an AI-enabled threat and its impact on a consumer, then pinpointing where defenses need to go.

“As AI systems become more capable, the consequences of their mistakes can extend well beyond a bad answer,” said Dr. Squire. “The people building them have a responsibility to understand how they can fail and who gets hurt when they do, and to put safeguards in place before that harm happens.”

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

The taxonomy reflects how the risks themselves are changing. It used to be a criminal going after a person directly, but now AI sits in the middle, which adds new players and new ways for things to go wrong. An assistant acting on someone’s behalf can be manipulated into doing damage, and a chatbot can mislead with complete confidence. Underneath, the trouble often starts in how an AI handles instructions and memory, or in the other services it’s connected to.

The research currently maps 26 harms across five relationship types and 19 intermediary layers, with 24 defenses designed to address risks at different points. Examples range from AI-generated voice and video impersonation to agents making harmful financial decisions, exposing personal information or acting on outdated context. It also examines attacks in which malicious instructions are hidden in content an AI system processes, potentially influencing what an agent does or what a chatbot tells a user.

One of the framework’s central findings is that responsibility for preventing AI harm is spread across several parties. Some risks can be handled by security software on a person’s own device. Others have to be dealt with further upstream, by the companies that build AI products and the systems behind them, including how an AI remembers things and which other services it connects to. Sorting out which is which makes it clear where a defense belongs and who has to build it. It also undercuts the idea that people can stay safe on their own just by spotting suspicious content or double-checking what an AI tells them.

Related:Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

This question of who’s responsible gets more urgent as AI moves from producing information to acting on it. A chatbot that gets an answer wrong can mislead someone, but at least that person is part of the exchange. An agent with access to a person’s accounts and the services linked to them can cause real consequences without that kind of back-and-forth. Protections need to be built around what these systems actually do, which starts with understanding how the two differ.

This research is part of a wider effort at F-Secure to build trust into the AI era. F-Secure Trust, announced alongside a strategic alliance with Quantum AI Lab QuTwo, is the company’s work on protecting people in a world where AI agents increasingly act for them. TrustGuard is designed to help protect people during AI interactions, while TrustPath aims to secure their digital journeys from discovery to delivery. The AI Harms Taxonomy gives that work a research foundation by spelling out the risks the protections need to address, and it makes clear that meaningful safeguards also depend on the companies building and running AI systems.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

Today’s digital threats go far beyond just scams. F-Secure’s Illuminate Research team studies people and technology as they actually interact, exploring the messy realities of trust, deception, and online resilience in the AI era.

The AI Harms Taxonomy is available on the Illuminate Research Hub.

F-Secure is a human-first, AI-powered consumer cyber security experience company with 38 years of expertise in tackling digital threats. We help digital service providers turn trust into a high-value growth engine — protecting their customers while enabling them to live their best digital lives in a world of relentless, AI-driven scams. With billions of digital interactions secured each year, tens of millions of consumers protected globally, and over $10bn in partner value created, we deliver proven impact at scale.
